articleTitle: OpenAI rolls out GPT-6 with visuals, interactive features and faster responses
articleFeaturedImageAlt: ChatGPT can now respond with more visual and interactive elements, instead of relying mainly on text.
description: GPT-6 brings a new ChatGPT experience with faster responses and interactive features, allowing users to explore information through charts, graphics, forms and other tools directly in a conversation.
body_raw: OpenAI has begun rolling out its much-awaited GPT-6 globally in ChatGPT. The company is introducing a new Intelligent UI that allows the chatbot to combine text with visuals and interactive elements. The update was initially available to Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise users, while Free and Go users will start receiving it on Thursday, October 8. GPT6 in ChatGPT introduces Intelligent UI, a new capability that allows ChatGPT to answer quickly with fully interactive user interfaces that make everyday answers more visual, make learning complex topics easier, and can swiftly create a tool to solve a task right in the moment, the company said in its blog announcing the development. What is Intelligent UI? According to OpenAI, GPT-6 has been designed to move ChatGPT beyond a text-based interface. Intelligent UI allows ChatGPT to generate graphics, charts, forms, tappable buttons, and interactive experiences directly within a conversation. OpenAI said that now ChatGPT can automatically choose a format based on a question at the same time, it can offer a conventional text response when deemed necessary. For instance, a user asking about a bicycle will get an interactive diagram that breaks it down into its different parts. ChatGPT can also create tools like calculators, bill splitters, and simple games within the conversation. The company claims that the feature could also make complex topics easier to understand by allowing users to change inputs and explore how the results change. OpenAI said that it has built an intelligent UI based on a library of native, streamable components and a compiler that processes interfaces as GPT-6 generates them. As an outcome, interactive elements appear progressively instead of waiting for the entire response to be generated. The company also said that it trained GPT-6 to make decisions about the content, layout and level of interactivity required for a particular question. Reasoning delivered more quickly Another key highlight is how GPT-6 manages reasoning. OpenAI said that the model can begin answering while it continues to think or use tools, meaning it adds useful information progressively instead of waiting until its reasoning process is complete. Further, the company revealed that during an internal evaluation of high-value everyday agentic tasks, GPT-6 Extra High began responding in roughly the same amount of time as GPT-5.6 Medium while achieving a higher overall score than GPT-5.6 Extra High. The Sam Altman-led company also claims improvements in web-based research. GPT-6 Instant begins responding 44 per cent sooner on average than GPT-5.6 Instant when web search is required. According to the company, the new model is also better at determining when a search is necessary and finding information that supports its answers. On safety measures OpenAI said that GPT-6 comes with updated safety measures. The model is said to be more resistant to multi-turn attempts to bypass safeguards and has improved protections against high-risk misuse involving cyberattacks, biological threats, etc. Besides, it is also trained to better recognise its limitations and communicate when it does not have the information or tools needed to answer a question. For ChatGPT, paid plans use GPT-6 Sol, while free and Go users will get GPT-6 Luna. The latest rollout applies to the chat experience OpenAI says the models powering ChatGPT Work and Codex are not changing as part of this release. According to OpenAI, GPT-6 is part of its longer-term effort to make software adapt to users rather than forcing users to navigate fixed interfaces. The company claimed that over 1.2 billion people use ChatGPT each week.

articleTitle: 2027 first: Why Congress walked away from UP MLC polls after a year’s prep
articleFeaturedImageAlt: 2027 first: Why Congress walked away from UP MLC polls after a year’s prep
description: After months of groundwork and preparations, the Congress decided to stay out of the 11-seat contest, prioritising its alliance with the Samajwadi Party and the 2027 Assembly polls.
body_raw: After a year of preparations for the Uttar Pradesh Legislative Council elections, the Congress has decided not to field candidates in 11 Graduate and Teachers constituencies going to polls, choosing instead to focus entirely on the 2027 Assembly elections. Newly appointed state Congress president Aradhana Misra told The Indian Express that the decision had been taken before she assumed office. The party had decided not to contest the MLC elections, keeping the 2027 Assembly elections in mind. Our focus is entirely on the Assembly polls. If those who had been preparing to contest wish to fight as independents, that is their decision. The party, however, has decided not to contest, Misra said. The elections will take place on October 23. Five Graduates constituencies - Lucknow, Varanasi, Agra, Meerut and Allahabad-Jhansi - and six Teachers constituencies - Lucknow, Varanasi, Agra, Meerut, Bareilly-Moradabad and Gorakhpur-Faizabad - will go to polls. A campaign already in motion The partys withdrawal comes as the nomination process has concluded. It had undertaken considerable preparations for the Council elections. In October last year, the Congress had indicated probable candidates for several seats, appointed observers and coordinators, and set up a control room. Several aspirants had begun working nearly nine months ago, when the process of preparing voter lists for these constituencies began. In these constituencies, where only registered graduates and teachers can vote, prospective candidates generally begin their campaigns well ahead of polling, helping eligible voters get enrolled and building constituency-level networks. Unlike Assembly or Lok Sabha elections, MLC elections in these constituencies are not fought on party symbols. However, candidates backed by political parties are counted as part of their respective partys electoral strength. With the Congress staying out, the contest is now largely between the BJP and Samajwadi Party, though a number of independents are also in the fray. Some within the party feel that preparations by the state unit to contest the MLC elections were not adequately coordinated with the central leadership, particularly amid discussions over organisational changes in the UP unit. With little time left before the election process, party sources said, the leadership eventually decided it was better to leave the contest to the SP. The partys calculation is that avoiding a direct contest with the SP in the Council elections will help maintain the alliance ahead of 2027 and allow it to concentrate its organisational and political resources on the larger electoral battle. Probable candidates stay in the race Several candidates who had been preparing to contest on the Congress ticket have decided to contest as independents. Arvind Singh Patel, who had been preparing to contest from the Varanasi Graduate constituency, filed his nomination on October 5. Speaking to The Indian Express, he said, I filed my nomination on October 5. Congress leaders from the district and adjoining districts accompanied me. I will not withdraw and will instead contest as an independent. I have put in a lot of effort and money into preparing for this election. October 6 was the last date for filing nominations, with 51 candidates filing their papers on the final day. The total number of nominations across the 11 Graduate and Teachers constituencies rose to 188 from 137 till October 5. Scrutiny of nominations was on October 7, while October 9 is the last date for withdrawal of candidature. The 100-member Uttar Pradesh Legislative Council currently has 10 SP members, putting the party at the 10 per cent threshold required for the Leader of the Opposition LoP post in the Upper House of the state legislature. The BJP-led alliance, meanwhile, has 83 members in the Council - 79 of BJP, and one each from Apna Dal S, RLD, Suheldev Bharatiya Samaj Party, and Nishad Party - giving it a clear majority.

articleTitle: Mobile phone bursts inside man’s pocket, consumer commission grants Rs 41,139
articleFeaturedImageAlt: mobile phone consumer court
description: The commission held that there was no rebuttal to the complainant's allegations and said that the mobile phone was defective and there was deficiency in service.
body_raw: A consumer commission in Uttar Pradesh recently directed a mobile phone manufacturer and a local electronics retailer to either replace a mobile phone or refund its cost after the phone allegedly burst inside a mans pocket in 2023, causing injury. President Hasnain Qureshi and member Purnima Singh Rajpoot also directed the opposite parties to pay compensation of Rs 36,139 and Rs 5,000 as litigation expenses. As there is no rebuttal of the pleadings of the complainant and therefore it is held that the mobile set was defective and there was deficiency in service, the order read. Phone burst According to the complainant, he purchased the mobile phone for Rs 29,500 in 2020. He alleged that the phone started heating up. After he complained, he was allegedly told that such heating sometimes occurred. After he complained, he was allegedly told that such heating sometimes happens. The phone allegedly heated up again, but his complaint to the local retailer was allegedly ignored. The complainant said that the phone burst while inside his pocket, injuring his thumb. He then lodged a police complaint. The complainant further alleged that the incident damaged photographs and videos from his marriage. He claimed that he was hospitalised after learning about the damage and that he and his wife had to hold another marriage celebration and arrange fresh photography and videography. He sought Rs 51 lakh towards the expenses of recreating the marriage ceremony and Rs 48 lakh as compensation for the shock, depression and treatment he claimed to have suffered. His total claim was Rs 99.29 lakh, though he restricted it to Rs 50 lakh citing the commissions pecuniary jurisdiction. The manufacturer filed its response beyond the prescribed period, which the commission said was of no importance, while the local retailer did not contest the case. The commission held that there was no rebuttal to the complainants allegations and concluded that the mobile phone was defective and there was deficiency in service. It noted that the complainant remained hospitalised and incurred Rs 36,139 in treatment expenses, as supported by the medical records. The commission directed the opposite parties to either replace the mobile phone with a new one or refund Rs 29,500. It also awarded Rs 36,139 towards medical expenses and Rs 5,000 as litigation costs. Takeaway Manufacturers and sellers can be held liable when a defective mobile phone causes injury to a consumer. Where the defect and resulting loss are not rebutted, consumer commissions can order replacement or refund of the product and award compensation for proven medical expenses and litigation costs. For consumer-related grievances, individuals may contact the consumer helpline in their respective states and union territories Uttar Pradesh helpline 1800180030 or call the National Consumer Helpline at 1915 for assistance. articleTitle: IMC 2026: Ericsson to export made-in-India antennas to Europe and other global markets
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Ericsson
description: As 5G networks evolve, Ericsson is looking to India as a manufacturing and export hub.
body_raw: Ericsson on Wednesday, October 7, announced plans to ramp up local production of antennas and other telecom equipment in India, while also exporting made-in-India gear to global markets such as Europe, for the first time. The Swedish manufacturer said that more than 15,000 antennas and 25 million components have been produced in India since July 2025. Its antenna portfolio is designed to support 5G standalone and AI-ready networks as well as future network evolutions. Ericsson made the announcement regarding its India-manufactured, export-ready antennas at the tenth edition of the India Mobile Congress 2026 organised jointly by the Department of Telecommunications DoT and the Cellular Operators Association of India COAI. The four-day annual telecom conference and exhibition is being held at Yashobhoomi, New Delhi from October 7 to October 10, 2026, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi expected to formally inaugurate the event today October 8. Ericssons export-ready antennas manufactured in India were first rolled out in 2025. Since then, the company said it has continued to expand local capabilities across sourcing, engineering, manufacturing and exports, serving customers in India and international markets. As mobile networks move towards 5G Standalone, AI-driven operations and future network architectures, antennas are becoming increasingly important to network performance. Ericssons push to manufacture more of this telecom equipment locally also aligns with Indias broader drive to strengthen domestic telecom manufacturing and build the country into a global export hub for such gear. India is an important part of Ericssons global innovation, engineering and manufacturing footprint. The production of more than 15,000 antennas and 25 million components shows how quickly this ecosystem is developing and the contribution it can make both in India and globally. Together with our partners, we are developing the capabilities needed for the next generation of high-performing, energy-efficient and AI-ready networks, Andres Vicente, CEO, Southeast Asia, Oceania and India, Ericsson, said onstage at the companys booth in the IMC 2026 Exhibition Hall. We are building an end-to-end antenna ecosystem that combines local sourcing and manufacturing with Ericssons global engineering capabilities. As networks become more intelligent and programmable, antenna performance will be increasingly important in getting the most from spectrum, sites and network investments. Expanding these capabilities in India strengthens both our ability to serve customers locally and Indias contribution to Ericssons global operations, Mikael Eriksson, Head of Ericsson Antenna System, Ericsson, said in a statement. Ericssons antenna system is designed as a solution for network impact, helping communications service providers improve coverage and capacity, strengthen uplink performance, use spectrum more efficiently, and reduce network energy consumption. The companys expanding antenna portfolio also supports the industrys transition toward more intelligent, programmable and energy-efficient networks. Ericsson said it will continue to strengthen its antenna ecosystem in India, and advance local engineering, manufacturing, and export capabilities while supporting communication service providers in building high-performing, energy-efficient, and future-ready networks.

articleTitle: Expert Explains | How Eastern Maritime Corridor can diversify India’s energy flows
articleFeaturedImageAlt: India energy security
description: The EMC is relevant given India’s quantum of Russian oil imports and energy import bias towards the west coast. It can reduce transit time to a Russian port by one-third via Chennai-Vladivostok, compared with the Mumbai-St Petersburg route.
body_raw: The conflict between US-Israel and Iran impacting the Strait of Hormuz and the Houthi attacks in the Red Sea and the Bab-el-Mandeb Strait have brought Indias energy security into sharp focus. India is the worlds third-largest energy consumer and second-largest energy importer, importing around one-third of its total energy supply. It ranks as the worlds third-largest crude oil importer and the fourth-largest importer of liquefied natural gas LNG. Oil imports stand at approximately 240-250 million tonnes annually, with an import dependency of nearly 85-90. LNG imports are about 26-27 million tonnes, with roughly 50 dependency, while liquefied petroleum gas LPG imports are around 20-21 million tonnes, with approximately 60 dependency. This clearly establishes that Indias energy system is structurally dependent on maritime supply chains. This vulnerability is further exacerbated by Indias coastal imbalance. Approximately 65-70 of Indias oil imports, 75-80 of LNG imports, and 55-60 of LPG imports are handled on the west coast. This concentration is reinforced by infrastructure nearly 60-65 of refining capacity and about 70-75 of LNG regasification capacity are located on the West coast. Regasification refers to the industrial process of warming LNG from its cryogenic storage temperature -162C back into its standard gaseous state for distribution and consumption. As a result, Indias energy system is overwhelmingly dependent on the Arabian Sea and exposed to the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab-el-Mandeb chokepoints. The westward tilt also creates a serious national security vulnerability, as the Jamnagar and Vadinar refineries, which together represent a third of Indias total refining output, are within striking distance of swarm drone attacks from Pakistan. Indias unique advantage with Russia In recent years, Russia has emerged as a critical energy partner for India. Since 2023, Russian imports have accounted for roughly 30-40 of Indias total oil imports. In 2025, India imported approximately 45.38 billion of crude oil from Russia, averaging around 1.7 to 1.9 million barrels per day. This trend continued into 2026, with Indias oil imports from Russia peaking in mid-2026 at an estimated record share of about 50.8 of total imports 2.47 million barrels per day in July 2026. This energy relationship, however, is also coast-asymmetric. India has diversified its suppliers but not its routes. Russian oil is largely shipped from its Baltic ports via the Suez Canal - which connects the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea through Egypt - to Western Indian ports. As a result, even diversified supplies remain exposed to maritime chokepoints and broader geopolitical disruptions. It is in this broader context that Indias unique connectivity advantage with Russia becomes particularly significant. The Russians have subsumed the erstwhile Northern Sea Route, which ran from Murmansk to Provideniya, into the Trans-Arctic Transport Corridor TATC project, which spans from St Petersburg in the west to Vladivostok in the east. Along its route, the TATC aims to integrate major Russian ports, including Murmansk and Arkhangelsk, to create a unified transport system combining sea, rail, road and inland waterways, connect the key economic centres of Eurasia and form a seamless logistics corridor. India is connected to both ends of the TATC. On the western side, it is linked via the International North-South Transport Corridor INSTC, and on the eastern side via the Chennai-Vladivostok Maritime Corridor, also known as the Eastern Maritime Corridor EMC. The critical internal connector in this system is Russias Unified Deep-Water System, which integrates inland waterways, links European Russia to Arctic ports, and carries approximately 75 of Russias internal cargo. Relevance of Eastern Maritime Corridor The EMC is particularly relevant given Indias energy import bias towards the west coast. Launched in 2019 by Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok, the EMC was accompanied by Indias announcement of its Act Far East Policy and a 1-billion credit to Russia. The EMC can reduce transit time to a Russian port by one-third via Chennai and Vladivostok, compared with the route between Mumbai and St Petersburg. Trade will take only 24 days to traverse the 10,470-km-long EMC at a speed of 10 knots, compared with 36 days required to cover the 16,070-km conventional route to St Petersburg through the Suez. This efficiency is increasingly vital amid persistent geopolitical disruptions and chokepoint vulnerabilities in the Red Sea and the Strait of Hormuz. In 2024, around 94 million tonnes of Russian exports, including 63 million tonnes of oil and petroleum products and 21 million tonnes of bulk cargo, were delivered to Indian ports via the Suez Canal. Even partial diversion of these flows through the EMC could significantly reduce exposure to chokepoints and enhance supply resilience. Through the EMC, India will gain direct access to the mineral-rich Russian Far East and the Arctic, one of the worlds last largely untouched resource repositories. These resources are becoming increasingly accessible for exploitation as ice melts due to climate change-induced global warming and other local factors. They include 13 of the worlds undiscovered conventional oil reserves and 30 of its undiscovered natural gas, as well as large deposits of coal base metals such as nickel, copper, zinc, lead, iron ore, and tin precious metals and stones, including gold, silver, platinum, palladium, and diamonds and industrial minerals such as phosphate for fertilisers, bauxite for aluminium, and rare earth elements. Russias Arctic Zone is the countrys largest territory. At 4.9 million sq km, it is 1.5 times the size of India, yet has fewer than one-twelfth as many people as Delhi. The Russian Arctic is larger than the combined Arctic regions of the other seven Arctic countries. It accounts for 15 of Russias gross domestic product and 20 of its exports, and holds three-quarters of the countrys natural gas resources and more than one-fifth of its oil reserves. Given the Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership between India and Russia, a long-term partnership in energy and minerals through the EMC could strengthen Indias energy security and help address its rare earth and mineral shortfalls. Ocean freight through the EMC is also expected to be more than 50 cheaper compared with the Suez route, thanks to the shorter distance and the absence of canal transit charges. Indias major trading partners, China, Japan, and South Korea, also lie along the EMC, while more than half of Indias trade passes through the South China Sea. India and Russia have explicitly linked the EMCs development to their ambitious goal of reaching 100 billion US dollars in annual trade by 2030. While the EMC holds transformative potential for bilateral trade, its commercial success hinges on one critical missing piece a predictable, scheduled direct liner shipping service, where cargo vessels operate on fixed schedules, predefined routes, and regular stopovers at designated seaports. The corridors economic potential cannot be realised at scale without addressing its systemic constraints. The EMC was announced as operational in November 2024 by the Union Minister of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, and cargo is moving. Yet there is no direct, regular liner service connecting the major ports of India and the Russian Far East. India-Russia trade reached a record high of 68.7 billion in FY 2024-25 but remains highly asymmetric. Indian exports stood at merely 4.9 billion, dwarfed by Russian exports to India of about 63.8 billion. Challenges and possible solutions In the absence of a direct scheduled service from Vladivostok to Chennai, container logistics often rely on inefficient transhipment via third-party Asian ports such as Ningbo or Shanghai. For instance, recent services organised by operators such as FESCO have recorded transit times of around 34 days due to these indirect routings. This lack of a direct schedule results in unpredictable transit times and volatile freight rates, making it impossible for exporters to commit to delivery schedules or accurately calculate logistics costs. Consequently, many businesses are forced to rely on slower yet more predictable western routes. Compounding these logistical hurdles are physical infrastructure gaps, such as a lack of specialised transhipment terminals in Vladivostok for key commodities, alongside ongoing banking sanctions that create friction in payment mechanisms. This creates a classic chicken-and-egg problem. Shipping companies are reluctant to launch a dedicated, high-frequency service until cargo volumes are large enough to make it profitable. At the same time, exporters hesitate to shift their supply chains to the corridor without a reliable, published sailing schedule. This dilemma is closely linked to the severe imbalance in trade flows EMCs current cargo profile consists almost entirely of Russian bulk commodities, including crude oil, coal, and fertilisers. To be commercially viable, a scheduled container service must address the critical backhaul problem. EMCs economic purpose must therefore evolve. Vladivostok must become not only a Russian export gateway to India but also a viable distribution hub for Indian goods, including pharmaceuticals, engineering goods, chemicals, and agricultural products, destined for the Russian Far East and the wider domestic market. Overcoming these constraints requires shifting the focus from mere infrastructure announcements to practical, collaborative logistics solutions. To break the chicken-and-egg cycle and absorb the initial commercial risk, several policy and market measures can be deployed. Governments and port authorities could offer temporary subsidies, preferential port charges, and guaranteed berthing windows to incentivise early adoption. Minimum-volume commitments from major exporters and importers could provide the baseline assurance shipping lines need. Furthermore, joint service agreements between Russian and Indian shipping companies could distribute financial risk, while an anchor-cargo model could allow containerised freight to utilise the same maritime corridor established by bulk trade. Recent industry dialogues in 2026 emphasise that authorities and logistics partners must act immediately to organise reliable routes. Businesses need a clear understanding of the schedule now, not next year, to make the corridor competitive with established alternatives. Ultimately, the EMC should be seen not as a fully operational maritime route but as a logistics platform whose commercial potential is constrained by the lack of regular sailings. An occasional voyage is not the same as an economically viable corridor an irregular vessel may carry a single cargo, but only a scheduled service can sustain trade flows. The EMCs next stage should be judged not by whether ships can sail from Chennai to Vladivostok, but by whether exporters and importers can rely on a vessel departing every week or two. Establishing this reliable, direct liner service is essential to turning the EMC from a strategic aspiration into a genuine, sustainable driver of diversified bilateral trade between India and Russia.

articleTitle: From ‘quantum-enhanced’ to ‘quantum-safe’: Why banks are preparing in advance for the new big threat
articleFeaturedImageAlt: banking sector quantum computing, Indian banking sector, banking sector artificial intelligence, Indian banking sector cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, quantum computing, Indian express explained, explained news, current affairs
description: As AI dominates current cybersecurity concerns, a far greater threat looms over banking: quantum computing. We explain what the technology is and why financial institutions are preparing for it now.
body_raw: The banking sector is moving its focus towards cybersecurity as artificial intelligence AI poses threats to financial systems. But regulators have also stepped up, mandating cyber preparedness across the sector. The Reserve Bank of India RBI issued a new cybersecurity and technology-resilience framework for commercial banks in July, setting requirements for IT governance, cyber-risk management and incident response, while the Securities and Exchange Board of India SEBI introduced an IT Resilience Index for market infrastructure institutions in August to measure the robustness of their critical IT systems and identify weaknesses early. While these measures may help address the threats confronting the sector today, a new type of threat is beginning to emerge - one that could challenge the mathematical foundations of some of the encryption used to protect digital systems quantum computing. What is quantum computing? Traditional computing stores and processes data in a unit called a bit, which can have a value of either 0 or 1. In quantum computing, the unit is called a quantum bit, or qubit. Unlike a classical bit, a qubit can exist in a combination of 0 and 1, a property known as superposition. Quantum systems can also exploit another property called entanglement, in which the states of different qubits become closely correlated. Quantum algorithms are designed to manipulate these quantum states so that the probability of useful answers is amplified, and that of the incorrect answers is reduced. This can give quantum computers a significant edge over traditional computers for certain types of problems.  Their significance comes from particular problems for which quantum algorithms can provide a major computational advantage. They have the potential to solve certain problems in minutes or hours that would take conventional machines millennia to complete. While this could have striking use cases, it also opens the door to a whole new set of threats. The cybersecurity concern stems from the fact that sufficiently powerful quantum computers could solve some mathematical problems that underpin widely used public-key cryptographic systems much more efficiently than classical computers can. Why does quantum computing threaten banks encryption? Right now, we are talking about AI threats, right? In a couple of years, we will be talking about cryptographic threats due to quantum computing. We will be talking about a lot of other things that are not even there in the market yet, Sarthak Dubey, Co-founder and COO of Mitigata, a full-stack cyber resilience firm, told The Indian Express. What people have been talking about quantum becomes a very major risk starting, say, 2030, he added. Modern cryptography protects digital communications by relying on mathematical problems that are extremely difficult for conventional computers to solve. Some widely used public-key systems, such as RSA RivestShamirAdleman and elliptic-curve cryptography, rely on problems related to integer factorisation and discrete logarithms. Indias financial ecosystem is heavily digitised through the Unified Payments Interface UPI, Aadhaar, real-time gross settlement RTGS, and national electronic funds transfer NEFT. The quantum threat is not that a quantum computer would hack a payment system. Rather, it could undermine cryptographic building blocks used across the digital infrastructure for functions like authentication, secure communication, key exchange, and digital signatures. However, cybersecurity and traditional computing in general are based on a particular set of mathematical logic. For example, RSA relies on the difficulty of factoring very large numbers, while elliptic-curve systems rely on the difficulty of solving certain discrete-logarithm problems. These problems are computationally difficult for classical machines, but could be much easier for a sufficiently capable quantum computer. Essentially, when we talk about the existing ways of security, there are encryption mechanisms that keep systems safe and secure in certain ways, that keeps your data secure in certain ways. And there are ways to decrypt them, which requires a significant amount of compute, and a significant amount of hardware power to make sure that you are able to decrypt those particular encryptions and get into that particular system, said Dubey. Now, with quantum, and what people call the quantum deadline, is that by 2029 or 2030 the quantum computers would be smart enough to decrypt any of the historical encryptions that are present, he explained. Several technology companies and governments have been working towards transitioning their systems well before such a capability emerges, although there is no universally agreed date for when a cryptographically relevant quantum computer will arrive. Why banks cannot wait for the quantum computer One reason why financial institutions cant just wait for quantum computers to become powerful enough is a threat called Harvest Now, Decrypt Later, or HNDL. Under this model, an attacker can intercept and store encrypted information today, with the expectation of decrypting it once sufficiently powerful quantum computers arrive. This makes data that needs to remain confidential for many years particularly vulnerable. According to the Digital Threat Report 2025-26 by CERT-In, CSIRT-Fin and SISA, the broader quantum threat has yet to reach full-scale realisation, but HNDL strategies are already active. This is why the transition to post-quantum cryptography PQC - encryption algorithms resistant to attacks from quantum computers - has to begin before the threat materialises. The more immediate task in preparing for the quantum era involves identifying where vulnerable cryptography is being used, and replacing it before sufficiently capable quantum systems emerge. This involves creating an inventory of cryptographic systems, identifying the most sensitive and critical data, testing quantum-resistant algorithms, working with technology vendors and ensuring that systems can switch between cryptographic standards without requiring a complete rebuild. This last capability, known as crypto-agility, is the ability of an organisation to replace cryptographic algorithms and protocols as security requirements change. For banks, this is crucial because their technology infrastructure is spread across legacy systems, cloud environments, third-party vendors, payment platforms and multiple layers of security infrastructure. How imminent is the threat? While the new threat sounds scary, it is at least a few years away. India has only a handful of quantum computers, though the technology is rapidly developing through startups, academics, and government initiatives such as the National Quantum Mission launched in 2023 with an outlay of Rs 6,003.65 crore. The mission aims to develop indigenous quantum-computing capabilities in stages, moving from 20-50 physical qubits in the initial phase towards systems with larger numbers of qubits over the longer term. Despite this, most projects are either under development or under small-scale testing. Were currently seeing only a handful of such systems being developed. This is led mainly by institutes like the IISc Indian Institute of Science, Bengaluru, or through startups like QpiAI. Most are under 10-qubit and are still under development, so it may take a few more years to undergo testing and be operational, said the executive from the Bengaluru-based startup cited earlier. Others remotely access such systems developed by bigger names such as IBM and Amazon Web Services for research and developmental purposes. Globally, too, quantum threats have not become widespread yet but remain an active concern, as suggested by Big Techs endeavours to bulk up security systems. They are researching on, and have started deploying post-quantum cryptography algorithms into their products, as well as stepping up protection against HNDL strategies. Governments and financial regulators are taking similar steps. In the US, the National Institute of Standards and Technology NIST has already finalised post-quantum cryptography standards and is urging organisations to begin the migration process. The G7 has also developed a roadmap for transitioning the financial sector towards post-quantum cryptography, while the European Union has called for member states to begin the transition by the end of 2026, with high-risk use cases moved to quantum-resistant cryptography as soon as possible and no later than the end of 2030. Indias quantum-safe roadmap India has begun building a policy framework around this transition as well. The Department of Science and Technologys quantum-safe roadmap sets out a phased approach for moving the countrys digital ecosystem towards post-quantum cryptography. For critical sectors such as banking, financial services and insurance, it envisages foundational work by 2027, migration of high-priority systems by 2028 and full adoption of post-quantum cryptography by 2029. The expert committee under RBIs Quantum Secure and Adaptive Financial Ecosystem Q-SAFE initiative released in May aims to examine the implications of quantum technology for the financial sector, and recommend a roadmap to quantum-secure it. NITI Aayogs roadmap for transforming India into a quantum-powered economy released in 2025 also identifies financial modelling, fraud detection and encryption among potential applications of quantum technology in finance. This creates a two-sided policy challenge for India the country has to protect its digital infrastructure from a technology that could eventually disrupt existing cryptography, while simultaneously building the domestic capabilities that could make quantum computing economically useful.

articleTitle: Flydubai attack: Saudi probe could test global aviation rules and pilot hiring processes
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Israel Mideast Emergency Landing
description: Saudi Arabia has opened an air safety probe into the September 30 cockpit attack on a flydubai jet, while the UAE runs a separate criminal case.
body_raw: Saudi Arabia has started an air safety investigation into last weeks cockpit attack on a flydubai jet, three people close to the matter told Reuters. The probe will run alongside a separate criminal case led by the United Arab Emirates. Flight FZ1073, a Boeing 737 MAX bound for Israel, was in Saudi airspace on September 30 when the co-pilot allegedly tried to bring the plane down by attacking the captain with an axe. The jet dropped sharply but survived, and all 172 people on board were unhurt. Experts say the case could test a global system that aims to make flying safer without blaming anyone. What Saudi Arabia has said According to Reuters sources, Saudi Arabia has told aviation agencies abroad that it will carry out a safety probe under international rules. One of the sources said it was not clear whether Saudi investigators would make their findings public. Saudi Arabias National Transport Safety Center, which leads accident probes in the country, did not reply to a request for comment. The Saudi government and the aviation regulator also did not respond, Reuters said. Safety probes are normal after an accident, but they are not required when a deliberate act is involved, as is suspected here. Who else is involved The US National Transportation Safety Board has named a representative to the probe, Reuters reported. The agency would play a key role because the aircraft was built in the United States. Under international rules known as Annex 13, the UAE will also take part automatically, as the jet is registered there and flydubai is based in Dubai. UAE officials did not respond to Reuters. The UAE has opened its own criminal investigation, and its prosecutor general has called the incident a terrorist attack. The co-pilot, identified as Hamam al-Hammami, an Omani national, had planned to crash the flydubai flight into Tel Avivs Ben Gurion International Airport. Photo AP enhanced via AI Israel, whose citizens made up nearly all of those on board, has offered to join the Saudi probe but has not been invited, Ofer Vaknin, head of Israels Aircraft Safety Investigation Authority, told Reuters. He added that Israel may not need to take part, as the aircraft itself had no operational or safety fault. Why the Saudi probe matters Safety officials say a deliberate act can still teach the industry something, Reuters reported. A probe into this case can look at areas such as how pilots are hired and how cockpits are kept secure, even though prosecutors lead when a crime is suspected. That is the main reason the Saudi probe is closely watched. It also matters because Saudi Arabia did not have to open one. Safety probes are not required when a deliberate act is involved, and until now it was unclear if the country would go ahead. Experts say the case could test a system of global cooperation that makes safety recommendations without trying to assign blame. Past cases show how this has worked, and where it has come under strain 2020 After Iran shot down a Ukrainian jet, US and Iranian aviation officials still took part together in the playback of cockpit recordings at the offices of Frances BEA agency, participants said. Reuters said such work has generally stayed out of diplomatic disputes. 2015 The BEA went ahead with a safety probe into the Germanwings crash, caused by the pilot, after a dispute with prosecutors over access to evidence. Friction between safety investigators and prosecutors has grown in recent years. Saudi Arabia and Israel have no diplomatic ties, yet experts say the UN-backed system, decades old, has worked across political divides. The Annex 13 rulebook gives observer status to countries with many deaths or injuries among their citizens, but it does not say what happens when nobody is hurt, as in this case. That gap leaves open the question of whether Israel will be invited to join.

articleTitle: Average 73% decline in wildlife population sizes between 1970 and 2022: WWF report
articleFeaturedImageAlt: wildlife population, wildlife population sizes, wildlife population sizes decline, wildlife sizes decline, wildlife, Wildlife Protection, wildlife conservation, World Wide Fund for Nature, Indian express news, current affairs
description: There has beena 73% decline in the average population sizes of monitored vertebrates — mammals, fish, birds and amphibians —  over 52 years between 1970 and 2022, according to the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF) biennial Living Planet Report, 2026.
body_raw: The average size of monitored vertebrate - mammals, fish, birds and amphibians - populations declined 73 over 52 years between 1970 and 2022, according to the World Wide Fund for Nature WWF biennial Living Planet Report, 2026. As part of the Living Planet Index LPI, average changes in the size of wild populations of vertebrate species are measured over time, tracking variations in relative abundance rather than absolute numbers. This means that the size of these populations fell by, on average, 73 during the assessment period, and it does not reflect the number of individual animals lost, nor the number of populations lost. Habitat loss and degradation, overexploitation of resources, climate change, impact of invasive species, pollution and disease are some of the dominant drivers of changes across ecosystems and wildlife populations, the Living Planet Report stated. The way the world produces and consumes food is the single largest driver of biodiversity loss. The food and agriculture system is the leading cause of habitat destruction, overharvesting, and a major source of greenhouse gas emissions. Even as the report noted the declining trends in wild populations, it also noted that nature can recover if society follows a clear pathway to trigger positive tipping points in the energy, food and finance systems that drive biodiversity loss. The Living Planet Report 2026 is both a stark reminder of the scale of the biodiversity crisis and a message of hope. While the Living Planet Index continues to highlight significant declines in monitored wildlife populations, the report also shows that these declines are not inevitable, said Ravi Singh, Secretary General and CEO, WWF-India. Species recoveries, including those of tigers in India and globally, demonstrate what sustained conservation action, collaboration and long-term commitment can achieve, he added. The LPI, produced by the Zoological Society of London, includes 35,803 population trends of 5,790 vertebrate species from 1970 to 2022. The strongest declines, 85, were seen in freshwater ecosystems, followed by terrestrial ecosystems, at 69 and marine ecosystems at 59. Although the overall trend is negative due to the magnitude of the declining trends, half of the populations included in the LPI are stable or increasing, WWF said. The report highlights recoveries in populations of green turtles, bluefin tuna, tigers and southern African elephants, which, it said, demonstrate that targeted conservation interventions can deliver proven results. The report noted rise in global wild tiger numbers between 2010 and 2025 - from 3,200 to around 5,700 individuals.

articleTitle: Protect the referee, even as you question the decision
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Protect the referee, even as you question the decision
description: The ECI is our archon. Its job is not to decide who should win — 140 crore Indians decide that.
body_raw: In every game, you can abuse the player. You cannot abuse the referee. If you do, the game ends. Today in India, we are abusing the referee. The Election Commission of India ECI is not just another bureaucracy. It is the core of democracy. To protect it is not to support any party it is to support the game itself. This wisdom is not new. It is in our Vedas, it was in Rome, and it was in Greece. The Rig Veda does not start with a king. It starts with two institutions Sabha and samiti. Samiti was the people - the voters. Sabha was the council of elders, the learned, the impartial who ensured the samiti could meet freely and choose freely. The Atharva Veda prays Sabha cha me samiti cha ma avatu - may my sabha and samiti protect me. The sabha had no army, no kingdom. Its power came from only one thing - trust. If the sabha was seen as biased, the samiti collapsed and the janapada broke. The ECI is our modern sabha. It has no seats to contest, no vote bank to protect. Its only capital is credibility. When we chip away at that credibility for political points, we are not hitting at an office in Nirvachan Sadan, but at the idea of sabha itself. The Vedas also gave us a method Tarka and shastrartha. Debate fiercely, but accept the decision of the sabha. The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad shows King Janaka hosting a great debate where Yajnavalkya is questioned by everyone, including women scholars like Gargi. He answers. The debate ends, and his authority is higher, not lower, because he submitted to questioning. The ECI must be questioned. But after questioning, it must be obeyed. That is dharma. The Romans were the greatest bureaucrats. They knew democracy needs a clean voter list more than a popular leader. They created the office of censor. The censor was not the consul who fought wars. He was more powerful. He prepared the census - the list of citizens. He could remove a senator by marking him with nota censoria. He was elected for 18 months, but his list lasted for 5 years. Why did Romans give so much power to two men who did nothing but count? Because they understood If the voter list is corrupt, the republic is corrupt. When we in India politicise the Special Intensive Revision SIR of electoral rolls, or the deletion and addition of voters, we forget Rome. A clean roll will always be painful. Someones name will be deleted. Someones booth will shift. That pain is the price of a republic. Attack the error with data, appeal to the ECI, go to court - but do not attack the censor itself. If the censor falls, the republic becomes an empire. Athens, the mother of democracy, had a brilliant safeguard. They did not even trust elections fully. Most offices in Athens were filled not by election, but by lot - by lottery among citizens - under the supervision of the eponymous archon. Why? Because they feared that elections could be manipulated by orators. Their safeguard was procedure. The archon did not decide who won he ensured the procedure was followed. The ECI is our archon. Its job is not to decide who should win - 140 crore Indians decide that. Its job is to ensure the lottery of democracy - the EVM, the VVPAT, the ink, the booth - remains pure. Every dharma is two-sided. If the players must not abuse the referee, the referee must also remember why it wears black. In the Vedic sabha, the elder did not speak more than necessary - he spoke through decisions, after listening to both sides. In Rome, the censor was respected because he applied nota censoria equally, even to his own kin. In Greece, the archon was trusted because he drew lots in the open agora, not behind closed doors. The referee protects itself best by transparency, by same-rule-same-speed for all jerseys, and by a dignified restraint that lets the order speak louder than the press note. The moment a referee starts explaining too much, defending too much, or being seen too much, the crowd begins to doubt the whistle. The referees work best when we see them stable, silent, and steady. I am a doctor, not a psephologist. In the ICU, I see what happens when sodium - a single ion that no one notices - falls from 141 to 123. The body seizes and the brain starves. Sodium is invisible till it is low. The ECI is the sodium of our democracy. Invisible when it works, catastrophic when it fails. You can disagree with an order. That is your right in a democracy. File an affidavit, produce data, go to the Supreme Court. That is Vedic tarka, Roman provocatio, Greek elenchus. But do not call for burning down the office that guards the list. Rome tried that. When Augustus destroyed the power of the censors, the republic never returned. Protect the referee, even as you question the decision. That is the only way the game continues. The writer is an endocrinologist and public health physician based in Mumbai

articleTitle: In every trans woman’s life, there is a Dorothy
articleFeaturedImageAlt: In every trans woman’s life, there is a Dorothy
description: To shift the collective consciousness and urge the public to view every person as human, Tamil cinema needs hundreds of more films like Dorothy, Super Deluxe, and Natchathiram Nagargiradhu
body_raw: A society disturbed by a kiss must first ask why it is unable to see a trans womans pain, love, and humanity. The Tamil film Dorothy, directed by Karthik Subbaraj, engages with a society still struggling to recognise transgender people as complete human beings. What troubles us is not the debate surrounding the film, but what this has chosen to focus on. A story exploring caste, patriarchy, family, systemic violence, toxic masculinity, and gender politics has been reduced to one question How can a trans woman kiss a man? Why does that kiss spark such moral panic? Calling it two men kissing reveals a refusal to recognise a trans woman as a woman. But beyond that, why should intimacy cause such discomfort? Set in the 1990s, Dorothy reminds us of the real-life Dorothys whose stories were never documented, living through an era where gender, caste, and class inflicted severe violence on womens bodies. Through a sharp intergenerational lens, Subbaraj confronts a centuries-old system now struggling to digest the truth. This conflict forces a deeper inquiry into identity Who is Dorothy to Subbu? Is she a mother? A sister? A sister-in-law? Before demanding answers, society must face a simpler question Do you accept Subbu as Dorothy? Change is not an overnight process, but opposing and ignoring the struggles of another human remains deeply inhumane. A section of viewers forgets how Subbu struggled to guard her kaitiakitanga, her protective, nurturing femininity in a male-dominated world, only to obsess over a single kiss in the final scene. In truth, Dorothy represents the collective feminine that nurtures and protects a trans womans emerging identity. In real life, Dorothy takes many forms Mothers, mentors, female educators. In every trans womans life, there is a Dorothy most often, she is another woman. Music is a vital pillar of this sanctuary. For decades, mainstream Tamil cinema offered transgender and queer people little more than ridicule. In Dorothy, Ilaiyaraajas score feels like a balm to those wounds. Music provides a space where trans women safely explore their identity, historically through Ilaiyaraaja and Swarnalatha compositions like Enulle enulle, and Muthumani, now a trans anthem. In many ways, Ilaiyaraaja himself embodies Dorothy through the emotional shelter his art bestows. The films visual grammar speaks volumes. Karthiks choices such as the slow-motion parotta and salna sequence or the sharp presence of the chappathi kalli prickly pear cactus vividly convey the weight of toxic masculinity enforced upon trans bodies. This depth extends to performance and casting. Sanaths performance deserves appreciation for its vulnerability and commitment. Yet, when cisgender actors consistently receive accolades for portraying transgender characters, it raises an undeniable question Where does that leave trans actors who have spent years fighting simply to be cast? At the same time, Dorothys inclusion of trans actors and the international platform given to artists like Jeeva is meaningful. True representation must extend beyond who plays the lead it must be about who gets access to opportunities. Dorothy is a gift and a necessary step forward. To shift the collective consciousness and urge the public to view every person as human, Tamil cinema needs hundreds of more films like Dorothy, Super Deluxe, and Natchathiram Nagargiradhu. Negha is an actor, writer, and co-founder of Queer Casting, Angamuththu is a law student

articleTitle: The universe whispers through ghost particles
articleFeaturedImageAlt: The universe whispers through ghost particles
description: His work has used neutrinos to probe some of the universe’s hitherto most inaccessible environments, helping open a new window on the cosmos.
body_raw: For centuries, astronomy has essentially been the science of observing light. However, some of the universes most consequential events take place in environments so dense or violent that photons cannot escape. Could the universe be observed through something other than light? In 1930, when Austrian physicist Wolfgang Pauli proposed the existence of an elusive particle to explain a mystery in radioactive decay, he was laying the foundations for a new way of exploring the cosmos. The ghost particle called the neutrino was detected two decades later, and the quest to understand it has since been rewarded with a string of Nobel Prizes. On Tuesday, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, which awards the Nobel Prize in Physics, recognised another pioneer in the field - Belgian-American astrophysicist Francis Halzen. His work has used neutrinos to probe some of the universes hitherto most inaccessible environments, helping open a new window on the cosmos. Neutrinos have tiny masses, carry no electric charge and interact so weakly with matter that billions pass through the Earth - and our bodies - without leaving a trace. These particles can escape from the dense interiors of exploding stars and other extreme cosmic environments, carrying information about places that conventional telescopes cannot see. Halzen recognised this potential. His pioneering work led to the IceCube Observatory, an enormous neutrino detector buried deep beneath the Antarctic ice. Rather than building a conventional telescope, scientists effectively turned a cubic kilometre of natural ice at the South Pole into a detector, embedding more than 5,000 optical sensors in it. Almost every neutrino passes straight through the ice. But on the rare occasion when one sheds its shyness, the resulting flash of light can give information on the particles travel path. In 2013, IceCube provided evidence for a flux of high-energy neutrinos originating beyond the solar system. Halzens work demonstrated that sometimes the way to see farther is not to build a more powerful eye, but to learn to detect what the universe is whispering through particles that pass silently through it. The next frontier is multi-messenger astronomy, in which neutrinos can be studied alongside light, gravitational waves and cosmic rays. Together, these cosmic messengers could reveal the workings of black holes, exploding stars and other extreme objects that remain invisible to any single form of observation.

articleTitle: She led the way to the top, that’s her legacy
articleFeaturedImageAlt: She led the way to the top, that’s her legacy
description: Harmanpreet helped India believe it belonged at the top. Mandhana has to make sure that belief does not fade — and turns into a habit of winning.
body_raw: Harmanpreet Kaurs contribution as captain of the womens cricket team cannot be measured only by the ODI World Cup trophy she lifted last year. It can be seen in the way the team began to carry itself on the biggest stages. When Harmanpreet took over, India had already reached two ODI World Cup finals. But there was still a sense that the team had to prove it belonged among the best. During her captaincy, the results began to follow more consistently. India reached the 2018 T20 World Cup semifinal, the 2020 T20 World Cup final and the 2023 T20 World Cup semifinal before going all the way in the 2025 ODI World Cup. The journey was not smooth. Harmanpreets batting became less consistent, and her decisions were often questioned. But she remained at the centre of the team through the difficult periods. Her leadership was driven by her passion for the game and a strong belief in the players around her. The World Cup win turned that belief into reality. Now, as Smriti Mandhana takes over, she inherits a team that has tasted success and knows what is expected at the highest level. Mandhana cannot and should not try to recreate Harmanpreets leadership style. She will have to lead in her own way. But she will be expected to protect the confidence that has been built and take it further. That is the challenge. Harmanpreet helped India believe it belonged at the top. Mandhana has to make sure that belief does not fade - and turns into a habit of winning. After back-to-back group-stage exits at the T20 World Cup, winning a title in the shortest format will be a priority.

articleTitle: RBI’s focus on inflation is timely
articleFeaturedImageAlt: RBI’s focus on inflation is timely
description: On Wednesday, with the Monetary Policy Committee of the Reserve Bank of India raising the repo rate by 25 basis points, it moved up from 5.25 per cent to 5.5 per cent. A higher repo rate is expected to make borrowing more costly for everyone and thus acts as a drag on economic activity. The […]
body_raw: On Wednesday, with the Monetary Policy Committee of the Reserve Bank of India raising the repo rate by 25 basis points, it moved up from 5.25 per cent to 5.5 per cent. A higher repo rate is expected to make borrowing more costly for everyone and thus acts as a drag on economic activity. The decision to make the first hike of the repo rate since February 2023 was not only unanimous - all six members of the MPC voted in favour - but also widely expected. The less obvious but perhaps more consequential change was the shift in the RBIs stance from neutral to calibrated tightening. The last time the RBI assumed this stance was exactly eight years ago. The RBIs primary mandate, as Governor Sanjay Malhotra has underlined, is to ensure price stability while keeping in view economic growth. Since the last policy review in August, the situation has changed on both these counts, necessitating a change in policy. On economic growth, the Indian economy has surprised everyone by showing resilience despite a worsening global context. The 7.8 per cent growth in Gross Domestic Product during the first quarter April, May, June surprised on the upside when the data was released at the end of August. This has led the RBI to bump up the full-year 2026-27 forecast from 6.7 per cent, as pencilled in the August policy, to 7.1 per cent now. But notwithstanding the domestic growth momentum, the situation has become considerably more challenging from the point of view of inflation, thanks to the sudden re-escalation of the West Asia conflict in September and the consequent hardening and volatility in global crude prices. Making the domestic inflation outlook worse are the deficient Southwest monsoon and El Nino conditions. Retail inflation has been going up steadily through the year, breaching the 4 per cent RBI target level. In fact, the RBI now expects it to touch 6 per cent by the end of December with full-year inflation around 5.2 per cent. Given that growth is robust even as inflation is trending upwards and beyond the RBI target, raising the repo rate in a bid to dampen overall demand in the economy and prevent inflation becoming more broad-based is timely. What is even more welcome is the shift in the RBIs stance. It suggests that the RBI is squarely focussed on dealing with a possible spike in inflation. Simply put, interest rate cuts are off the table for the time being, and the RBI has signalled the start of a rate hike cycle, given that globally other central banks are expected to raise interest rates in the coming months.

articleTitle: Leaked papers, cancelled government exams, no new dates: MPSC protests grow in Maharashtra
articleFeaturedImageAlt: MPSC protests continue, MPSC paper leak, MPSC protests, Maharashtra Public Service Commission (MPSC), Devendra Fadnavis government, MPSC protests intensify, MPSC chairman Vivek Bhimanwar, Pune news, Pune, Maharashtra news, Indian express, current affairs
description: Fadnavis tries to damage control, indicates also open to change of MPSC chief. But problems with successive exams, including those held last year for which recruitment is in motion, fuel anger
body_raw: Rahul Mahale, 29, had a simple plan give the State Services Main Exam this month, write the Group-B Main in December, exit the long preparation phase finally, and end the monetary drain it caused on his parents. Then, his hopes vanished. Mahale is among the thousands of aspirants sitting for exams conducted by the Maharashtra Public Service Commission MPSC, who have been protesting in Pune-an MPSC exam hub-since October 2. The exam that Mahale was preparing for, having passed the Prelims for the State Civil Services, has been postponed with no new dates announced, since irregularities were found in tests conducted by the MPSC. My demand is that the wrongdoers be removed, and the commission adhere to strict exam schedules and transparent conduct, Mahale says. Topping the demand for him and others is the resignation of MPSC Chairman Vivek Bhimanwar. With the government on the backfoot since the NEET paper leak protests, the Opposition, including the Congress, NCP SP, Maharashtra Navnirman Sena and the Cockroach Janta Party, has lent its weight to the MPSC protests. Maratha quota activist Manoj Jarange-Patil has also spoken up for the aspirants. At least one leader of the ruling coalition, Shiv Sena MP Omraje Nimbalkar, has visited the protest site. He promised the aspirants that he would take up their demand to remove the MPSC chief personally with the CM. On Monday, in one of its biggest concessions to the demands of the aspirants, the Fadnavis government sent a recommendation to Governor Jishnu Dev Varma proposing a committee to examine the conduct of former and incumbent MPSC chairpersons and members. The CM had earlier said Bhimanwar held a constitutional post and hence could not be removed arbitrarily. His recommendation to the Governor was made under Article 317 of the Constitution, which deals with the removal and suspension of chairpersons and members of public service commissions. On Wednesday, hearing a petition by some Pune residents, the Bombay High Court said it was the governments duty to ensure that public recruitment exams are conducted impartially, adding If they students lack opportunities and believe there has been hanky panky, they have the right to agitate. Because they have given hours of study. The protesters are students. not anti-social elements. A drug inspector exam On June 12, results were declared for the drug inspector posts exam conducted by the MPSC in March, selecting 506 applicants for the interview round. A little over a month after the results came out, NCP SP MLA Rohit Pawar held a press conference claiming that the paper had been leaked. It took another month before the MPSC admitted this had happened, and on August 25, it cancelled the recruitment process. By then, of the 506 who qualified for the interview stage, interviews had been conducted for 488 and a provisional general merit list of 485 had been declared. Soon after, the State Services Main Exam 2025 conducted by the MPSC in November last year for 139 vacancies, whose result shortlisting candidates for interviews was declared on August 25 this year, came under a cloud. Widespread protests alleged irregularities in the evaluation of questions requiring descriptive answers-a new format introduced only last year-and questioned the unusual variations in marks. On September 10, Rohit Pawar held another press conference, where he claimed MPSC chief Bhimanwar was close to Fadnavis, and that his record was marked by several controversies. Bhimanwar defended himself saying he took charge of the MPSC only in April this year, and that the alleged irregularities predated his tenure. On September 11, in a further escalation, members of the Maratha outfit Sambhaji Brigade blackened the face of then MPSC secretary Mahendra Harpalkar at the commissions head office in Navi Mumbai. On September 28, the MPSC announced postponement of the State Services Main Exam 2026, which was to begin on October 3, citing requests from aspirants, parents, student organisations and elected representatives. It also said it would re-evaluate the answer sheets for the 2025 exam, and deferred the Maharashtra Civil Engineering Main Examination 2026 and the Maharashtra Group-B Non-Gazetted Main Examination, without announcing revised schedules for any of the three. Damage control By mid-August, Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis had already announced a complete review of the MPSC system. As part of this, a seven-member committee was asked to visit each Revenue Division, consult students, representatives of educational institutions and other stakeholders, and submit a report by the end of the year. With tempers rising, on October 2, the government transferred Harpalkar. While the government seems to have relented on its position regarding Bhimanwar now, the protesters are also divided over their main demands. If for one group, the main thing is the MPSC chiefs removal, another wants the descriptive pattern of exams scrapped, while yet another opposes any return to the objective format. One of the members of the second group of protesters, Dhuldev Tele, 27, says the wide variation in the Mains marks showed that the MPSC lacked the mechanism and experts to evaluate descriptive papers fairly. But Amar Khose 21, who says he has spent lakhs of rupees preparing for the State Services Main Exam since 2023, is opposed to a change in format. Preparing for an optional subject alone cost him Rs 70,000, he says, and now the MPSC has decided it will not be a part of the 2027 exam. If the Mains shift to the objective pattern too, it will be a major setback for lakhs like me who have studied hard for the descriptive format, Khose says. Madhuri Netake 29, an aspirant from Karjat, says the cancellations could not have come at a worse time. Most protesters belong to agrarian families from rural regions like Marathwada, Vidarbha and Western Maharashtra, which are already battling drought. The financial burden is just getting heavier, she says.

articleTitle: Inside Visakhapatnam spying case: Pakistani women operatives lured, blackmailed naval personnel, probe finds
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Inside Visakhapatnam spying case: Pakistani women operatives lured, blackmailed naval personnel, probe finds
description: 2 arrested, 16 under scanner as investigators piece together how Pak-based operatives used social media and WhatsApp to orchestrate honey-trap.
body_raw: Investigators probing allegations of spying in Visakhapatnam claim to have pieced together how intelligence operatives from Pakistan trapped and then blackmailed civilians and navy personnel to gather information about the movement of vessels and submarines. According to investigators, around six months ago, a woman operative allegedly posed as a shipping firm employee and struck up a conversation with Annam Sai Varaprasad, 28, a civilian hired on a contract basis to drive naval officers vehicles at the Visakhapatnam naval base. The woman messaged him on his social media accounts, investigators said, adding that though he was initially suspicious, he allegedly continued the conversation. She told him she was from a neighbouring state. At first, the conversation focused on his personal life where he lived and why he was not married. Then, investigators said, she asked about his work, his salary, and the kind of vehicles he drove. Eventually, the woman allegedly shared sexually explicit content with Varaprasad and promised to visit Visakhapatnam soon to meet him. As the conversation progressed, she allegedly managed to extract information about the officials he drove. From then on, he was threatened that he would be reported to his employers and arrested. Investigators said what followed was blackmail to provide information about the locations of various naval assets, the deployment of officials, etc. The platform for their communication shifted from social media to WhatsApp. However, Varaprasad had basic security clearance and lacked access to observe and report on classified assets, naval ships docking, and submarines arriving or leaving, investigators said. The Andhra Pradesh Polices Counter Intelligence Cell and naval officials monitored him for over a month before his arrest on October 6. Officials are also examining his phone to check if he received payments through cryptocurrency, investigators said. According to investigators, Varaprasad allegedly shared details of a trainee sailor, Pradeep Mukharjee, 31, whom he previously met at the Visakhapatnam base. He too was allegedly trapped by a Pakistan-based intelligence operative, who posed as a medical professional. Threatened with arrest and legal complications after they allegedly exchanged sexually explicit messages, he too shared information about the Vizag and Coimbatore facilities, where he was attending a training course, investigators said. He was allegedly forced to share OTPs to activate WhatsApp accounts of Pakistani operatives, and was threatened with dire consequences on a voice call if he stopped cooperating, investigators said. These WhatsApp numbers were then used to lure and trap at least 16 others, using a similar modus operandi. They targeted employees posted in Kerala, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Gujarat, Goa, Delhi, Tamil Nadu, Chhattisgarh and Bihar, investigators said, and information sought included movement of naval ships and submarines arriving and leaving. Andhra Pradesh Counter-Intelligence Cell officials said that after it was established that Varaprasad and Mukherjea allegedly shared information and helped operatives trap others, they registered a case against them on September 2 and put them under surveillance. On October 1, simultaneous raids at the homes and residences of 18 persons, including 13 naval personnel, were conducted in an operation named Operation Firewall 2026, and 12 teams supported by officials of the anti-terrorist squads of several states, navy intelligence officers, and local police seized phones, electronic devices, and documents. Authorities are investigating the 16 people to determine their level of involvement and have arrested Varaprasad from Visakhapatnam and Mukherjea from Coimbatore.

articleTitle: ‘We don’t distinguish between nations’: Coast Guard chief on rescue operations
articleFeaturedImageAlt: ‘We don’t distinguish between nations’: Coast Guard chief on India’s sea rescue mission
description: Speaking to the reporters ahead of the 12th edition of the national level Search and Rescue Exercise (SAREX-2026) to be conducted off Paradip coast on Thursday, he said several nations look up to India in the event of a crisis.
body_raw: Director General of the Indian Coast Guard ICG Paramesh Sivamani on Wednesday underscored the forces commitment to saving lives at sea, saying it does not distinguish between nations while carrying out an effective search and rescue SAR operation. Speaking to the reporters ahead of the 12th edition of the national level Search and Rescue Exercise SAREX-2026 to be conducted off Paradip coast on Thursday, he said several nations look up to India in the event of a crisis. We have enhanced our capacity, redefined the procedure and fine-tuned the standard operating procedure over the years. We have established a very robust system of SAR and all the nations in the Indian Ocean Region look up to Bharat in case there is a crisis or in a volatile situation that requires a SAR, said the ICG chief. Stating that they have built up the SAR capabilities from scratch, Sivamani said they have ensured that the ICGs prowess of executing a good SAR operation is there for a larger good of humanity. Whenever there is a crisis and our ships and aircrafts are required to the spot. we do that immediately, he said. During the inaugural event of SAREX, the ICG chief also emphasised that the future of maritime SAR hinges on advanced technological integration, real-time information sharing, and seamless inter-agency synergy. Sivamani stressed the imperative for enhanced vessel tracking, robust distress-alert management, data-driven operational decision-making, and accelerated asset mobilisation. He also underscored that operational lessons derived from past missions and multi-agency exercises must directly translate into heightened mission readiness and response capabilities. The SAREX-2026 exercise will witness participation and observation by 32 delegates from 30 foreign friendly nations. The multi-agency exercise aims to validate operational preparedness, enhance international interoperability, test joint response mechanisms, and foster the exchange of best practices-reaffirming the preservation of life at sea as the paramount objective of every mission. The 24th National Maritime Search and Rescue Board meeting was also held on the occasion and it deliberated on strengthening national and international SAR frameworks, recognising that maritime emergencies transcend geographic boundaries and necessitate synchronised coordination among global Rescue Coordination Centres and maritime safety agencies. Minister of State for Defence Sanjay Seth, who inaugurated the event, called upon all participating agencies and international partners to reaffirm their shared commitment to safeguarding lives at sea and to strengthen the spirit of cooperation that underpins effective search and rescue across the region. Invoking the principle of One Earth, One Family, One Future, he said collective efforts can build a safer, more resilient and more cooperative maritime community. Speaking on Indias efforts to strengthen its search and rescue capabilities, Seth said Indias journey in Satellite-Aided Search and Rescue has progressively evolved from Low Earth Orbit Search and Rescue LEOSAR to Geostationary Search and Rescue GEOSAR and now towards Medium Earth Orbit Search and Rescue MEOSAR.

articleTitle: Rahul Gandhi stood guard, Priyanka lay on the road — then the police moved in
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Rahul stood guard, Priyanka lay on the road — then the police moved in
description: The Opposition is learnt to be planning another protest on Thursday, keeping the details under wraps so that it can catch the police off guard.
body_raw: The dramatic events on Wednesday started off rather innocuously with a lunch for Opposition INDIA bloc leaders hosted by Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge at the Sagar Ratna restaurant in Janpath in central Delhi. While the police outside the restaurant prepared to stall any movement of the MPs, the mood inside was full of optimism. The leaders of the INDIA bloc spoke of how they were moving ahead in the right direction and that the government was on the back foot. Most of the leaders belonging to South Indian states ordered dishes associated with North Indian states, while those from the North and other parts of the country ordered what is broadly clubbed as South Indian cuisine, sources said. The variety on the plates ranged from idli and dosa to uttapam and North Indian and South Indian thalis. Twelve leaders sat on the main table, including the Gandhi siblings, Kharge, K C Venugopal, RJDs Manoj Jha, IUMLs E T Mohammed Basheer, CPIs P Sandosh Kumar, CPIMs John Brittas, and representatives of other parties. Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi shared with others the food he had ordered, said those present at the lunch. Following the lunch, the MPs exited the restaurant and announced to the media contingent that had gathered outside that they would make their way to Jantar Mantar in three deluxe buses parked outside to keep up the pressure on the government for the second straight day, demanding that they be allowed to meet Chief Election Commissioner CEC Gyanesh Kumar and the Election Commissioners. The Opposition, it seemed, was prepared for the long haul, stacking the buses with energy drinks, snacks, and plenty of water. As the buses left Janpath and slowly inched towards Jantar Mantar, less than a kilometre away, the word had gone around among Congress workers that the top leadership was heading towards a flash protest. Hundreds of Congress workers joined them, walking alongside the buses and raising slogans. Soon afterwards, several Congress MPs, including Imran Masood, Deepender Hooda, Imran Pratapgarhi, and Amrinder Singh Raja Warring of the Congress, climbed atop their bus and waved a Tricolour, giving the protest march the colour of a celebratory roadshow. Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra were dragged away by Delhi Police-for a second time in as many days-after opposition MPs kick-started Day 2 of protests demanding CEC Gyanesh Kumar quit over irregularities in the SIR process. Read   - The Indian Express IndianExpress October 7, 2026 Once the destination was just metres away, the mood changed and became more confrontational as the police stopped the buses from entering the road to Jantar Mantar. The police had already barricaded it and a face-off appeared on the cards. Then came the tipping point, as the situation hurtled towards a skirmish. Near the Windsor Place roundabout, Congress workers, including those from the partys student and youth wings, were pushed back as the police tried to stop them from progressing. As several Congress workers sustained minor injuries in the ensuing melee, those in the buses decided to get down. How could we stay inside when our workers were being bashed up? asked an MP. This, sources said, marked a change of plan. We thought we would sit in the bus till night, said an Opposition leader. Sit-in and punctured tyres The parliamentarians led by Rahul Gandhi got off their buses and attempted to begin an impromptu sit-in. Priyanka Gandhi Vadra lay on the road, shielded by other MPs and party workers, while her brother stood guard, pushing back the police personnel attempting to break up the protest.
