articleTitle: Cramped spaces, deposit disputes: Delhi students tell cops what’s wrong with their PGs
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Police interact with students at a PG in Delhi. (Express Photo)
description: Students in Delhi’s major PG hubs raised concerns during a police outreach drive after the Satya Niketan hostel collapse.
body_raw: Tushar wants to leave his paying guest accommodation in East Delhis Laxmi Nagar after seven months of living there and move in with a friend. But the second-year Delhi University student is worried he will have to forgo the Rs 20,000 security deposit he paid when he moved in. His rent agreement has an 11-month lock-in clause. My warden says that if I leave the PG before the lapse of 11 months, my Rs 20,000 security deposit will not be returned. Im not sure how to deal with this, said Tushar, a B.Com student from Uttar Pradesh. His concern was among several issues raised during a Delhi Police drive to meet students living in PGs and rented accommodation in the Capitals major student hubs - Mukherjee Nagar in North Delhi, Laxmi Nagar in East Delhi, Rajinder Nagar, Karol Bagh and Patel Nagar in Central Delhi. The drive, undertaken by police teams from every police station, followed the September 6 collapse of a building housing a private hostel in Satya Niketan, which claimed seven lives, including those of five students. Waterlogging, wires and poor maintenance Thousands of students who flock to Delhi to study in colleges and coaching institutes live in PGs because of the acute shortage of on-campus accommodation. Kuldeep, who studies at a coaching institute in Karol Bagh and stays in a nearby PG, said, For most students, security deposit is the most common problem because people sometimes have to leave or change their PGs, he said. Cramped spaces in many private hostels have also been worrying, Kuldeep said. But the Satya Niketan incident has made students more worried about safety and accountability. Its cramped inside the PGs. But what is bothering us most after this incident is the question of who is accountable to us, he said. Muskan, who has been living at a PG in Old Rajinder Nagar for over a year, said her concerns revolved around basic standards of living poor hygiene, inadequate water supply and electricity maintenance, sagging electrical wires and waterlogging her PG. After meeting students at PGs, reading rooms and libraries in these student hubs, police compiled the issues raised by students and prepared an Action Taken Report ATR, which was submitted to the Delhi Police Headquarters, according to the officials sources. Officers said the most frequent grievance aired by students in these interactions was over security deposits. Apart from these, students also flagged waterlogging, seepage, cleanliness in kitchens, maintenance of the buildings, and dark or poorly lit stretches around PGs. Rohit Rajbir Singh, DCP Central, said police were briefing PG owners and property dealers about the issue of security deposits, which he said was a major concern for students who spend considerable amounts on accommodation. Letters were sent to civic agencies seeking structural audits of properties for the safety and security of students. The Delhi Fire Services was approached for fire-safety surveys. Libraries were directed to follow safety norms, obtain fire no-objection certificates and install CCTV cameras, Singh added. Police also began regular engagement with Residents Welfare Associations to improve CCTV coverage and ensure that PGs and rented accommodation followed safety guidelines, he said. Steve, a B.Com student living in Mukherjee Nagar, said that police had also shared contact numbers with them during their interaction at his PG. The police officers had come to my PG a few days ago and told us about precautionary measures in case an emergency situation arises. They also gave us the contact number of the station house officer, he said. The officer also told us to take precautions to prevent incidents of mobile phone snatching. He also told us to not befriend strangers, Rudra said.

articleTitle: World Bank ranks India among top 10 in AI readiness
articleFeaturedImageAlt: AI
description: India among top 10 emerging markets in AI readiness: The World Bank report titled 'India and Artificial Intelligence: Seizing the Development Opportunity, ' released in October 2026, ranked India among the top 10 emerging-market performers in AI readiness.
body_raw: World Bank Ranks India Among Top 10 in AI ReadinessThe World Bank Group has recently released a report titled India and Artificial Intelligence Seizing the Development Opportunity under the India Development Update IDU. According to the World Banks latest report, India has emerged among the top 10 leading emerging-market performers in artificial intelligence AI readiness, supported by its large technical workforce, globally integrated IT sector and digital public infrastructure. Recent developments in Indias economy place it in a medium-term and global context. The report also suggested that even though aggregate long-term impacts remain uncertain, existing analysis shows that labour market substitution risks are lower than in advanced economies so far due to a smaller share of cognitive jobs, with significant potential for productivity jobs. According to the World Bank, AI holds significant promise for enhancing productivity and transforming public service delivery in India. However, the institution noted that the technologys long-term effects on employment and overall economic stability remain uncertain. To reach its full capacity, the report suggested that this can only occur through broadening AI adoption beyond large urban firms, building worker capabilities, strengthening infrastructure, leveraging AI in public services, and establishing adaptive governance frameworks. Private AI investment in India soared to 4.1 billion 36,231.7 crore in 2025, more than triple the previous year, reflecting surging investor confidence in the nations tech ecosystem. At the same time, employment across Indias Global Capability Centres expanded to 2.36 million, prompting the World Bank to note AIs potential for driving development while cautioning over its uncertain long-term impact on labour markets. A policy research working paper titled Beyond the AI Divide A Simple Approach to Identifying Globaland Local Overperformers in AI Preparedness, published by the World Bank, notes that in the landscape of the global AI Divide, nations perform along three distinct economic tiers.At the top, high-income economies such as Singapore and the United States dominate global rankings through deep capital and mature regulatory frameworks. Below them, upper-middle-income countries such as China and Malaysia act as regional tech gateways that weaponize state infrastructure to rapidly scale compute power. Meanwhile, lower-income economies such as India and Rwanda go beyond their economic weight, defying resource constraints through aggressive policies, massive engineering talent, and digital public infrastructure to close the gap. A core team of analysts, including Ran Li, Vincent Tsoungui Belinga, Aurlien Kruse, Tanvir Malik, Naresh Kumar, Mohini Gupta, Utz Johann Pape, Ayago Esmubancha Wambile, and Nishtha Kochhar, authored the report under the guidance of World Bank leads Hoon Sahib Soh, Sebastian Eckardt, and Paul Procee.

articleTitle: Two days to election: Can Maharashtra opposition alliance stop infighting?
articleFeaturedImageAlt: A meeting of Maha Vikas Aghadi at Tilak Bhavan, to discuss the Legislative Council elections and other important issue, in the presence of Congress State President Harshvardhan Sapkal, NCP (SP) MP Supriya Sule, NCP (SP) State president Shashikant Shinde, Shivsena (UBT) leader Anil Parab, Shivsena (UBT) leader Ambadas Danve, and Shivsena (UBT) leader Milind Narvekar, in Mumbai on Wednesday
description: With the October 9 deadline for withdrawals approaching in the Legislative Council elections, allies have little time to avert “friendly fights”
body_raw: Opposition parties may be trying to remain on the same page nationally when it comes to taking on the BJP, but a recurring problem has been resolving their differences at the regional level. In Maharashtra, the Opposition Maha Vikas Aghadis MVA plan to contest the October 23 Legislative Council elections together is under strain, with the Congress and the Shiv Sena UBT set to face each other in Amravati Teachers constituency, while the Sena UBT and the NCP SP are pitted against each other in the Marathwada Graduates constituency. The other seats where elections are being held are Pune Graduates, Nagpur Graduates, and Pune Teachers. The differences have cropped up within days of the three parties deciding to contest the five Council seats together. With Tuesday the last day to file nominations - candidates have till October 9 to withdraw their nominations - the parties have failed to reach an agreement in these two constituencies. In Amravati Teachers constituency, the Congress has fielded Aditi Pohare, while the Sena UBT has put up Dattatray Lahane. Lahane filed his nomination on October 6 in the presence of Sena leaders. The Congress had announced Pohare along with sitting MLCs Abhijit Wanjari from Nagpur Graduates and Jayant Asgaonkar from Pune Teachers on October 3. Pohare joined the Congress days before her candidature was announced. She is the daughter of Harshvardhan Deshmukh who heads the Shri Shivaji Education Society in Amravati. The society has a large number of teachers among its staff, giving Pohare a local base in a constituency where the candidates are elected by registered teachers. The Sena UBT, however, says it was Lahane for the Amravati seat. After announcing his candidature, Sena UBT MP Sanjay Raut made it clear that the party would not give up the seat simply to avoid a contest with the Congress. We are contesting two seats, Amravati and Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar Marathwada. You call it a friendly fight or whatever you want. We are contesting them, he said. Raut argues that the Sena UBT was not seeking all the seats the Congress was claiming. He said his party was willing to leave the Nagpur Graduates and Pune Teachers seats to the Congress and was even prepared to give up Pune Graduates to the NCP SP, despite the work done by its leaders to register voters there. All three parties have worked separately to build their voter base in the Graduates and Teachers constituencies and each has its own claim to some of the seats, Raut has said. Congress leader Vijay Wadettiwar said voter registration was an important factor in these elections. These elections are not based on ordinary voting. The side that registers more membersvoters has greater weight, he said. He said the Congress had not claimed Pune Graduates when the Sena UBT had a sitting member there, while the Sena UBT had not claimed Pune Teachers as the Congress had a sitting member there. When there is a sitting member, it is not right for another party to demand that seat, he said. The position of the NCP SP in Amravati remains less clear. On Monday, one of its district presidents attended Lahanes nomination programme, while another local leader said the senior leadership had not taken a final decision. The contrasting positions suggested that the party was not comfortable with the situation. A direct contest The second dispute has become more direct. The Sena UBT has fielded Dilip Ghuge from the Marathwada Graduates constituency. Ghuge filed his nomination on October 5. The following day, Dr Pratapsinh Patil of the NCP SP announced that he was filing his nomination as the authorised candidate of the Sharad Pawar-led party and the MVA. Patils campaign also shows how the contest could play out. In a social media post on Tuesday, he said his candidature was not merely about filing a nomination but about starting a new fight for graduates, students, unemployed youth, and ordinary people in Marathwada. Taking aim at Satish Chavan, who has represented the seat since 2008 and is contesting this time as the candidate of the NCP and ruling Mahayuti alliance, Patil asked what had changed for graduates in the past 18 years, raising issues such as employment, education, examination paper leaks, and students future. However, the Sena UBTs decision to contest the seat has complicated the equations and upset the NCP SP, which has traditionally regarded Marathwada Graduates as an NCP seat. NCP SP leaders in Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar have argued that the party won the constituency for three consecutive terms and should therefore continue to contest it. NCP SP MP Supriya Sule sought to play down the differences. Asked about the disagreement over the Council seats, she said there was no dissatisfaction within the MVA and that the issue will become clear after further discussions. Raut has rejected the argument that the NCP SP somehow has an automatic claim over the seat. He has pointed out that before joining the NCP following the split in the party, Chavan was a Congress member and the political situation has changed since then. Understanding fails to hold Earlier this month, the MVA decided to contest the five seats going to polls on October 23 together. The Opposition alliances strategy was discussed at a meeting attended by Congress leaders Naseem Khan and Harshwardhan Sapkal, NCP SP leaders Shashikant Shinde and Harshwardhan Patil, and Raut. The Congress at the time said the parties were looking at the constituencies held by the NCP, the NCP SP, and an Independent, and would take a call on the candidates after determining their chances of winning. That understanding now appears to have failed in two constituencies. In both cases, the parties have moved ahead with nominations rather than waiting for a final decision at the alliance level. However, the Opposition alliance still has time till October 9 to avoid friendly fights and give itself the best possible chance to defeat the Mahayuti. Otherwise, the folly of friendly fights might become apparent when the votes are counted on October 27.

articleTitle: ‘6-7 police stations called me’: Mumbai, Nagpur CJP members allege pressure
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Protesters stage a protest under the leadership of CJP Founder Abhijeet Dipke, seeking Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation over voter roll deletions at Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Park, Dadar, in Mumbai on Friday. (ANI Photo)
description: Plainclothes police noted names at a Mumbai meet and visited homes in Nagpur, members allege, ahead of the Jantar Mantar protest seeking CEC Gyanesh Kumar's resignation. Police say they are "doing our job".
body_raw: Even as Cockroach Janta Party CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke on Tuesday accused the Chandrapur police of serving notices on party workers to keep them away from the partys Delhi protest, members in Mumbai and Nagpur alleged similar pressure. In Mumbai, members said plainclothes police noted names at a party meeting and warned of FIRs. The partys city coordinator said six or seven police stations had called him. In Nagpur, a coordinator said police came to his home. The CJP has called the protest at Delhis Jantar Mantar on October 10 to demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Dipke announced it after a rally at Mumbais Shivaji Park on October 2. On September 23, The Indian Express had published an investigation on the rupture within the Election Commission, with two Election Commissioners Vivek Joshi and Sukhbir Singh Sandhu flagging 14 objections in 10 months on issues that strike right at the heart of the electoral process. At a press conference in Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, Dipke had alleged that the Chandrapur notices asked workers not to join the protest, and that police questioned them on how they would pay for the trip. He called this dictatorship and asked how police could already say, as the notices did, that the agitation would turn violent. In Mumbai, CJP member Mayur Sharma said police in plain clothes came to the partys meeting at Sana Banquet Hall in Dongri on Wednesday. We had a meeting at the Banquet hall, and the police had arrived in plain clothes and noted the names of the people present in the meeting. They showed us Dipkes post in which he had posted the notice. 7-8 police officers in plain clothes threatened us with an FIR if we attend the protest, which is scheduled to be on October 10 at Jantar Mantar, he told this newspaper. Pranay Ahire, the CJPs Mumbai coordinator, told The Indian Express I have received a call from 6-7 police stations asking what my plans for the 10th of October are. I have not revealed my plan for that day. This is very sad that they are tracking our movements. Another member, Azzaruddin, said he was told a notice would be served on him. Many comrades have received calls or threats that notice will be served if we are planning to attend the protest. I received an ultimatum too, he said. In Nagpur, CJP west zone coordinator Durgesh Kuhike told The Indian Express that police visited his home and asked how many people from the city were likely to travel to Jantar Mantar. CJP volunteers alleged that officials also indirectly sought the numbers and identities of those planning to join. Samya Korde, a Bombay High Court advocate and member of the Shetkari Kamgar Paksh, said police may have identified protesters from records of protests in July. Many of us had attended protests in July. Some of us might have been detained, some of us came under surveillance and FIRs were registered in July. Based on that they might have tracked down protesters. Calling regular citizens is completely unconstitutional. If they are doing that it should be stopped, Korde said. Asked about the allegations, a police official said, We are doing our job.

articleTitle: Barefoot in a blue saree, a widow ran for a job, and the stadium roared
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Jharkhand widow
description: Kavita Kumari, whose video has gone viral, says she knew she had done well once people started cheering her on
body_raw: Everyone in the stadium started clapping and hooting as soon as a woman in a blue saree, tucked at the waist, removed her slippers and ran barefoot to finish a 1,600-metre run. Someone watching the trial run amid the Home Guard recruitment shot a video, focusing on the woman as she passed other candidates one by one. It went viral on social media. The woman is Kavita Kumari, a widow from Jharkhand for whom a Home Guard job could spell a change in fortunes. Kumari starts her day with an early-morning practice run on uneven ground near her village, Soso, in Ramgarh district. On October 4, she travelled to Sidhu Kanhu Stadium for a free trial conducted by an academy run by athletes, where candidates could get a sense of the ground and assess their fitness in conditions closer to those they would face in the recruitment test. The same stadium is scheduled to host the physical test for the Home Guard recruitment from October 24 to November 5. Barefoot, in a saree, Jharkhand widow runs 1,600m in 8 minutes. The finish line A Home Guard job  - The Indian Express IndianExpress October 7, 2026 Kumari, clad in a saree and chappals, was among those who showed up. I was very nervous as soon as I reached the stadium. People were looking at me in a saree, and I was looking at them in tracksuits with bags, bottles and shoes on their feet. This just made me uncomfortable, but I took part in the run, she said. To pass the running test in the female category, a candidate has to run 1,600 metres in 10 minutes. Kumari said she completed it within eight minutes, earning an Excellent grade with full marks. Till people applauded me, I had no idea about what I had done. I just removed my chappal and started running barefoot. While I was running, I had no thoughts other than the Home Guard job. Someone took my video and posted it on social media. I hope I will run with the same energy and confidence on the physical exam day, she said. Ankit Singh 25, who runs Ankit Runner Academy in Ramgarh and organised the October 4 trial, said the purpose was not merely to conduct a practice run but to familiarise candidates with the stadium. The ground, he said, has a slope on one side, with portions that are sandy, gravelly and uneven. Candidates need to know how the ground behaves before the actual physical test. That is why many of them come from 15 to 20 kilometres away to practise here. That day, around 1,900 candidates took part, including nearly 1,100 women. Many of the women came from rural areas, and some wore sarees. There were around 50 to 60 women in sarees that day, he said. He said that for women from rural areas, wearing a tracksuit and running shoes and going out to practise is not always easy. The idea was to give candidates an experience of the actual ground so that they would know what to expect on the recruitment day, he said. The notification for Jharkhand Home Guard recruitment was issued in April this year, with 284 vacancies in Ramgarh district against more than 16,000 applications. The first phase of the recruitment includes a physical test comprising a 1,600-metre run, long jump, high jump and shot put, following which the written examination will be conducted. The recruitment also reserves 50 per cent of the overall posts for women, with 5 per cent reserved for widows. A long list of misfortunes Kumari said she got married in 2009 while she was a minor. Now around 30, she lost her husband, Deepak Kumar Mahato, three years ago. Deepak was a migrant worker in Gujarat after working in Mumbai, she said. During Covid, he was unwell, and he returned home. He continuously fell sick and died in 2023. I had to look after my in-laws, maintain the home and children and run the home financially, she said. Six months after Deepaks death, the family also lost his younger brother. My sister-in-law left home after her husbands death, she said. Kumari told The Indian Express that the family has a debt of around Rs 6 lakh after spending a substantial amount on treatment. She said she worked as a security guard at private offices in Ramgarh town but left the job as her shifts ended late and she could not find transport back to her village. Now she works as a labourer, mostly at a brick kiln, to repay the debt and support her two children, who study at a private school in Ramgarh. While preparing for the physical test, Kumari said she relied on YouTube to learn and practise. I ask my children to open YouTube and play the videos for me, as I hardly know how to use it. I watch the videos and prepare for the exam. I do not have a single penny to spend on dresses, shoes or tuition fees, so I have to prepare on my own, she said. After the video reached a wider audience, several people and politicians reached out to support her. Dumri MLA Jairam Kumar Mahato spoke to Kumari over the phone and sent her a tracksuit and running shoes. Ajay Karmali 38, a Home Guard posted in Ramgarh, is Kumaris coach and runs the HMT Physical Academy in Dulmi, about 5 km from her village. He started the academy around four or five months ago, offering free physical training to villagers. Kumari found him through his social media posts and called him to ask if she could join. Karmali said he encouraged her to run at the stadium before the recruitment test so that she could become familiar with the ground and gain confidence. Though she did not have a running uniform, she hopes that she will soon get the Home Guard uniform, he said.

articleTitle: As reservoirs shrink, this Maharashtra district moves to guard remaining water
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Beed reservoir levels water crisis
description: Officials from the revenue department, the Maharashtra State Electricity Board, and the police will check water theft from reservoir backwaters in Beed three times a day.
body_raw: As water levels in reservoirs in Maharashtras Beed have sunk to 16.38 per cent and groundwater levels are falling sharply, the district administration has ordered inspections of waterbodies and stepped up action to protect drinking water sources. Speaking to The Indian Express, District Collector Vivek Johnson said dedicated teams comprising officials from the revenue department, Maharashtra State Electricity Board MSEB, and the police have been formed to check water theft from reservoir backwaters and monitor the situation. The inspections will be conducted three times a day. There are 164 reservoirs across the district, including small, medium, and large projects. We have been facing water theft from certain locations in the backwaters of reservoirs. To check these thefts, we have ordered joint inspections, Johnson said. According to Johnson, the officials have been checking illegal water theft for the last three months. However, it was found that some farmers were reconnecting pump connections even after action was taken against them. As part of the intensified action, the administration has started dismantling electricity distribution points at select locations from where water is being stolen. These transformers are being removed and stored in the MSEB godown, while transformers supplying power to regular connections will remain operational, the collector said. Johnson also directed talathis and gram sevaks to maintain a strict vigil over water theft from small and medium water supply projects. At larger reservoirs, including Majalgaon and Manjara, dedicated teams have been deployed to monitor illegal water lifting, he said. 37 rainfall deficit in Beed The intensified monitoring comes at a time when Beed is facing a significant rain shortfall and declining water availability. Data from the district information office shows that against the expected average rainfall of 566.1 mm till September 30, the district received only 356.6 mm, or about 63 per cent. The rainfall deficit has also translated into a sharp decline in groundwater levels. The average water level recorded in observation wells has fallen to 7.36 metres, which is 4.55 metres deeper than the average level recorded in September over the past five years. A decline in groundwater levels was recorded in all 126 wells surveyed, with Georai tehsil recording the steepest fall of 6.64 metres. Reservoir storage also remains low. Of the 164 projects in the district, usable water storage is at 16.38 per cent. The Majalgaon project has 28.53 per cent storage, while medium projects have 12.49 per cent and minor projects only 5.49 per cent. As many as 32 projects have completely dried up. Currently, the average capacity of all 164 large, medium, and small reservoirs is roughly 16 per cent. Apart from these, there are several minor sources such as open wells, borewells, jackwells and small lakes. Their water availability in the coming months depends on the groundwater table, Johnson said. The administration is therefore already relying on tankers to meet drinking water requirements. As many as 150 tankers are currently supplying water twice a day across the district, Johnson said. 40of water sources acquired As of September 29, wells or borewells had been requisitioned in 28 villages and at 32 other locations. We have acquired 40 per cent of water sources, he said. The pressure on drinking water supplies is particularly evident in Parli Vaijnath, where the municipal council has begun planning for the coming months. We have a population of roughly 1.2 lakh. Considering the current reservoir capacity and evaporation rate, we have planned to supply water once every eight to 10 days to ensure water availability till June 2027. The implementation will start on October 8, Trimbak Kamble, Chief Officer of the Parli Vaijnath Municipal Council, told The Indian Express. Livestock and fodder stock also affected The water shortage is also affecting livestock. Available fodder stocks are expected to last for an average of only 37 days. The situation is particularly critical in Patoda, where stocks are estimated to last 21 days, and Ashti, where they are expected to last 27 days. Parli has the highest availability, with fodder stocks estimated to last around 70 days. The impact of the rainfall deficit has also been felt during the Kharif season. Sowing was completed on 7,87,218 hectares, or 97.31 per cent of the expected 8,08,946 hectares. Soybean sowing exceeded the target at 137.90 per cent, while cotton sowing stood at 78.36 per cent. Preliminary assessments have indicated crop damage of more than 75 per cent across all 11 talukas, with the affected area estimated at around 5.14 lakh hectares. Amid the water and agricultural stress, the district has also received funds for irrigation-related works. A total of Rs 2,341.33 lakh has been sanctioned for three projects in Ashti, Beed, and Georai under the Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana 2.0. The projects are expected to cover 10,642 hectares. For the administration, however, the immediate challenge remains protecting the limited water available in reservoirs and groundwater sources. We are now making a drought management plan for all villages in the district and mapping their primary and secondary water sources. Around 40 sources are currently being regularly monitored, Johnson said.

articleTitle: ‘Trust court, go study’: Bombay HC appeals to MPSC protesters, seeks fair exams, recruitment
articleFeaturedImageAlt: MPSC paper leak protest bombay high court
description: The court has asked the Maharashtra government to to ensure "free, impartial and fair" examinations are conducted, as it asked the protesting students to trust the court and 'go study'
body_raw: The Bombay High Court on Wednesday asked the Maharashtra government to address the grievances of the protesting Maharashtra Public Service Commission MPSC aspirants to ensure free, impartial and fair examinations and appealed to the agitators to go back to their studies. It also reminded the MPSC paper leak protesters of state action if they do not relocate, noting that they do not have the required permission. If they protestors wish to continue with the agitation, then they will have to take permission to continue and relocate. If they do not relocate, then the state will have to take reasonable steps, the HC bench of Chief Justice Mahesh Chandra Tripathi and Justice Advait M Sethna noted. The court was hearing a writ plea by two Pune residents, claiming daily disruptions faced by Pune residents due to agitations by MPSC aspirants at Alka Talkies Chowk, Ahilya Study Centre, and SM Joshi Bridge. Onus is on the state government to ensure recruitment happens and is streamlined, CJ Tripathi orally said, seeking its roadmap within three weeks. It Pune is at a centre for education and most students are genuinely interested in studies and not interested in these protests. The entire atmosphere is now vitiated, and there should be sincere effort in restoring trust.I will make a request to all students, see the plight of parents who have sent you to Pune and go back to education.Innocent children are on roads and their grievances should be addressed and free and fair examination takes place..They should trust the court which is now seized of the matter and do not cause grievance to citizens in peace-loving Pune city, CJ Tripathi orally said. Remarking that students should ask for permission for agitation to ensure citizens are not troubled, the judge added, If they get the idea that there has been something hanky-panky, they have the right to agitate, because they have given hours to study. AG Sathe, appearing for the state government, responded that the governments course of action would be placed on affidavit. We appreciate that. They are students, not anti-socials. Their main grievance is that the examination has to be conducted fairly. The detailed enquiry and everything should be brought on record. We will ensure effort is made and find who the culprits are. Court is genuinely entrusted as guardian and students should go back to faculty and university, the HC remarked and posted further hearing to November 25.

articleTitle: Barapullah Phase III traffic mess: Delhi plans U-turn, road widening, Google Maps fix
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Barapullah Phase 3 traffic jam, Barapullah Phase 3 congestion, Barapullah flyover traffic,
description: The corridor opened last week but has already seen long traffic snarls, prompting the Delhi government to look at short-term measures.
body_raw: With congestion building up soon after Barapullah Phase III opened last week, the Delhi government is now relying on a series of quick measures-deployment of traffic police at merging points, a new U-turn, redesigning the point where traffic merges, widening the road and removing a footpath, while also working with Google Maps to ensure real-time route information is provided to the commuters. Citing an engineering flaw in the construction, which had not taken into account the traffic situation expected after 10 years, PWD Minister Parvesh Sahib Singh said on Wednesday, The government is currently working on immediate traffic-management measures, while discussions on a longer-term solution continue. see box Singh blamed the previous AAP-led Delhi government for the flaw in the construction. The Barapullah Phase III flyover project began in 2015. That means its design had already been approved in 2014-2015, when the AAP government had come to power in Delhi. The entire design was approved during their tenure. How many lanes the flyover would have, all of this was decided by them, he said. Asked whether there was any warning sign that such a situation could arise, Singh said, We had no such study. We had no estimate. The new corridor connects Mayur Vihar with Sarai Kale Khan and links to the existing Barapullah network, creating a continuous stretch of around 10 km towards the AIIMS roundabout. However, the promise of a 15-minute, signal-free ride has run into a bottleneck at Sarai Kale Khan, where vehicles arriving from Mayur Vihar, those joining from the Sundial loop, and traffic approaching from the DND side converge before entering the older and narrower Barapullah flyover. The project was originally scheduled for completion in 2017 but opened only in 2026 after construction delays. Over these nine years, while vehicle numbers rose significantly, East Delhi and the wider NCR also grew, changing vehicular movement between East Delhi, Noida, Ghaziabad, and South Delhi. Singh also said that the issue was not limited to the road itself. The interaction of Barapulla with DND Flyway, NH 24, Ring Road, RRTS connectivity, Sarai Kale Khan and the surrounding railway and Metro network has created a much larger integrated traffic movement. Traffic Police had earlier flagged another problem Google Maps was showing the new corridor as relatively clear, directing motorists towards a stretch that was already congested. This was adding to the load as some vehicles that could otherwise use DND or NH 24 were being routed towards Barapullah. Singh said the PWD was in touch with Google Maps and that its algorithm could take about 15 days to reflect the changed traffic situation. He also raised questions over the financial and contractual decisions taken during the previous AAP government. An additional payment of around Rs 640 crore was made to the contractor through arbitration. The projects prolonged delay, cost escalation, and arbitration-related payments need to be examined together, Singh said. The AAP called for a CBI investigation. The BJP government itself admits that Barapulla Phase nIII has serious issues of planning, design and traffic integration. It must answer why it sanctioned Rs. 1,635 crore without a proper technical assessment. The CBI must investigate the matter, an AAP spokesperson said. Instead of blaming the previous government, the BJP should explain the technical assessment and the basis on which Rs. 1,635 crore of public money was sanctioned, the spokesperson added.   The quick fixes  Traffic police deployment Personnel to be deployed at peak hours to regulate the three merging traffic streams.  Sundial merge Traffic Police has suggested redesigning the merger point to improve vehicle flow.  New U-turn A dedicated U-turn near Gurdwara Bala Sahib for Siddharth Extension residents, reducing dependence on the ramp to the old Barapullah. Footpath removal A footpath between Sarai Kale Khan and ITO is being removed to improve traffic movement.  Road widening The government is working on widening the affected stretch to accommodate the increased flow.  Google Maps changes PWD is coordinating with Google Maps to ensure routing reflects the current congestion and traffic patterns.

articleTitle: 22-year marriage not consummated, Calcutta High Court grants divorce, Rs 10 lakh alimony
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Calcutta High Court marriage divorce consummate alimony
description: The husband claimed before the Calcutta High Court that the marriage was never consummated as the wife allegedly said that she was not interested in physical intimacy.
body_raw: The Calcutta High Court recently granted divorce to a man after a 22-year marriage that was never consummated and directed him to pay Rs 10 lakh as permanent alimony to his wife. The court noted that the couple lived together as husband and wife for barely a month after their marriage in 2004 and separated after that, barring a brief period when they were required to stay together by a court order. Justices Debangsu Basak and Aryak Dutt held that the marriage was not consummated and that there was no valid reason or evidence of physical incapacity preventing consummation. There is no valid reason for the marriage not being consummated. There is no material on record suggesting that any of the parties were incapable of consummating the marriage. The materials on record suggest that they voluntarily withdrew from the society of the other, the October 5 order read. Lived together for 1 month The man claimed that the couple married in April 2004, but allegedly never consummated the marriage, and they started living separately after the wife left the house within one month. The husband later filed a divorce case on the grounds of cruelty and desertion in July 2016. He said that his wife refused to consummate the marriage, saying that she was not interested in intercourse because her figure would become shapeless and nobody would notice her after that. The mans counsel, advocate Kaushal Paul, submitted that there was an interim period in which the parties were required to live as husband and wife in the wake of an order of the high court. He added that the couple, however, never cohabited and neither was the marriage consummated during that period. The husband did not reside at the house with the wife at the time, the counsel added. On the contrary, the woman, through advocate Prantick Ghosh, argued that the husband did not give any particulars of her alleged cruelty. He also stated that the husband had not given particulars of the dates of the alleged non-consummation of the marriage. No amicable settlement The high court noted that the marriage was proved to have not been consummated and that the wife had admitted in her cross-examination that there had been no cohabitation between the couple. It also mentioned having made efforts to help the couple arrive at an amicable resolution of their disputes, but they could not agree to settle the same. The bench acknowledged that both lawyers tried their best to help the parties arrive at an amicable settlement and went out of their way in the process. The bench found that there was an irretrievable breakdown of marriage. The cruelty which was occasioned in the facts and circumstances of the present case emanates out of denial of conjugal rights and non-consummation of marriage, it added. The court also considered the assets available to the husband and found it appropriate to grant permanent alimony of Rs 10 lakh, payable in four monthly instalments starting November 15, 2026. It noted that the wife was gainfully employed.

articleTitle: Yoga, exercise, sleep: Why old health practices are being rebranded as ‘neurowellness’
articleFeaturedImageAlt: The neurowellness vocabulary may be different, but many of the practices behind it have been around for generations.
description: In a world where the modern brain is overworked and overstimulated, experts explain why people are paying for experiences designed to help them do less.
body_raw: W ellness, for all these years, has largely been about the body-eating better, exercising more, losing weight, building muscle and looking healthier. But that conversation is shifting. People are now asking different questions about their wellbeing Why cant I sleep properly? Why am I constantly overwhelmed? Why is my attention so fragmented? Why cant I switch off even when I am technically resting? The search for answers has given rise to a new wellness buzzword neurowellness. The term may be new, but much of what it includes is already familiar. Meditation, yoga, pranayama, breathwork, sound healing, spending time in nature, social connection, and simply allowing yourself to rest-all these have existed for years. So what exactly is new? Moreover, why are these familiar practices suddenly being presented as ways to care for the brain and nervous system? DISCLAIMERThis article is based on information from the public domain andor the experts we spoke to. Always consult your health practitioner before starting any routine. A mind thats not allowed to clock out Dr Munia Bhattacharya, Senior Consultant, Clinical Psychology, Marengo Asia Hospitals, Gurgaon, describes neurowellness as an emerging umbrella term within the wellness industry rather than a formally established clinical concept. The term may be new, but the need is not, she says. Broadly speaking, it means caring for the brain as part of overall wellbeing-from sleep and concentration to emotional regulation, stress management, and recovery. The idea is especially relevant to how people live now. We are living in a world where the body gets a fitness routine, but the brain gets whatever time is left, says Dr Bhattacharya. The modern brain is being asked to process an extraordinary amount of information notifications, emails, social media, work demands, family responsibilities and an almost continuous stream of information. We have created a lifestyle where the body can stop, but the mind is rarely allowed to clock out, she says. And this may explain why someone can appear to be functioning perfectly well while still feeling mentally depleted. In my clinical practice, I increasingly meet people who are not necessarily presenting with a diagnosable psychological disorder. They are functioning. They are working, meeting deadlines, managing families and maintaining their responsibilities, says Dr Bhattacharya. Yet, she says, they may arrive saying, My mind doesnt switch off, I cannot concentrate like I used to, or I am exhausted even after sleeping. She hears another sentence increasingly often. Nothing is really wrong, but I dont feel like myself. We have become remarkably good at functioning while feeling unwell, she says, adding that a healthy brain is not one that is productive every minute of the day. It can focus when needed, rest when needed, experience emotions, adapt to change, and recover from stress.   Old practices, new reasons This is perhaps the biggest distinction between the term neurowellness and all the wellness trends that preceded it. Tarun Gulati, Director, Ganga Kinare Resorts and Hotels, says meditation, yoga, pranayama, sound healing and time spent in nature have long been a part of peoples lives. What is new is not necessarily the practices, but what people are looking for from them, he says, mentioning that they want to sleep better, switch off from work, quieten the mind and come back feeling less overwhelmed. Shane Gunasekara, Director, Kurundu Wellness at Cinnamon Life in Colombo, Sri Lanka, observes a similar shift among guests. We are constantly connected to our phones, work pressure and deadlines, we travel more, sleep patterns are disturbed, and even when we are resting, our minds are still busy, he says. That changes the reason someone might seek out an old practice. People are no longer coming to a spa only because their back is tight or because they want a massage. They understand that beyond muscle relaxation, they also need to calm down, unwind and manage stress, he adds. To address this, Kurundu Wellness introduced Traditional Himalayan Sound Healing with Sakron Boonjing and developed its Sleep Enhancement Ritual. Making ancient practices relatable There is also a language shift. Dr Chandni Tugnait, MD A.M, Psychotherapist, Life Alchemist, Coach and Healer, Founder and Director, Gateway of Healing, says the growing scientific understanding of practices such as meditation and breathwork has given a vocabulary that appeals to a different generation of consumers. Theres now a much clearer picture of what meditation and breathwork are actually doing to the body, not just settling the mind in some vague way, but genuinely calming the nervous system, she says. That matters because the way something is framed and packaged can determine whether people are willing to try it. But I wouldnt call it pure repackaging. Sit through a breathing exercise and your body responds exactly the way it always has, long before anyone gave it a fancy name or a scientific framework to sit inside, says Dr Tugnait. What has changed is whos willing to try it. Someone who would never touch anything labelled spiritual will happily do the same breathwork if its framed as nervous system regulation, backed by a chart and a heart rate number, she says. She sees some of the trend as a rebranding exercise-but not entirely. So call it a rebrand if you want, honestly, in some ways it is exactly that, she says, adding, Underneath it, though, is something genuinely old, tested quietly for generations, just finally handed a name this particular audience trusts enough to actually sit down and try. Neurowellness and nervous-system regulation The two phrases appear together, but they describe different things. Dr Atampreet Singh, Senior Director and Head, Neurology, ShardaCare-Healthcity, says, Neurowellness is a broader approach to supporting brain and nervous-system health through habits such as adequate sleep, regular physical activity, balanced nutrition, social connection, stress management, cognitive stimulation and emotional wellbeing. However, nervous-system regulation refers to the bodys ability to appropriately respond to stress and then return towards a calmer baseline once the stressor has passed, he adds. Regulation does not mean being calm all the time it means being flexible in how you respond to different situations and recovering after stress. Dr Singh explains that several aspects of neurowellness can support this process. Regular exercise can help improve stress resilience and mood, while consistent, good-quality sleep is important for emotional and physiological recovery. Slow, controlled breathing, mindfulness, relaxation practices and activities that promote social connection may also help reduce physiological arousal. A healthy diet and limiting excessive alcohol, nicotine and stimulants can further support overall nervous-system health, he says. That distinction is important because wellness content can sometimes make regulation sound like a state in which a person should remain permanently calm. That is not what it means. Asking a more fundamental question The changing language of wellness reflects a broader change in what people want from it. Dr Bhattacharya says wellness was once commonly discussed in terms of diet, exercise, weight, and physical appearance. Now, people are asking about attention, sleep, stress and emotional exhaustion. These are not simply lifestyle questions, she says. They tell us something about how modern life is affecting the way we think, feel and function. This is also why the idea of a wellness experience is changing. Gulati says people are becoming less interested in wellness as a checklist. They dont necessarily want to attend a yoga class just because it is on the schedule. They want the experience to make a difference to how they feel. That is why multi-day programmes are becoming relevant, he says. At Ganga Kinare, programmes include combinations of yoga, meditation, kriya, pranayama, sound healing, therapies, wellness cuisine and nature experiences. I think people are looking at wellness less as an activity and more as a way of changing their pace for a few days, says Gulati. Gunasekara has noticed a similar change at Kurundu Wellness. Earlier, a guest might have booked a massage, attended a meditation session or experienced a sound bath as separate activities. Now, we are seeing guests looking for a more complete journey rather than one isolated treatment, he says. Its Sleep Enhancement Ritual, for instance, combines several elements The experience begins with a warm welcome ritual, followed by a light-pressure head massage and Thai stretching techniques to help the guest slow down, release tension and prepare the body and mind for deeper rest. This then flows into the sound-bathing experience. You can simply lie down, listen and allow yourself some time away from everything else. The experience doesnt finish there. Afterwards, guests can continue with hot and cold therapy through our steam, sauna and vitality pools with water jets, before finishing with a healthy cup of tea and a light snack. I think this kind of complete journey is becoming very important in modern wellness, says Gunasekara. It is no longer about experiencing one treatment in isolation, but about creating a journey that allows the guest to slow down, disconnect and leave feeling deeply relaxed. How priorities are changing Perhaps the most noticeable change is in the outcome people are seeking. People still want the traditional benefits of wellness-muscle relaxation, physical recovery, skincare and feeling physically better. But the desired endpoint is increasingly intangible. At Ganga Kinare, Gulati says programmes such as Nidra Samadhi centre on sleep, relaxation, stress and fatigue, while Dhyana Sadhana takes a more meditative approach involving yoga, meditation, kriya and pranayama. It tells us something about how peoples priorities are changing, he says. A wellness holiday doesnt necessarily have to result in a visible physical transformation. Sometimes, sleeping properly for a few nights, having a quieter mind and feeling like yourself again is the outcome people value most. Gunasekara says the same shift can be seen in conversations with guests, who increasingly talk about sleep, stress, mental tiredness and wanting to disconnect. Of course, guests still want traditional outcomes - releasing muscle tension, improving recovery, taking care of their skin and feeling physically better, but the conversation is becoming broader, he says. For Gunasekara, this is where wellness is heading-not choosing between physical and mental wellbeing but understanding that people increasingly want to experience them together and leave feeling satisfied and fulfilled. Why pay for doing nothing? An interesting contradiction lies at the heart of the neurowellness boom. People are paying for experiences designed to help them do less. According to hospitality experts, genuine downtime has become hard to find. Even when we go on holiday, we are often still checking our phones, answering messages or thinking about work, says Gulati. So simply being in a beautiful destination doesnt always mean that you have actually switched off. Gunasekara agrees. You can buy many things, but if you are constantly tired, mentally overloaded or unable to switch off, it affects your work, family time, holidays and physical wellbeing, he says. That may explain why structured wellness experiences are becoming more attractive. Someone else provides the setting, removes some decision-making, and creates protected time to step away. I think people are increasingly willing to pay for that because they recognise the value of having someone else take care of the setting and structure while they focus on themselves, says Gulati. He believes this may even be creating a different definition of luxury. It is not necessarily about having more things. It is about having the time, privacy and space to step away from everything for a while and genuinely feel rested. Neurowellness without the marketing Take away the apps, gadgets, retreats and optimisationneurowellness becomes all about basic mental wellbeing sleeping properly, moving regularly, taking breaks from constant stimulation, focusing on one thing at a time, allowing some boredom, staying socially connected and making space for emotions and activities you enjoy. As Dr Bhattacharya puts it, It does not have to involve expensive programmes, complicated routines or another gadget to track how well we are functioning. The basics are simple Treat sleep as a healthy behaviour rather than leftover time at the end of the day, she says. She also recommends periods of uninterrupted attention and regular movement, noting that physical activity is not only about physical fitness. And perhaps most importantly, the brain needs time without constant input. Five or ten minutes without a phone, podcast, television or constant input can be surprisingly restorative, says Dr Bhattacharya. We should not be afraid of a little boredom. The brain does not need stimulation every waking minute. The same goes for pleasure and connection. Reading, gardening, music, family time, meaningful conversation, or simply sitting quietly do not need to have a measurable benefit to be worthwhile. As Dr Bhattacharya says, Sometimes, the most powerful thing we can do for the brain is not ask it to perform better, but give it permission to rest. DISCLAIMERThis article is based on information from the public domain andor the experts we spoke to. Always consult your health practitioner before starting any routine.

articleTitle: Rahul Gandhi detained again: How does detention differ from arrest, what rights do detainees have?
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Congress leader Rahul Gandhi is detained at Akashvani Bhawan on Tuesday. (Gajendra Yadav)
description: The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita does not define 'detention' per se. Instead, it gives police a set of powers that allows them to stop, remove or temporarily hold people in certain situations, including when a crime has actually taken place.
body_raw: Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi was detained on Wednesday October 7 as Opposition leaders protested in New Delhi demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the Election Commissions Special Intensive Revision SIR exercise. This was the second time in as many days that the Congress leader had been detained - on Tuesday, too, he along with Opposition leaders including Priyanka Gandhi Vadra was taken into custody by Delhi Police after protesting for nearly eight hours inside Akashvani Bhavan in New Delhi. On Wednesday, before Gandhis latest detention, police had registered a case of trespass into the Akashvani Bhavan premises. Since October 2, Delhi police have detained hundreds of protesters, including Advocate Prashant Bhushan, and AISA national president Neha Bora. Legally speaking, what exactly is detention? How does it work? And what rights does law provide to police and detainees? How does detention differ from arrest? Police, under the law, are empowered to maintain law and order, particularly during protests and demonstrations. In practice, this may sometimes look like an arrest and at other times a detention, often because these terms are used interchangeably. Arrest is a formal act of police taking a person into custody in connection with an offence, marking the beginning of criminal proceedings. Once a person is arrested, a range of constitutional and statutory safeguards immediately come into play. The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita or BNSS, which replaced the Code of Criminal Procedure or CrPC does not define detention per se. Instead, it gives police a set of powers that allows them to stop, remove or temporarily hold people in certain situations, including when a crime has actually taken place. This is why disputes arise after protests. Someone may be taken away by police, kept in custody for several hours, and released without any case being registered. To the person involved, it can feel very much like an arrest. Legally, however, police may say that they were exercising preventive powers rather than arresting the individual for an offence. Senior Advocate Sanjay Hegde drew a distinction between a formal arrest and the short-term custody often seen during protests. They are temporarily not allowed to leave wherever they are detained, and they are not put under a formal arrest either, he told The Indian Express. Advocate Soutik Banerjee told The Indian Express that the distinction is often used to avoid the scrutiny that accompanies a formal arrest. The police know that the power to arrest cannot be exercised casually when there is no cognizable offence punishable with more than seven years being committed by the protestors. If they are arrested, courts will come down heavily on them. That is why they choose to abduct people and release them within hours, he said. A cognizable offence is one for which police can arrest without a warrant. Section 170 of the BNSS allows preventive action before any offence is committed. A police officer, knowing of a design to commit any cognizable offence may arrest, without orders from a magistrate and without a warrant, the person so designing, if it appears to such officer that the commission of the offence cannot be otherwise prevented. Section 172 of the BNSS says that a police officer may detain or remove any person resisting, refusing, ignoring or disregarding a lawful direction. The officer must then take the person before a magistrate or, in petty cases, release them within 24 hours. Unlike the earlier CrPC, this provision expressly allows police to detain or remove a person who refuses to comply with a lawful direction. Section 1722 BNSS is new. The CrPC had no equivalent, Senior Advocate Hegde said. The CrPC let police prevent cognizable offences and arrest to prevent them. It did not bind citizens to obey police directions, nor let police detain those who refused. Section 172 adds both. The idea came from state police statutes, not the CrPC. The 24-hour limit was itself a late addition. He added that the law on safeguards applicable to such short-term detentions remains largely untested no short-term detention and the consequences of not following safeguards have been litigated up to the Supreme Court. This position is different from preventive detention which allows a person to be held without trial under special laws such as the National Security Act. Banerjee said that the practice of briefly taking protesters into custody should not be confused with preventive detention powers under the law. He said This so-called detention has no place in law and is wholly illegal. Of course there are preventive detention powers available, but they are subject to strict rigours of the law and cannot be casually applied spontaneously. None of the abductions and excursions to Narela or Kingsway Camp in buses is carried out under legal provisions for preventive detention. When can police detain people? Most protest-related detentions begin with a claim that police are trying to prevent a law and order problem. Often, there is already a prohibitory order in place. On October 2, the Delhi Police imposed Section 163 of the BNSS across New Delhi. If protestors refuse to disperse or continue activities prohibited by such an order, police may invoke preventive powers to remove them from the spot or hold them temporarily. Disobeying such an order is itself an offence under Section 223 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita or BNS, which replaced the Indian Penal Code or IPC. That is the point at which a detention can turn into an arrest with an FIR first information report. Courts have, however, said that such actions cannot be arbitrary. Police must be able to explain why restricting a persons liberty was necessary. The Supreme Court, in Joginder Kumar v State of UP 1994 held that the existence of the power to arrest is one thing and the justification for the exercise of it is quite another. In Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar 2014, the court told police not to arrest automatically in offences punishable up to seven years. In Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan v Union of India 2018 the court held that restrictions on protests should be regulatory rather than eliminating the right to protest altogether. What rights does a detained or an arrested person have? Once the state restricts a persons liberty, a number of protections become relevant. Article 22 is a fundamental right under the Constitution that deals with protection of an accused against arrest and detention. It requires production of an accused person before a magistrate within 24 hours information about the grounds of arrest and the right to have legal representation. The Supreme Court, in multiple cases, has held that written grounds of arrest must be furnished. Just last month, the court held that if an arrest violates the safeguards prescribed under Article 22, it would be unconstitutional. Article 221 also provides for the right to consult and be defended by a lawyer of ones choice. Section 38 BNSS allows an arrested person to meet an advocate of his choice during interrogation, though not throughout interrogation. If a person cannot afford a lawyer, free legal aid is provided to them at the States cost. Section 435 of the BNSS bars the arrest of a woman between sunrise and sunset, except in exceptional circumstances and with the prior permission of a judicial magistrate. The Supreme Court in DK Basu v. State of West Bengal 1997 laid down safeguards for all cases of arrest or detention. Officers must wear visible name tags. An arrest memo must be attested by at least one witness. Injuries must be recorded, and family members should be informed. The court also made clear that these safeguards are not merely advisory and officers who fail to comply can face departmental action or even contempt proceedings.

articleTitle: ‘Lost Rs 250 cr in 13 years’: Rajpal Yadav to SC, hints at film on cheque-bounce cases
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Rajpal Yadav has agreed to sell his ancestral property to pay his dues in a long-running series of cheque-bounce cases.
description: Rajpal Yadav told the Supreme Court that he has a title in mind for a film on cheque bounce case.
body_raw: In a relief for Bollywood actor Rajpal Yadav, the Supreme Court on Wednesday, October 7, reportedly accepted his proposal to pay his dues in a long-running series of cheque-bounce cases by selling off his ancestral property. The apex court gave him a breather after he produced demand drafts worth Rs 1.15 crore, as mandated by its last order. During the hearing, Rajpal informed a bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana that he has found a prospective buyer for his ancestral property, who will deposit Rs 85 lakh in the court registry by Monday, October 12, news agency PTI reported. The latest development comes two days after the court came down heavily on the actor for failing to comply with the last opportunity it had offered him on September 15. Also Read  Your place is in jail SC comes down heavily on Rajpal Yadav as he fails to deposit Rs 2 cr Supreme Court grants conditional relief to Rajpal Yadav Pointing out that it is not satisfied with Rajpals conduct, the apex court remarked that it was only giving him breathing time. We are not satisfied with this. This conduct does not satisfy us. Consider that we are neither impressed by your bona fides nor the merits of the case. We are only giving the accommodation in order to give equitable relief to the complainant, Justice Bagchi reportedly told him. Rajpal was present in court and addressed the bench, I have worked on some 200 to 250 films. Over the last 13 years, I have also incurred losses amounting to Rs 200-250 crore.
