articleTitle: Knowledge Nugget | Why does a dedicated growth fund matter for SMEs?
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Knowledge Nugget | Why does a dedicated growth fund matter for MSMEs? upsc, upsc cse, upsc ias, upsc 2027
description: The Union Cabinet has approved Small and Medium Enterprise (SME) Growth Fund recently. Why was this fund needed? How significant are MSMEs to India’s economy and what are other government supported credit support initiatives for them? Go beyond the nugget to understand updated MSMEs classification.
body_raw: Take a look at the essential events, concepts, terms, quotes, or phenomena every day and brush up your knowledge. Heres your UPSC Current Affairs knowledge nugget for today on Small and Medium Enterprise SME Growth Fund. Knowledge Nugget Small and Medium Enterprise SME Growth Fund. Subject Indian Economy Why in the news? The Union Cabinet on Tuesday approved the Small and Medium Enterprise SME Growth Fund SGF with an outlay of Rs 10,000 crore to provide equity support to small and medium enterprises. The fund was first announced in the Union Budget for 2026-27. Key takeaways 1. Under the initiative, the government will provide an aggregate commitment of Rs 10,000 crore to the Alternative Investment Fund AIF established under the SGF framework. 2. A majority of the funds investments will be directed towards small and medium manufacturing enterprises, with a focus also on SMEs operating in industrial clusters in Tier-II and Tier-III cities. 3. As per the government Investments across industrial clusters, including those in Tier-II and Tier-III cities, will support balanced regional industrial development, reinforce local supply chains and generate high-quality employment opportunities. Why was a dedicated SME fund needed? 5. According to the government, while several existing funds provide equity support to businesses, most of them focus on early-stage enterprises and largely cater to micro enterprises. 6. This has left a structural gap in the availability of growth-stage equity capital for small and medium enterprises. 7. While various initiatives have enhanced access to credit for SMEs, a gap remains in the availability of long-term risk capital required by enterprises seeking to scale, innovate, expand internationally, adopt advanced technologies, undertake acquisitions, and transform into industry leaders, the government said in a statement. 8. The SME Growth Fund is designed to address this critical financing gap by providing patient growth equity capital to high-potential SMEs with demonstrated business viability and scalability, it added. 9. The Centre expects the fund to help SMEs scale up, improve productivity and strengthen export competitiveness by enabling manufacturing enterprises to expand capacity, adopt advanced technologies and achieve greater scale. 10. Vinod Kumar, President, India SME Forum said the Rs 10,000 crore SME Growth Fund can set in motion a powerful cycle, where stronger manufacturers place larger and more consistent orders with smaller suppliers, enabling those businesses to invest in better machinery, improve quality, build skills and create jobs. 11. As these capabilities deepen across industrial clusters, more MSMEs can meet the standards required by large domestic buyers and global supply chains. The cumulative outcome can be higher domestic value addition, greater export competitiveness and reduced dependence on imported components and finished products, Kumar said. Why are MSMEs significant? 12. Small-scale industries make up about 95 per cent of all industrial units and form a significant part of the economic structure of the nation. Mahatma Gandhi said that The salvation of India lies in cottage and small scale industries. 13. Indias 63 million MSMEs employ more than 320 million people, contribute about 31 per cent of GDP, 35 per cent of manufacturing output, and 49 per cent of exports. 14. MSMEs are one of Indias most important non-farm employment generators, particularly for semi-skilled and less-skilled workers. 15. MSMEs are also particularly important for labour-intensive exports such as textiles and apparel, leather and footwear, gems and jewellery, engineering goods, handicrafts and processed products. 16. They can i spread industrial activity beyond metropolitan centres. ii create employment closer to workers homes. iii support smaller towns. iv integrate rural economies with manufacturing. v create opportunities for women, artisans and first-generation entrepreneurs. What are the major government credit support initiatives for MSMEs? 1. In India, micro and small enterprises benefit from a 25 per cent public procurement quota and MSMEs overall are eligible for priority sector lending, with a sub-target for micro firms. 2. Banks and other financial institutions including NBFCs are guaranteed to offer collateral-free credit to MSMEs. 3. The scheme covers up to Rs. 5 crore w.e.f. 01.04.2023 per borrowing unit of collateral-free credit facilities term loans andor working capital provided to micro and small businesses by qualified lending institutions. 4. Budget 2025 proposed customised credit cards with a 5 lakh limit for micro enterprises registered on the Udyam portal. 5. In May 2026, the government approved ECLGS 5.0, with a credit guarantee cover of 2.55 lakh crore to support businesses affected by external shocks. 6. ECLGS 5.0 provides additional credit of up to 20 of an MSMEs peak working capital used in Q4 FY26, subject to a ceiling of 100 crore per borrower. The government provides a 100 guarantee on this additional credit, with a one-year moratorium and a five-year repayment period. 7. Budget 2026 proposed an additional 2,000 crore top-up for the Self-Reliant India Fund SRIF to maintain access to risk capital for micro enterprises. SRIF was established in 2021 as a fund-of-funds vehicle to infuse equity and risk capital into viable MSMEs. 8. An MSME can be profitable on paper and still fail if a large buyer doesnt pay on time. Delayed payments to MSMEs were estimated at 8.14 lakh crore in FY24, down 7 from the previous figure of 10.76 lakh crore.At the same time, the estimated unmet credit requirement was around 25 lakh crore. 9. Budget 2026 proposed several measures to expand the use of the Trade Receivables Discounting System TReDS. TReDS allows MSMEs to receive finance against their unpaid invoices instead of waiting for buyers to make payments. BEYOND THE NUGGET Updated MSMEs Classification 1. The Government of India updated the classification limits for Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises MSMEs effective April 1, 2025. 2. The criteria use a composite measure of investment in plantmachineryequipment and annual turnover for both manufacturing and service units. 3. Investment limits have been increased 2.5 times and turnover limits are doubled from previous thresholds. 4. The investment limit to be classified as a micro enterprise is now up to Rs 2.5 crore. For small enterprises, this limit is up to Rs 25 crore, and for medium ones, it is Rs 125 crore. 5. Similarly, the turnover limit for these classifications goes up to Rs 10 crore for micro enterprises, Rs 100 crore for small ones, and Rs 500 crore for medium enterprises. The same limits apply equally to manufacturing and service sector businesses. Post Read Questions Consider the following statements with reference to India UPSC CSE, 2023 1. According to the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development MSMED Act, 2006, the medium enterprises are those with investments in plant and machinery between  15 crore and  25 crore. 2. All bank loans to the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises qualify under the priority sector. Which of the statements given above isare correct? a 1 only b 2 only c Both 1 and 2 d Neither 1 nor 2 Answer b Faster economic growth requires an increased share of the manufacturing sector in GDP, particularly of MSMEs. articleTitle: Thai woman accuses Kanpur ‘husband’ of Rs 60 lakh fraud, hiding another marriage
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Kanpur
description: The businessman was arrested after the woman alleged he assaulted and pressured her to convert; police invoke anti-conversion law
body_raw: Travelling 3,000 km from Thailand to Kanpur, a 35-year-old woman went looking for the man she said she married - and the Rs 60 lakh she had lent him. The man, a tannery businessman named Mohammad Irfan, had stopped answering her calls and cut off contact. When she went to his Kanpur home, she allegedly discovered that he was already married and had children. The woman approached Kanpur Police on Tuesday, alleging that Irfan and his family members assaulted and threatened her when she confronted him and pressured her to convert to Islam. Based on her complaint, Kanpur Police arrested Irfan and registered an FIR against him at Anwarganj police station under charges including assault. Police also invoked provisions of the anti-conversion law against him. We have arrested Irfan in connection with the case. The womans allegations are being examined, and necessary verification is being carried out, said Assistant Commissioner of Police, Kanpur, Manjay Singh. He added that Irfan has admitted to marrying the woman and is being produced before the court. The woman has been sent for medical examination and the report is awaited. We got married two years ago According to police, the woman, who runs a restaurant and a canteen in Thailand, met Irfan through social media around four years ago. She told police he introduced himself as a prominent Kanpur businessman involved in the tannery business who frequently travelled abroad for work. The woman said Irfan would stay at her house whenever he travelled to Thailand and that they subsequently entered into a relationship. Around two years ago, he proposed to her and the two later married in Thailand, she claimed. She said Irfan continued visiting her every two months. During this period, he allegedly took around Rs 60 lakh from her in several installments, saying he needed the money to expand his business. She told police that she arranged the money by borrowing from relatives and friends. When she later asked Irfan to return the money, he allegedly gave her different excuses. She also said she asked him to stay with her in Thailand, but he refused. She alleged that Irfan returned to India this year and stopped responding to her calls and messages. With her businesses in Thailand facing financial difficulties and her struggling to repay the loans she had taken to provide money to Irfan, she decided to travel to India to recover the money. She came to Kanpur with an acquaintance on a tourist visa on October 5 and visited Irfans house as she knew his address. It was there that she allegedly learned for the first time that he was already married and had children. She alleged that when she confronted Irfan, he and his family members abused and insulted her, and Irfan told her that she would first have to convert to Islam if she wanted to stay with him.

articleTitle: Exclusive: Planning Kainchi Dham visit? You’ll soon need to register first
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Kainchi Dham
description: Proposal discussed at meeting involving district administration, police and other stakeholders, including temple committee and taxi union, Express has learnt
body_raw: The Nainital district administration is set to introduce a registration system for pilgrims visiting Kainchi Dham, initially on weekends, as the Kumaon shrine grapples with a sharp rise in visitors and traffic congestion, The Indian Express has learnt. The proposed system will be modelled on the registration mechanism used for Uttarakhands Char Dham pilgrimage and is expected to allow the administration to know in advance how many devotees are expected at the shrine on a given day and regulate the flow when crowds swell. Currently, there is no registration requirement to visit Kainchi Dham. Pilgrims can arrive at the shrine and enter for darshan without any prior registration. Nainital District Magistrate Lalit Mohan Rayal told The Indian Express Wednesday that a joint report by him and the Senior Superintendent of Police will be sent to the state governments Tourism Department recommending the system. The proposal is to introduce registration at Kainchi Dham, similar to what is done for Char Dham, Rayal told The Indian Express. A joint report of the DM and SSP will be sent to the government. The proposal was discussed at a meeting involving the district administration, police and other stakeholders, including the temple committee and taxi union on Tuesday. For now, the administration plans to restrict the system to weekends, when the shrine sees its largest crowds. We will keep it for weekends, Rayal said. Later, when the regular season comes, we will assess the expected crowd and implement it according to the estimated footfall. It will take about a month for the government to develop the portal and everything else, he said, adding that the administration would seek to replicate the existing Char Dham model at Kainchi. How the Char Dham system works The Char Dham registration system the administration is looking to replicate runs through Uttarakhands Tourist Care portal and mobile application. Pilgrims first create an account, then create a tour by entering their travel dates, number of pilgrims, and the Dhams they intend to visit, along with the dates they plan to visit each shrine. They then enter the required details of each pilgrim. Once registration is complete, pilgrims receive a Yatra Registration Letter with a QR code, which they must keep with them. At the destination, designated counters at the shrine verify the registration. The official system describes registration and verification as compulsory for the Char Dham and Hemkund Sahib pilgrimage. Individuals, families, and tour operators can use the system. Pilgrims can register online through the portal or mobile application physical registration facilities and assistance through Yatri Mitra are also available for those unable to complete the process online. The Char Dham system also allows pilgrims to obtain darshan slot tokens, while vehicle registration is part of the system for those travelling by personal or public vehicles. The Kainchi administration now proposes to adapt this broad framework, rather than simply asking pilgrims to provide their names at the temple gate. Behind the decision The proposal follows an unprecedented surge in visitors to the shrine, associated with spiritual leader Neem Karoli Baba. Rayal said the administration normally expects around 25,000 visitors a day at Kainchi Dham. During the long weekend beginning October 2, however, the daily footfall crossed 35,000. The extra visitors overwhelmed the road connecting Kainchi with Bhowali and Mukteshwar. Both the pilgrims and the locals use the same road to Kainchi, which also goes up to Mukteshwar, causing a traffic jam for hours, Rayal said. The congestion stretched through Bhimtal, Bhowali and Kainchi over the long weekend, with vehicles crawling for kilometres and journeys taking hours longer than usual. The administration is now pursuing both crowd management and additional road capacity. A key development discussed at the meeting was the proposed alternative route around Kainchi. Rayal said the Forest Department has now given the required permission for the 18-km Ratighat bypass, which will provide a more direct route towards Almora, Ranikhet and Kausani and help separate through traffic from the road leading to Kainchi. The bypass has received permission from the Forest Department, Rayal said. Earlier, the in-principle approval had been given. Now the practical permission on the ground has also come. Around eight kilometres of the bypass have already been hot-mixed, while work remains on roughly 10 kilometres. Rayal said the state government is currently considering a Rs 21-crore estimate for hot-mixing the remaining stretch. There is a discussion in the government today regarding the Rs 21-crore estimate for hot-mixing it, he said. Once that is approved, the road should become functional in four to six months. According to figures accessed by The Indian Express, 24.34 lakh people visited Kainchi Dham in the first six months of 2026, compared with around eight lakh visitors during the entire previous year. Rayal earlier attributed the latest surge partly to the end of the monsoon, when tourists who had avoided the hills because of rain and landslides began returning, and partly to the release of Hanuman Ansh, a film based on the life and teachings of Neem Karoli Baba.

articleTitle: In own state, ‘upset’ Fadnavis cites ‘pathetic’ school, hostel infra for protests

description: Directing questions at the officials, Fadnavis made his displeasure known at the meeting and said, "If schools and hostels are in such poor condition, agitation will happen."

articleTitle: 83-year-old Lonavala man held for ‘shooting dead’ grandson over property dispute
articleFeaturedImageAlt: grandfather kills grandson
description: Officers from Lonavala City Police Station reached the spot and initially registered the case as an accidental death.
body_raw: Lonavala city police have arrested an 83-year-old man for allegedly shooting dead his 33-year-old grandson, a lawyer, following a property dispute in Bhushi village, and then trying to pass off the killing as an accident. A case has been registered against five members of the family. The deceased has been identified as Advocate Abhay Manik Marathe. The accused, his grandfather Motiram Marathe, was arrested after police found inconsistencies in the familys version of events. Abhays father, Manik Marathe, is a former Lonavala municipal council corporator. The family owns Hotel Motiram in Bhushi village. Addressing a press conference on Tuesday, Superintendent of Police Sandeep Singh Gill said, Motiram Marathe holds a valid arms licence for a 12-bore gun, which he used for hunting. According to the family, the incident took place on Monday. They told police that Abhay was cleaning his grandfathers gun when the trigger was accidentally pulled and a bullet hit him in the chest. Officers from Lonavala City Police Station reached the spot and initially registered the case as an accidental death. However, police grew suspicious on inspecting the scene. The injury on Abhays chest, the bloodstains and the firearm itself did not appear to match the familys account. The body was sent to Sassoon Hospital for a post-mortem examination, and police consulted medical experts. Officers also questioned the Marathe family members, along with the manager and staff of the hotel. The inquiry revealed that Abhay and his grandfather had been involved in a property dispute. Motiram wanted to sell their land and distribute money among family members, however, Abhay had different plans for the land development, which led to the dispute, Gill said. Police said that the two had a heated argument and that the grandfather allegedly shot Abhay when the latter charged at him. Abhay was reportedly inside the hotel premises. Based on these findings, police registered a case against five people, including Motilal Marathe, and arrested him. Attempt to destroy evidence According to police, the family tried to cover up the crime after the shooting. CCTV cameras near the spot were allegedly removed, along with the DVR unit that stored the footage. Hotel staff were also allegedly threatened against speaking about the incident. Officials are now probing the property dispute within the Marathe family, the sequence of events after the shooting, and the attempts to destroy evidence, inspector Pramod Kshirsagar of the local crime branch said.

articleTitle: Between starlight and Antarctic ice — another neutrino is on its way
articleFeaturedImageAlt: physics, nobel, ice
description: Thanks to Nobel Prize winner Francis Halzen and his team, the ice is ready
body_raw: For an astronomer, light is the easy part Hold up a lens or a mirror and starlight is yours. Neutrinos are another matter. Born in the most violent places in the cosmos, these ghost-like particles pass through planets, people and most detectors almost without a trace. It took decades to turn a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice into a telescope for these deep-space messengers. This years Nobel Prize in Physics goes to the man who stayed with that hunt Francis Halzen, a Belgian-born physicist at the University of WisconsinMadison. Why chase a particle so hard to catch in the first place? You could see things in the universe you couldnt see any other way, Halzen once said in an interview. Neutrinos barely interact, so they escape from deep inside their sources while light gets stuck on the way out. Think of a journalist trying to reach the one official who was in the room where a major policy was made. The press conference is easy to attend that is astronomy with visible light. But the insider who knows what was really decided avoids reporters. Catching a neutrino is harder still. The gigantic IceCube Neutrino Observatory near the Amundsen-Scott South Pole station in Antarctica has lowered 86 cables into the ice, the deepest reaching almost 2.5 kilometers down. To place them, scientists had to melt holes in the ice with hot water. Each cable sports sixty sensitive light detectors, like beads strung on a thread. On rare occasions, a neutrino strikes a nucleus of an atom in the ice, and the collision generates high-energy particles. The resulting particles move faster than light travels in ice, and generate an eerie, bluish flash, much like a sonic boom of a supersonic jet. That glow, the signature of a far traveling neutrino, is what the sensors on the strings pick up. Such an instrument couldnt be built overnight. What Halzen himself once called a cute idea took smaller trials to hone the skill and show what a larger detector could potentially deliver. Conceived in the 1980s, the last cable in IceCube was dropped in 2010. Since then, it has been eavesdropping on far-away violent phenomena in the universe. Some strange galaxies, unlike our own Milky Way, host massive black holes that churn the gas in their cores and spew spectacular jets. These jets accelerate high energy particles called cosmic rays, which collide and produce neutrinos. These neutrinos point back to where cosmic rays are produced. The discoveries at IceCube have been helping astronomers to peek inside the core of these galaxies. In 2017, a single neutrino hurtled through the observatory, and its path indicated it was coming from the direction of the constellation Orion. Alerted astronomers worldwide swiveled their telescopes in that direction and found a blazar, a giant galaxy whose central black hole, weighing hundreds of millions of suns, spits out a jet aimed straight at Earth. The discovery gave a major boost to multi-messenger astronomy, where scientists use visible light, neutrinos, and gravitational waves to study the same cosmic event, pulling together the clues from all the light we cannot see. IceCube has also confirmed a prediction from the 1960s about how an antineutrino interacts with an electron. Halzen, the principal investigator of this unique venture, has long been drawn to astroparticle physics, the area of research that marries astronomy with particle physics. Born in 1944, he studied at KU Leuven, Belgium, where he completed his masters degree and PhD. Then, while working at CERN, Geneva, in early 1970s, he was invited to the University of Wisconsin-Madison, where he has been since. But IceCube was never a one-man project It is the work of an international collaboration of hundreds of scientists and engineers. Starlight can be caught with a mirror. Neutrinos take patience. IceCube received its first major expansion only this year, and physicists are already proposing a successor eight times its size. Somewhere out there, another neutrino is on its way. Thanks to Halzen and his team, the ice is ready. The writer, visiting professor, IISER Mohali, was an astrophysicist at the Raman Research Institute, Bengaluru

articleTitle: ‘Unrest, poverty brought them to India’: Court cuts jail term of 3 Bangladeshis
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Bangladeshi nationals illegal immigrants detention madras high court
description: The Madras High Court, while considering the sentence, noted their economic hardship, migration from Bangladesh for employment, daily-wage work and several years of residence in India.
body_raw: The Madras High Court has upheld the conviction of three Bangladeshi nationals for residing in the State without valid travel documents however, observing that the appellants, owing to the unrest in Bangladesh and the uncertainty of their future, came to India to sustain themselves and their families, it modified their fine-default sentence and ordered authorities to complete their deportation within 30 days. Justice N Nirmal Kumar was dealing with a plea of three Bangladeshi nationals challenging their conviction under the Foreigners Act, 2004. It is not in dispute that the appellants, owing to the unrest in Bangladesh and the uncertainty of their future, and being unemployed and impoverished, came in search of employment and livelihood to sustain themselves and their families. Admittedly, they are neither involved in nor convicted of any economic offence, nor have they enriched themselves so as to assume that they possess the means to pay the fine, the court said on September 28. The court further emphasised that the appellants had come to India in search of livelihood they had stayed in Tiruppur for quite some time, and the first and second accused had also given birth to two children. It noted that the appellants had also been employed in banian factories in Tiruppur on a daily-wage basis. Three Bangladeshi nationals arrested The case arose from the arrest of three Bangladeshi nationals by the Veerapandi Police in Tiruppur in February 2025. Police found them with two children at Iduvampalayam and, during inquiry, they admitted that they were Bangladeshi citizens who had entered India without valid passports, visas, or other travel documents. According to the accused, they had been living and working in Tiruppur for over six years and had twin sons born at Tiruppur Government Medical College Hospital in September 2023. They said they had migrated from Bangladesh because of political unrest, unemployment, and poverty and had come to India in search of livelihood. The police registered a case, and the prosecution examined six witnesses and produced 12 exhibits. The trial court convicted all three under the provisions of the Foreigners Act, 2004. It sentenced each to two years rigorous imprisonment and a Rs 10,000 fine, with three months simple imprisonment in default. They challenged the conviction before the high court. Appearing for the petitioners, advocates M Mohamed Saifulla and R Bakiyalakshmi argued that they had not committed any other offence, had lived peacefully in Tiruppur, and were willing to return to Bangladesh. They also questioned whether proper procedures had been followed regarding their detention and deportation. They stated that due to political unrest, unemployment, and poverty, they moved from Bangladesh to Tiruppur seeking employment for their livelihood. At the time of crossing the border post, they informed their entry. They are very poor Court The court held that the prosecution had established that the three appellants were Bangladeshi citizens. Their Bangladeshi national identitycitizenship documents and birth certificates were produced in evidence, and they had entered India without valid travel documents. The court found no reason to interfere with their conviction under the Foreigners Act, and confirmed the two-year rigorous imprisonment imposed by the trial court. They hold, to date, a Bangladesh voter ID and citizenship card. They are natural citizens living here and have also begotten two children for their livelihood and subsistence, they are living in Tiruppur to make earnings and livelihood. They are law-abiding citizens and have not come under any adverse notice from the law-enforcing authorities. Now they are willing to go back to their country, the court noted. However, while considering the sentence, the court took note of their economic hardship and circumstances. They had migrated from Bangladesh in search of employment, worked as daily-wage workers in Tiruppur, and had been living there for several years. Two children were also born to the first and second accused at a government hospital in Tiruppur. The court observed, There is no doubt that they are very poor, are seeking livelihood, have migrated in search of employment, and are in penury and unable to pay the fine amount. Considering their financial circumstances, the court reduced the default imprisonment for non-payment of the Rs 10,000 fine from three months to one week, while retaining the fine and two years rigorous imprisonment.

Head coach Gautam Gambhir lauded Agarkar and praised his conviction. Dear Ajit Bhai, an absolute honour to work with you. Those 3 ICC trophies are a testimony of your conviction Team first  Team ahead, always. I must say, History will be kinder to you. Thank you for everything. articleTitle: Internet rallies for Jaya Bachchan amid Kangana Ranaut’s dig over ‘Nahi Bataungi’ moment
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Jaya Bachchan
description: Jaya Bachchan went viral during an INDIA bloc protest in Delhi on October 6, 2026, after she pushed away a reporter’s microphone.
body_raw: Jaya Bachchan is once again in the headlines for her equation with the media. During the INDIA blocs protest over the functioning of the Election Commission, the Samajwadi Party MP and actor refused to comment on the issue that had prompted the opposition demonstration even as she was badgered by the reporter. Now, actor-politician Kangana Ranaut has taken a dig at her viral response. Sharing the video on her Instagram handle, Kangana wrote, When you sit on dharna so that you can make a point in front of the whole world but when they ask you what point you want to make? Jaya B ji. Nahi bataungi. What happened in the video? Jaya Bachchan went viral during an INDIA bloc protest in Delhi on October 6, 2026, after she pushed away a reporters microphone as he kept on asking her to respond even as she alleged that he was twisting the narrative. Members of the opposition INDIA bloc had marched towards the Election Commission of India in Delhi, demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar after Indian Express investigation that revealed objections by Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi to a declaration added to the online version of Form 6, the form used to enrol new voters. During the protest, a journalist questioned Jaya about a placard carried by fellow opposition members that appeared to refer to the Chief Election Commissioners office as the BJP office. Pointing to the placard being held by TMC MP Derek OBrien, the journalist asked, What is written on this? Jaya Bachchan repeatedly responded, Dont twist it. When the journalist said, I am not twisting anything, I am just asking what is written on it, Jaya sternly replied, Dont twist the matter. The reporter then asked, What is the matter? You please explain to me, prompting Jaya to simply push the microphone away. When the journalist questioned her again, Jaya said, Nahi bataungi. The reporter then asked, On what basis are you then saying that I have twisted the matter? Jaya responded, Whatever you asked Derek was twisted. She then walked away, choosing not to engage in the conversation any further. Derek, who was present throughout the exchange, also turned away. Jaya then laughed and said, I dont believe this. ALSO READ  Soundarya Rajinikanth says parents changing male-dominated dynamic at home My rocks during divorce Social media users hail Jaya Bachchan for her response The video quickly went viral, prompting a wave of reactions on social media. While Jaya has often faced criticism online over her interactions with the media, several users appeared to enjoy her blunt response this time around. Many users called her a Queen and Diva for her response. One user wrote, For once, we love you Jaya Ji, while another commented, Jaya is always iconic. Only celeb politician I like. Several others turned the exchange into memes, with one user suggesting, Say Nahi bataungi and move on. Another wrote, Waiting for new memes. Jaya had made headlines just days earlier when she was seen laughing out loud at a book launch event attended by her husband, Amitabh Bachchan, and writer Gulzar. In several videos from the event, Jaya was seen sharing a light-hearted moment with Gulzar, prompting social media users to say Yeh hasti bhi hai?.

description: UPSC Civil Services Mains Exam 2027: This week’s GS 2 answer practice explores the role of community participation in water governance and Legislative privileges. Check out our thought process.
body_raw: UPSC Essentialsbrings to you its initiative for the practice ofMains answer writing.It covers essential topics of static and dynamic parts of the UPSC Civil Services syllabus covered under various GS papers. This answer-writing practice is designed to help you as a value addition to your UPSC CSE Mains. Attempt todays answer writing on questions related to topics ofGS-2to check your progress. As we mark the 3rd anniversary of the UPSC Essentials magazine, we thank our readers for being part of this journey. Your trust, feedback and continued support have shaped the magazine and encouraged us to keep improving with every edition. Click Here to read the UPSC Essentials magazine for September 2026. Share your views and suggestions in the comment box or write to us at manas.srivastavaindianexpress.com. QUESTION 1 How can decentralisation and community participation improve the effectiveness and sustainability of water governance in India? QUESTION 2 Legislative privileges are intended to secure the effective functioning of legislatures, not to insulate them from public scrutiny. Discuss. QUESTION 1 How can decentralisation and community participation improve the effectiveness and sustainability of water governance in India? Relevance The question links with GS Paper 2 Governance, decentralisation, local self-government and participatory governance. It also provides scope to discuss cooperative federalism and multi-level governance in addressing water challenges. NoteThis is not a model UPSC answer. It only provides you with a thought process which you may incorporate into the answers. Introduction - Indias water challenge is multifaceted, encompassing not only infrastructure development but also governance, institutional capacity, and sustainable service delivery. - The Gujarat example demonstrates that water security improves when governance, infrastructure, and community ownership are pursued simultaneously. Body You may incorporate some of the following points in your answer Role of decentralisation and community participation - Water-related decisions can be decentralised to reflect local variables such as availability, quality, location, and household requirements. The notion of subsidiarity states that functions should be carried out at the lowest appropriate level. This strategy is used by Gujarats WASMO and other similar initiatives. - Institutions like Pani Samitis can help communities become active participants rather than passive beneficiaries. The Gujarat model demonstrates how local water governance institutions, with suitable infrastructure and external aid, may improve water conservation, harvesting, and recharge. - Decentralisation can improve operation and maintenance since local institutions are directly involved in water system management. This is especially critical as the task switches from simply providing tap connections to guaranteeing consistent, adequate, and dependable water service. - Community participation can assist ensure that taps are accompanied by steps to protect the underlying water source. Groundwater recharging, rainwater collection, and water supply must all be addressed simultaneously, rather than considering water provision as a standalone engineering project. - When local communities participate in planning and implementation, they can check service quality and continuity, as well as file grievances. This can help close the gap between administrative claims of infrastructure coverage and real service delivery on the ground. - Water availability and infrastructure requirements vary greatly by region. Local institutions can tailor responses to local hydrological and socioeconomic conditions rather than depending solely on centrally designed techniques. Conclusion - Effective water administration necessitates a shift from a centralized, infrastructure-centric strategy to participatory and decentralized service governance. Indias experience, particularly the Gujarat model and the developing Jal Jeevan Mission strategy, illustrates that infrastructure becomes more sustainable when people play an active role in planning, managing, and monitoring water systems. - Thus, decentralization can transform water governance from a government-provided function to a shared institutional and community duty. Sources From India to Global South, a Gujarat water-governance model, Many challenges of Jal Jeevan Mission Decentralisation is the only way ahead, Centre asks district collectors to regularly review Jal Jeevan Mission works, address gaps Points to Ponder What institutional mechanisms can facilitate effective participation in water management? What are the major challenges to decentralised water governance in India? Related Previous Year Question What are environmental pressure groups? Discuss their role in raising awareness, influencing policies and advocating for environmental protection in India. 2025 QUESTION 2 Legislative privileges are intended to secure the effective functioning of legislatures, not to insulate them from public scrutiny. Discuss. Relevance The question directly relates to GS Paper 2 Parliament and State Legislatures, constitutional provisions and legislative privileges. It helps to analyse the role of legislative privileges in preserving parliamentary functioning while protecting democratic scrutiny. NoteThis is not a model UPSC answer. It only provides you with a thought process which you may incorporate into the answers. Introduction - Legislative privileges are constitutional provisions designed to ensure that Parliament and state legislatures may carry out their tasks independently and effectively. - Articles 105 and 194 provide privileges and immunities to Parliament and State Legislatures respectively. However, these privileges are meant to facilitate legislative functioning, not create an unrestricted sphere of immunity from constitutional scrutiny or legitimate public criticism. Body You may incorporate some of the following points in your answer Why are legislative privileges necessary? - Privileges protect legislators from external interference and enable them to participate freely in legislative proceedings. Article 1051 provides freedom of speech in Parliament, subject to the Constitution and parliamentary rules corresponding protection exists under Article 194 for State Legislatures. - Collective privileges allow Houses to govern their proceedings and deal with conduct that disrupts their operation. - Immunities enable lawmakers to carry out their constitutional duties without fear of legal ramifications from valid legislative speech or voting. Why cant privileges be used as a barrier against scrutiny? - The Supreme Court must decide whether privileges under Articles 105 and 194 can supersede fundamental rights like free speech and expression under Article 191a. The position made before the Court is that privileges exist to defend the Houses operation rather than the reputations of MPs, governments, or ruling parties. - India adheres to constitutional supremacy rather than the model of unrestrained parliamentary authority. As a result, legislative privileges function within the constitutional framework and cannot automatically take precedence over fundamental rights. - The Supreme Courts jurisprudence has gradually acknowledged limits to legislative privilege. In Raja Ram Pal 2007, the Court determined that the exercise of parliamentary privilege is subject to judicial review. In Amarinder Singh 2010, it was determined that privilege could not be utilised to punish conduct unrelated to the operation of the House. - When privilege proceedings culminate in the arrest or imprisonment of citizens or journalists, Articles 14 and 21 are invoked alongside Article 19. The exercise of legislative power over personal liberty creates issues of fairness, due process, and arbitrariness. - A free press allows individuals to monitor legislative activity. The 2003 Tamil Nadu Assembly privilege event, which involved actions against journalists from The Hindu and Murasoli, exemplifies the conflict between legislative privilege and press freedom. The Supreme Court suspended the arrest warrants and referred serious constitutional matters related to Articles 1943 and 191a for review. Conclusion - Legislative privilege is a tool for protecting legislative democracy, not an end in itself. Its credibility is ultimately tied to the legislatures ability to function effectively. - A constitutional balance must consequently protect legislative authority while ensuring that privilege is not used to repress valid criticism, journalistic freedom, or fundamental rights. Such a balance strengthens, not diminishes, the authority of democratic institutions. Assess the reasons for the absence of legal codification of the parliamentary privileges. articleTitle: Man caught recording Bombay HC proceedings; fined, phone confiscated
articleFeaturedImageAlt: bombay high court video recording
description: The high court also noted that such recordings are "manipulated in ways unimaginable, and then distorted versions are posted on social media" and "in fact, it has become quite rampant."
body_raw: Noting incidents of court proceedings being recorded without permission, the Bombay High Court has ordered the confiscation of the mobile handset used and imposed a Rs 10,000 fine on a man after he was caught doing so. Emphasising that the incidents have been unfortunately on the rise, the Bombay High Court also noted that such recordings are manipulated in ways unimaginable, and then distorted versions are posted on social media and in fact, it has become quite rampant. A bench of Justices Girish S Kulkarni and Neela K Gokhale took suo motu on its own cognisance on October 5, noting that while the court was in session, around 1223 pm, a person sitting in the last row held a mobile phone, with its flash on. Suspecting he was recording court proceedings, the court staff, on the judges instructions, seized his phone and sent it for examination. The person, identified as Dilip Wagh, who works at the Education Inspectors office, was visiting the Government Pleader. He deleted the video recording after being caught. The video was later retrieved by the courts IT department. The HC noted that except for the HC registrys written permission, there was an express bar under HCs Rules to record court proceedings, which Wagh did not obtain, and he was fully aware of these basic expectations. There cannot be any objection for any member of the public to attend the Court and witness the Court proceedings, as they are open proceedings. However, certainly, restrictions on any member of the public to adhere to the rules and regulations governing the Court proceedings, when inside the Courtroom, need to be followed in letter and spirit, the HC noted. Thus, considering the seriousness, casualness and frequency of such instances happening, it is high time that actions as the law would mandate are taken by the Court, the order added. The judges stated they would be falling in our duty if they overlook the Rules by not taking any action. While the court accepted Waghs apology and did not initiate contempt proceedings, it ordered confiscation of the mobile handset, removal of all data with a registry panchanama, and its disposal as per legal procedures. He was also ordered to pay Rs 10,000 to the High Court Legal Services Authority within two weeks, and compliance was sought by October 19.

articleTitle: ‘Tried to kidnap me’: Nagaland woman pulled towards car by 3 men at Delhi 5-star hotel
articleFeaturedImageAlt: delhi crime
description: Police sources said the three men have been bound down and an FIR has been lodged in the case.
body_raw: Three men who allegedly harassed a woman from Nagaland and forcibly pulled her towards a Mercedes car in the parking lot of a five-star hotel in Chanakyapuri have been bound down by the Delhi Police, sources said. To be bound down means to be required to appear before an investigating officer on a given date. The incident took place around 3.15 am Sunday, police said. According to police officers, the three men were sitting in the car parked at the hotel and were playing loud music. As the woman and her friends came towards the parking lot, one of them objected to the music. When the woman moved towards the exit gate, one of the men sitting in the car pulled her hand towards the vehicle. As per the FIR registered in this case, the woman alleged that they were trying to kidnap her. The womans three male friends intervened, after which the men in the Mercedes allegedly started a brawl. When my friend came to save us, they beat him with hockey sticks and punched his face. When my two other friends came, they beat them with hockey sticks as well, the woman alleged in the FIR. One of the friends suffered injuries to his teeth., an officer said. The medico-legal case report of one of the victims friends cites swelling in the right hand. The accused allegedly fled from the spot in their car after police reached the location. The complainant had noted down the cars registration number, which helped investigators trace the men, police said. The three accused were booked at Chanakyapuri police station. The woman was taken to Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital, where she underwent a medical examination. Police said the case was registered on the basis of her complaint and the medical report. Police are examining CCTV camera footage from the hotel and other evidence to establish the sequence of events. The medical reports are also being examined to ascertain the injuries suffered by those involved, they said.

articleTitle: Paying Rs 5,000 by UPI after Oct 15? Who pays new charge and what RBI governor said today
articleFeaturedImageAlt: RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra
description: Starting October 15, select high-value UPI person-to-merchant transactions will attract an merchant discount rate (MDR) of 0.4%
body_raw: The National Payments Corporation of Indias NPCIs recent decision to introduce a merchant discount rate MDR on select Unified Payments Interface UPI transactions marks a significant shift in the economics of the countrys digital payments ecosystem. However, the Reserve Bank of Indias RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra has sought to make one thing clear - the new charge, according to him, is unlikely to dent the enormous scale of UPI. On UPI-MDR, a decision has already been taken, Malhotra said on Wednesday. As of now, we do not see any drop in UPI volumes, and I dont personally think that a small fee will have a major impact on the volumes. Starting October 15, select high-value UPI person-to-merchant P2M transactions will attract an MDR of 0.4. The charge will apply to transactions above Rs 2,000, with a cap of Rs 300 for transactions of Rs 75,000 and above. RBI repo rate news LIVE The crucial point, however, is where the burden falls. The MDR will be paid by merchants within the digital payment ecosystem, while consumers will not be charged. That distinction is important. UPI has become synonymous with frictionless digital payments, and any change to the cost structure of transactions inevitably raises questions about whether users and merchants will alter their behaviour. The RBI, at least for now, does not appear concerned that the introduction of a fee for certain transactions will undermine the platforms momentum. Growing volumes The latest numbers offer some support to that assessment. UPI transaction volumes grew 22.2 in the second quarter of 2026-27, although this was slower than the 24.2 growth recorded in the first quarter. While the central bank regulates the payment system, the government has created the legal framework. The current UPI MDR structure has been introduced by NPCI under that framework. The numbers point to continued expansion, but they also underline the scale of the challenge. UPI is not merely another payment mechanism. Its strength lies in its reach and volume, and the policy question is whether introducing MDR on a segment of transactions can coexist with that growth without altering the behaviour that has made UPI so pervasive. Malhotras argument is straightforward a small fee should not materially change volumes. But the real test begins after October 15, when the new framework will move from policy announcement to actual transactions. Bankers said the fact that consumers will not bear the charge directly could help limit any immediate impact on usage. Yet merchants are at the centre of the MDR framework, and the eventual effect on the digital payment ecosystem will depend on how they respond to the additional processing cost, they said. For now, the RBI is betting that UPIs scale and convenience will outweigh the impact of the new charge. The data shows that volumes continue to rise, even as the pace of growth has moderated. The coming months will reveal whether the RBIs confidence is justified. If UPI volumes remain resilient, the MDR may prove to be a limited adjustment to a rapidly expanding payments ecosystem. If growth weakens sharply, however, the decision could face tougher questions.

articleTitle: Implants ‘broke’ thrice after procedure, Punjab dentist to pay UK citizen Rs 79,000
articleFeaturedImageAlt: consumer commission dentist
description: The Punjab State Consumer Commission was hearing the dentist’s appeal against the district commission order directing him to refund Rs 64,000 spent on the dental implants and pay Rs 15,000 compensation.
body_raw: The Punjab State Consumer Commission has upheld a Rs 79,000 payout for a patient whose dental bridge allegedly broke three times after treatment by a Jalandhar-based dentist. While upholding the award of a district consumer commission, the state body did not buy the dentists argument that a person who spent a huge sum of money on dental implants would knowingly chew hard food that could harm his teeth. The Punjab State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission judicial member Harinderpal Singh Mahal and member Kiran Sibal were hearing an appeal filed by a Jalandhar dentist against an April 17, 2023 order of the District Consumer Commission, Jalandhar. The state commission, on September 28, noted the district commissions observation that it cannot be presumed that a person who has spent so much amount for fixing the implants would chew hard food knowingly fully well that it may cause harm to his teeth. The dispute began in March 2018 when the complainant, a UK resident, approached the dentist after his tooth bridge needed replacement. According to the complaint recorded in the order, the dentist advised two implants and a bridge costing Rs 64,000. After the complainant returned to the UK, the bridge became loose within about three months. Subsequent attempts to replace or repair it also failed. Bridge failed repeatedly According to the complainant, he was told after the first problem that the plastic crowns would have to be removed and replaced with stone crowns during his next visit to India. He returned in March 2019, but the replacement bridge broke in the middle after five months. He again approached the dentist and was advised to return the following year. In March 2020, another procedure was carried out, but the new bridge also failed and broke into two pieces. The complainant said he was again promised that the problem would be corrected on his next visit. He could not travel to India in 2021 because of the Covid-19 pandemic and eventually got a denture fitted by a dentist in the UK for 500, stated in the complaint to be equivalent to about Rs 50,000. The complainant claimed Rs 64,000 towards the implants, Rs 1,500 for X-ray and reception charges, Rs 10,000 in taxi fares and Rs 50,000 towards the replacement denture. The dentist disputed the complaint, saying the patient had been informed about the procedure and had signed a consent form. He said three implants had initially been advised at Rs 97,000, but the patient opted for two implants and an overhead bridge costing Rs 64,000. The dentist also contended that the bridge could have broken because the patient chewed hard or sticky food despite being advised against it. He said he had replaced the bridge without charging the patient and again advised him not to eat hard or sticky food. Commission rejects dentists plea The dentist argued that there was no defect in the implants and that it was the bridge that had broken. His counsel contended that any liability should therefore be limited to the cost of the bridge. The commission rejected the argument, noting that the record specifically mentioned charges for the dental implants but did not specify any separate amount charged for the bridge. It therefore found no basis to limit the liability as suggested by the dentist. The commission recorded that the bridge became loose about three months after the initial treatment, was replaced, and that a later porcelain-fused-to-metal bridge broke after five months before being replaced again. Finding no merit in the appeal, the bench dismissed it and upheld the district commissions direction to pay Rs 64,000 towards the amount spent on the implants and Rs 15,000 as compensation. The commission also directed that the Rs 39,500 deposited by the dentist while filing the appeal, along with any interest accrued, be remitted to the complainant after 45 days from the sending of certified copies of the order to the parties. Takeaway Consumers should keep treatment records, payment receipts, consent forms and communication with the dentist when undergoing costly dental treatment. If treatment repeatedly fails and a dispute arises over responsibility, these records can help establish what treatment was provided, what was paid for and what went wrong. Consumers facing similar grievances may contact the consumer helpline in their respective states Punjab helpline1800-425-1082 or dial the National Consumer Helpline at1915for assistance. articleTitle: Mathura gurukul students went inside water tank after foul smell, 4 dead
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Mathura ashram tragedy: 4 students die after inhaling toxic gas inside water tank
description: Police said two owners of Maharishi Panini Sanskrit Gurkulam have been taken into custody. A fifth student who also fell unconscious is stable
body_raw: Four students died after inhaling suspected poisonous gas inside an unused underground water tank at a gurukul in Mathuras Vrindavan late Tuesday night, when a group of students went into the tank to investigate a foul smell, police said. Two owners of Maharishi Panini Sanskrit Gurkulam have been taken into custody. The incident came to light after 11.30 pm. Mathura Senior Superintendent of Police SSP, Shlok Kumar, told The Indian Express that preliminary investigation so far has revealed that a group of students were cooking food on the ground floor of the ashram when a foul smell wafted out of the water tank nearby. The water tank, about 15 ft deep, was unused and was covered with a concrete lid. The SSP said the students initially tried to get rid of the smell by removing the small amount of water inside the tank with a bucket. One of the students then volunteered to go inside. He climbed down the stairs built into the tank but did not return or respond when the other students called out to him. Four others went down one after another in an attempt to bring him out. All of them fell unconscious, causing panic among other students waiting outside. Staff members and local residents then pulled all five students out of the tank, the SSP said. A police team had rushed to the gurukul by then. Policemen tried performing CPR and gave first aid to the students, but it did not help they were all rushed to the hospital. Four of the students - Manu Katare, 21, of Jabalpur Vishu and Aryan, 18, of Meerut and Kaushambi and Devansh, 17, of Vidisha - died during treatment in the early hours of Wednesday. The fifth student survived and is currently stable, Kumar said. SSP Kumar said they are waiting for families of the victims to file a complaint so they can register a case.

articleTitle: Delhi is India’s No. 2 concert market. So why are global artists skipping it?
articleFeaturedImageAlt: cold play
description: Organisers say state incentives, venue readiness, pollution, permissions and differences in audience behaviour are making cities beyond Delhi more attractive.
body_raw: In the past year, Delhi-NCR has seen a spate of mega concerts, from hip hop star Travis Scott and English singer-songwriter Ed Sheeran, and is set to host upcoming shows by Fred Again and Khalid. It is currently Indias second-largest concert market, accounting for nearly 17 of concerts and live events in the country - about half the share of Mumbai. Yet some international artists planning India tours are skipping the national capital altogether, choosing Mumbai and Bengaluru - and, in some cases, smaller cities such as Guwahati and Ahmedabad - instead. For instance, English rock band Gorillaz is heading to Guwahati, Bengaluru and Mumbai in January next year. Post Malone performed at Guwahati last year while Coldplay only did shows in Ahmedabad and Mumbai. Many other artists like Enrique Iglesias and John Mayer only did concerts in Mumbai. Guns N Roses is headed to Guwahati in November after Bengaluru. For organisers and industry executives, the choice of city is increasingly about more than just audience size. They pointed to several factors behind the decision, from state subsidies and audience spending patterns to concerns around womens safety and air pollution in Delhi. To be sure, the Delhi government has been pushing to strengthen the Capitals concert economy, seeking to attract major international and homegrown artists and the wider economic activity that comes with them. After it emerged that high stadium rentals were an issue, in October last year, the Sports Authority of India SAI made it cheaper to host events at its venues by 40-50. Cities compete for global artists Deepak Choudhary, managing director of the event company Eva Live, said different states are increasingly seeking to attract concerts through subsidies. Speaking about the Guns N Roses tour, he said, Mumbai, theyve already done. Then they are going to Bengaluru, which is an automatic number two. Subsequently, instead of Delhi, they are headed to Guwahati because Assam subsidised the cost. The state government supported in a large way through sponsorship, Chaudhary explained. In 2024, Canadian artist Bryan Adams had performed in Meghalaya. Both Meghalaya and Assam have concert tourism policies, which subsidise part of the cost of organising the concert and simplify related processes, in return of expected gains to the states economy. Naman Pugalia, Chief Business Officer, Live Events, BookMyShow, disagreed. What we are seeing is a very robust and continuous decentralisation of demand. Delhi continues to be a strong and important market, while these other cities have also shown endeavor and initiative. He added that this is the story of India. We are growing in all directions and we are going fast. But that does not mean Delhi is any less important, he said. Why putting on a show is harder in Delhi An industry executive argued that the condition of venue infrastructure is not good in Delhi and a lot of money is spent on refurbishment. For instance, the Indira Gandhi Indoor Stadium is a great venue. All it needs is to be maintained, have clean toilets, well educated and well spoken, helpful staff who have answers. When we go and ask them about the rigging capacity, they dont know. They dont have basic layouts on digital files, so we have to make even the basic models ourselves, the executive said. He added that coordinating with government agencies is much easier in other states. Mohit Bijlani, Founder of events management company Team Innovation, agreed. In a massive metropolitan capital like Delhi, traffic, venue accessibility, permissions and crowd movement can make large-scale shows more complicated to execute. Because it is the seat of administration, the capital naturally requires meticulous coordination across multiple regulatory bodies, which can add layers of administrative planning for a promoter, he said. Upneet Bhatia, who has worked as a project director for Ed Sheeran, Post Malone and Backstreet Boys, among other artists, said people dont come to a concert just for the artist. They come for the whole experience, she said. If they are spending so much money and time, venues need to have proper hygiene, free drinking water, a medical professional on ground, and support for traffic and parking. The industry executive also said air pollution is a key factor which weighs on the minds of artists and their teams. It is very important for an international singer to justify the ticket price by giving his heart and soul, and building a great production, right? So, they have to sing live. But they also need to be protective of their voice. This is why the artist could be a little apprehensive, she believes. Different cities, different concert crowds Organisers also feel that different audiences have different tastes. For instance, a rock band will prefer going to Bengaluru rather than Delhi, since it has a South-Indian based audience which is well travelled. Shillong will also be a strong option, since it is known as the rock and music capital of India. On the other hand, a Punjabi artist will prefer Delhi and may not be able to sell out in Bengaluru, Chaudhary of Eva Live said. He also said paying capacity is another consideration. If a person from Mumbai is willing to pay Rs 10,000 for a ticket, the audience will be willing to pay Rs 9,000 in Bangalore, and the same will be Rs 8,000 in Delhi. Another industry executive said Delhi also has a larger market for complimentary tickets, which can affect advance sales. In Bengaluru and Mumbai, if people know an artist or festival is coming, they are excited and buy tickets. In Delhi, people tend to wait until the last minute, hoping they will get a complimentary ticket from someone, the executive said.

articleTitle: How ‘Hanuman Ansh’ turned Neem Karoli Baba’s ‘quiet’ Kainchi Dham into a crowded, littered hotspot
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Hanuman Ansh Kainchi Dham
description: The surge has prompted concern among locals, with influencer Aishwarya Kandpal speaking out about the growing crowds, traffic, litter, and social media activity around the ashram.
body_raw: Kainchi Dham, the Uttarakhand ashram associated with Neem Karoli Baba, has seen a sharp rise in attention in recent months, with the site drawing larger crowds following the success of the film Hanuman Ansh, which has reportedly crossed Rs 400 crore worldwide. The surge has prompted concern among locals, with influencer Aishwarya Kandpal speaking out about the growing crowds, traffic, litter, and social media activity around the ashram. Kandpal, who identifies herself as a local and has a personal connection with Kainchi Dham, shared a lengthy note on Instagram urging visitors to be more mindful of the sites religious significance and its fragile mountain environment. Idk why Im posting this at almost midnight by maybe I just couldnt hold it back? As a local Im so enraged, so angry, so upset. If youre visiting - which I know A FEW HUNDREDS OF YOU ARE- read this before you go, she wrote in the caption. Explaining why she chose to speak about the issue, Kandpal began by acknowledging that the post was unlike the content she normally shares. She then described how dramatically Kainchi has changed from the place she remembers growing up around. I was at Kainchi two days ago. Most of you probably know it as Kainchi Dham - a name that the media and the internet latched onto post-2020, and then ran into overdrive after a recent feature film, she wrote. For us locals though, its always been the quiet, nondescript Kainchi. And the ashram of my Gurus, Maharajji and Siddhi Maa, she added. According to Kandpal, the site was once a relatively quiet place where locals would visit for prayer and religious activities. She also spoke about her familys longstanding association with the ashram. She said she has been fortunate enough to stay there and deliberately chose not to turn those personal experiences into social media content. My retreats, my experiences are personal, and I would like to keep it like that. Same goes for my parents and brother. Read the post   View this post on Instagram   A post shared by aishwarya kandpal  skincare  haircare indianskinblog   Both my parents have been serving at the ashram for years, and post-retirement, been spending a considerable part of the year staying within the sanctum sanctorum, helping with the ashrams day-to-day activities and being a part of the management. Their visits, however, much like those of scores of other locals, have become increasingly difficult, Kandpal said. Sacred place not meant to hold so many people Kandpal described roads packed with vehicles and constant honking, saying that her father, who is over 65, gets migraines from the noise. However, she stressed that her concern goes beyond the inconvenience caused to her family. Its about the ecology of a sacred place that wasnt exactly meant to hold so many people. According to her, the change is visible across the area, from roadside waste to the rapid growth of shops and traffic. The constant honking leaves birds and animals disturbed. The sides of the roads are lined with plastic bottles, wrappers, cigarette butts-you name it The whole area suddenly has a sea of new shops selling religious artifacts and the flood of people doesnt seem to end. Everyones scrambling, everyones in a rush. Theres pollution, extreme congestion, endless selfies and endless litter. Inside the ashram, Kandpal said she has also noticed visitors ignoring restrictions on photography and filming. I dont remember it being like this at all. And then you enter the ashram and see people doing exactly what theyve been asked to not do Phones out, cameras rolling, people filming themselves inside the premises and vlogging loudly on mics You cannot do that. Kandpal pointed out that photography, filming, and excessive noise are prohibited on the premises. Youre disturbing the sanctity of a hill thats been the tapobhumi of several revered saints since pre-independence times. Theres a strict no-photography, no noise, no film rule. For a reason. Kandpal also recalled what she described as the understated nature of the ashram and the teachings associated with Maharajji and Maa. Maharajji and Maa were always against any kind of lavish show of wealth Cellphones didnt exist for a long time so naturally they werent part of the ruckus. But photography, loud noise, donations, camps, flashy visits from VIPs or ministers were all STRCITLY prohibited in the ashram and still are, she said. The simplicity was a CHOICE. Precisely why the whole culture of coming here, filming everything, putting it online, turning every visit into content feels so completely at odds with the place. Concerns extend to surrounding hills Kandpals concerns also extend to the surrounding hills, where she said the increase in vehicles and visitors is putting additional pressure on the local environment. And then there are the mountains. There are cars and taxis backed up for miles, people honking constantly, bikes revving, trying to squeeze through whatever little space is left. Our fragile hills arent meant to handle so many people and so much litter left in their wake. No points for guessing how this leaves the birds and animals in the area completely, irrevocably disturbed. And I know this probably sounds like Im asking people to not come. Im not, she added. Kandpal clarified that she was not against people visiting Kainchi Dham. Instead, she said she wanted visitors to experience the place with the same sense of quiet and simplicity that she remembers from her childhood. Because firstly, I dont think I have any right to do that. Secondly, God belongs to everyone. And thirdly, its heartening that so many people have discovered the grace of this tiny ashram. So you shouldnt have to NOT come here. I ever so SIMPLY want you to experience the Kainchi I grew up around - quiet, nondescript, no frills and miles away from the prying eyes of the media and the internet, she said. Kandpal ended her post with a request for visitors to make small changes to their behaviour while travelling to and visiting the ashram. So maybe, just maybe Leave the phone on silent for a few, leave it in your bag, come in a group instead of taking five cars, keep the honking to a minimum, take your plastic back with you, and once you enter the ashram, remember why you came here, she said. The post has gained significant attention, with several users sharing similar experiences visiting Kainchi Dham and other spiritual destinations. One more thing to add. People must not visit a pilgrimage or ashram just because their a buzz around it - a famous person endorsed it or their is a superhit movie related to that place .people must visit ashrams or temples or sacred places only when they have an inner calling to visit . And people who are actually spiritual know the fact that God and his grace are present everywhere and every being , they just need to be a good person  not to show off . Visiting such places brings peace and calm but finding God and receiving his grace is a totally different thing, an Instagram user wrote. Another user compared the situation with Kasar Devi, saying, You said it so well. I recently went to kasar Devi and can understand what you are saying. The only solution to this problem is banning phones and cameras completely and you will see the rush dropping by 80. I pray for nature. A third user wrote, I am from Rudrapur and i have to think 10 times when i want to go there now.. its so much crowded now.. I miss the old Kainchi dham.. It was so peaceful few years back.

articleTitle: Custodial death compensation, Rs 80,000 for students in Mumbai – Fadnavis Cabinet’s key decisions
articleFeaturedImageAlt: devendra fadnavis cabinet decisions
description: Students studying in Mumbai city, Mumbai suburban, Navi Mumbai, Thane, Pune, Pimpri-Chinchwad and Nagpur will now receive Rs 80,000 a year
body_raw: The Maharashtra Cabinet has approved a series of measures covering student welfare, police custody deaths, traditional occupations and higher education, including higher annual assistance for Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe students, a compensation policy for deaths in police custody and an increase in the royalty-free minor mineral extraction limit for the Wadar community from 200 to 500 brass a year. Under the Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar Swadhar Scheme, annual assistance for SC and Nav-Buddhist students who are eligible for government hostels but do not get admission has been increased. Students studying in Mumbai city, Mumbai suburban, Navi Mumbai, Thane, Pune, Pimpri-Chinchwad and Nagpur will now receive Rs 80,000 a year - Rs 42,000 as food allowance, Rs 28,000 for accommodation and Rs 10,000 as subsistence allowance. The annual assistance will be Rs 68,000 for students studying in other divisional headquarters and C-class municipal corporation areas. Students studying at other district headquarters, and in institutions within five kilometres of municipal corporation limits, will receive Rs 57,000 a year - Rs 32,000 for food, Rs 17,000 for accommodation and Rs 8,000 as subsistence allowance. Those studying attaluka headquarters have been fixed at Rs 50,000. Students pursuing medical and engineering courses will additionally get Rs 8,000 a year, while those pursuing other courses will receive Rs 4,000. Rs 5 lakh compensation for custodial deaths The Cabinet approved a policy to provide compensation to the next of kin in cases where a person dies in police custody and it is established that the death was caused by assault, torture or coercion by police personnel. The compensation in such cases will be Rs 5 lakh. The policy also provides Rs 2 lakh for permanent disability of less than 50 per cent caused by physical or mental torture in custody, and Rs 4 lakh where the disability is 50 per cent or more. Higher assistance under Swayam scheme For ST students who do not get admission to government hostels, the Cabinet approved revised assistance under the Pandit Deendayal Upadhyay Swayam Scheme. Students studying in Mumbai city, Mumbai suburban, Navi Mumbai, Thane, Pune, Pimpri-Chinchwad and Nagpur will now receive Rs 80,000 a year, up from Rs 60,000. At other divisional headquarters and C-class municipal corporation areas, the assistance has been raised to Rs 68,000 from Rs 51,000. For students at other district headquarters, it will be Rs 57,000. At other locations, students will receive Rs 50,000. Medical and engineering students will get an additional Rs 8,000 a year for educational material, while students in other disciplines will receive Rs 4,000.

articleTitle: Vijay Deverakonda says Rashmika Mandanna tells him ‘I love you’ 10-15 times a day: ‘More mature’
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Vijay Deverakonda and Rashmika Mandanna have opened up about the importance of expressing love in a relationship.
description: Vijay Deverakonda and Rashmika Mandanna opened up about love, marriage and the importance of expressing feelings in their relationship during a podcast with Prakhar Gupta.
body_raw: Vijay Deverakonda and Rashmika Mandanna recently opened up about their bond, their marriage and how their understanding of love has evolved over the years. The couple also shared how little efforts keep a relationship going. DISCLAIMERThis article is based on information from the public domain andor the experts we spoke to. In a podcast with Prakhar Gupta, calling Rashmika the more mature one, Vijay says, Rashmika is more mature when it comes to relationships. Look at how shes talking. She makes sure she tells me I love you at least 10-15 times a day, and she tells me that its important for me to express it too. I constantly feel it, but I shouldnt think, Okay, she knows it, so I dont need to say it.   View this post on Instagram   A post shared by Rashmika Mandanna rashmikamandanna Why is it important to express love Most people assume the person they love already knows it. They have shown up, stayed, and handled the practical things, so surely the feeling is obvious. That assumption is where a lot of quiet distance begins, because as Dr Chandni Tugnait, MD A.M Psychotherapist, Life Alchemist, Coach  Healer, Founder  Director, Gateway of Healing says, love that is felt but never said often goes unnoticed by the very person it is meant for. She also explains why it is necessary to express feelings instead of assuming the other person already knows. Unsaid love gets misread A partner cannot see whats inside your head, and everyday acts of care are easy to read as habit or duty. Saying it plainly removes the guesswork and turns a feeling the other person had into something they can actually hold onto. It calms the background worry Many people carry a faint, constant question about whether they are still wanted. Hearing love expressed regularly answers that question before it grows, which tends to lower stress and make both people feel safer, including the one saying it, since voicing a feeling also strengthens it. It stops the relationship coasting In long relationships, affection is usually the first thing to be said less often, simply because life gets busy and the words start to feel unnecessary. Small, regular expressions work like maintenance, keeping two people connected instead of running on autopilot. It fills a quiet gap In many Indian households, love is shown through food, favours, and quiet sacrifice rather than words, and that language is real. Saying it aloud does not replace those acts, it simply makes sure the feeling behind them is actually heard. None of this means that the number of times matters most. Words work only when actions back them, and honesty counts more than frequency. But a feeling spoken at the right moment often does what months of silent effort cannot, which is to leave no room for doubt, she adds. The importance of physical touch As conversation flowed, Rashmika and Vijay kept brushing their feet against each other. That is when Vijay asks Rashmika what the most romantic thing that he has done for her is. Immediately, Prakhar Gupta replies, First of all, what youre doing right now. However, that was normal for the duo. This goes on 24x7, they say. Vijay later says, Some physical touch should always be there. That is one part of it. Rashmika also agrees with him. She says, I feel like we just live in a very romantic world, so. To this, Vijay adds, Maybe what is romantic for you is normal for us. Their upcoming movie Vijay Deverakonda and Rashmika Mandanna aregearing up for the release of their period dramaRanabaali, markinganother on-screen reunion for the actors. Directed by Rahul Sankrityan and produced by Naveen Yerneni and Y Ravi Shankar under the banner of Mythri Movie Makers, the period action drama is scheduled to release in theatres worldwide on October 16.
