articleTitle: Ahmedabad bridge meant to ease traffic ends up worsening it
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation, Railway Overbridge project at Makarba, Makarba, Makarba Railway Overbridge, Makarba Railway Overbridge project, Ahmedabad news, Gujarat news, Indian express, current affairs
description: The Makarba railway overbridge that CM Bhupendra Patel inaugurated on Sept 24 lands smack at a junction on Corporate Road. The civic body has demanded an explanation from the design consultant and is scrambling to find immediate solutions to the traffic chaos that has ensued.
body_raw: The Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation AMC has issued a show-cause notice to a design consultant firm involved in a railway overbridge project at Makarba that has caused traffic chaos, within two weeks of its inauguration. This traffic congestion in the rapidly growing commercial and residential area in southwestern Ahmedabad has forced the civic body to widen the connecting road to resolve the problem, and to implement immediate traffic solutions. The firm, Ahmedabad-based DELF Consulting Engineers India Pvt Ltd., is an extension of DELF-South Africa, according to its website. The company was the design consultant for the railway overbridge that Chief Minister Bhupendra Patel inaugurated on September 24 under the Phatak-mukt Bharat Abhiyaan, a campaign to free roads from railway level crossings. However, the four-lane bridge, which was meant to ease traffic snarls caused by the closure of the gates of Level Crossing 24 on the Ahmedabad-Botad broad gauge section of Western Railway, lands at a junction on Corporate Road-which has resulted in congestion and traffic chaos on the roads that connect to the Sarkhej-Gandhinagar Highway. AMC has instructed the projects design consultant, DELF Consulting Engineers India Pvt Ltd, to conduct a technical study of the current traffic situation and submit a detailed report, Dinesh Gaurav, Deputy Municipal Commissioner, Roads and Building Department, said. He said the design consultant had been instructed to analyse the root causes of the current traffic congestion and traffic flow patterns, and to submit a detailed report outlining both immediate corrective measures for the current situation and long-term solutions to permanently resolve the traffic issues. Gaurav said the design firm has been asked to explain the technical reasons behind the situation, and to compare the traffic flow now with the time when the study was conducted. Work on the bridge began in 2023. The show-cause notice says, The bridge lands in close proximity to the Corporate Road junction, leaving inadequate length for merging, weaving and dispersal of traffic. Based on the findings of the technical study and the clarifications provided by the design consultant, an appropriate technical evaluation will be carried out, and necessary further action would be taken, Gaurav said. Meanwhile, the AMC has implemented a capsule design layout to streamline traffic flow and reduce congestion at this point. Also,.AMC has undertaken the widening of the existing road from Corporate Crossroads to SG Highway to its full width. Efforts are underway to ensure that traffic flow on this route improves significantly upon the completion of this work, Gaurav said.

articleTitle: 2026 Physics Nobel: The science of ‘neutrinos’, ‘ghost’ particles that can reveal universe’s mysteries
articleFeaturedImageAlt: 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics, Nobel Prize in Physics 2026, Francis Halzen, IceCube Neutrino Observatory, high-energy neutrinos, astrophysical origin neutrinos, Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, University of Wisconsin Madison, South Pole ice neutrino tracking, cosmic particles discovery, physics Nobel winner 2026, Francis Halzen Nobel Prize, Nobel Physics Prize 2026, Francis Halzen, IceCube Neutrino Observatory, high-energy neutrinos, astrophysical neutrinos, Nobel Prize Physics winner 2026, neutrino discovery, Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, University of Wisconsin, South Pole neutrino observatory, 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics, Nobel Prize in Physics 2026, Francis Halzen, IceCube Neutrino Observatory, high-energy neutrinos, astrophysical origin neutrinos, Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, University of Wisconsin Madison, South Pole ice neutrino tracking, cosmic particles discovery, physics Nobel winner 2026, Francis Halzen Nobel Prize, Nobel Physics Prize 2026, Francis Halzen, IceCube Neutrino Observatory, high-energy neutrinos, astrophysical neutrinos, Nobel Prize Physics winner 2026, neutrino discovery, Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, University of Wisconsin, South Pole neutrino observatory
description: Francis Halzen, who was awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics, found a new way to study neutrinos — by turning a block of ice under the Antarctic into a detector for these tiny, elusive particles
body_raw: Neutrinos, very small sub-atomic particles produced mainly in nuclear reactions in stars, are among the most abundant particles in the universe, second only to photons or light particles. And they can reveal a huge amount of new information about the universe. The problem has been that they are extremely difficult to detect, the reason they are often described as ghost particles. The quest to detect neutrinos, and attempts to study them, have already led to several Nobel Prize wins. Another one was added on Tuesday, with the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics being awarded to Francis Halzen, a Belgian-American scientist who designed an elaborate set-up under ice sheets in Antarctica to detect these elusive particles. The IceCube facility in Antarctica is not the first observatory to detect neutrinos. Neutrinos were first proposed in the 1930s and first detected in the 1950s. Several observatories around the world are dedicated to detecting and studying these particles. Studying distant space What the IceCube facility managed to do was something unique. It was successful in detecting a special variety of high-energy neutrinos that was coming from far away in space. Till now, only those neutrinos that originated in the close vicinity of the Earth, primarily being produced in the Sun, were being detected. Most of the neutrinos passing through the Earth are produced in the nuclear processes inside the Sun. For scientists, the detection of extra-galactic neutrinos has opened a new source of information about the universe. Initially, visible light was the only tool available to scientists to study the cosmic phenomena. Then, detectors were developed for the full electromagnetic spectrum of radiation and for cosmic rays. The detection of gravitational waves in 2015 opened an entirely new window for scientists looking at the universe. Extra-galactic neutrinos add another dimension of possibilities. Together these different kinds of signals enable what is called multi-messenger astronomy, the ability to study the same cosmic event using different kinds of signals, said D Indumathi, a scientist at the Bengaluru-based Indian Institute of Astrophysics who was formerly associated with Indias effort to build a neutrino detector. Shy particles The reason neutrinos are so difficult to detect is that they have an extremely low propensity to interact with matter. The Nobel Prize committee described them as the shyest particle. They simply pass through very dense regions of matter without any disturbance. A very common example often cited is the fact that nearly 65 billion neutrinos pass through human finger nails every second without anyone ever noticing. Because they are also electrically neutral, they do not respond to electromagnetic fields the way charged particles do. The detections happen on the very rare occasions that they do interact with matter. That happens to, maybe, one in billions or trillions of neutrinos. That is why neutrino observatories the world over are very large facilities, built in extremely isolated, often underground locations, that maximise the chances of interaction and minimise noise. The elusive nature of neutrinos is also what makes them particularly interesting to study. They pass through regions of cosmic space that other signals may never be able to cross. Very dense regions in space, for example, can absorb or scatter all electromagnetic radiations, but neutrinos simply flow through. They can thus reveal processes happening within or beyond that dense region, which are otherwise inaccessible to scientists. The IceCube facility The 82-year-old Halzen, who had been studying cosmic rays since the 1960s, came to know of the attempts of Soviet researchers to build a neutrino detector in Antarctica, a press release from the Nobel Prize committee said. When a neutrino collides with an atomic nucleus in the ice, it creates an electric spark. This produces radio waves which could be detected using radio antennas. Halzen thought of a slightly different idea. He realised that light sensors could be installed in glacier ice. These sensors could produce flashes of light from collisions of neutrinos with the nucleus of ice atoms. The area around the South Pole was a favourable location. It was isolated and, at significant depths, there was a lot of darkness with no disturbance from other radiations or signals. He discussed his ideas with some of his colleagues and did most of the theoretical work on designing an observatory deep below the ice-sheets. IceCube is one cubic kilometer of ice equipped with over 5,000 light sensors on long cables, along with an overground facility where signals are collected. On the rare occasion when the neutrino interacts with an atomic nucleus of ice, a charged particle is produced. If that charged particle travels faster than the speed of light in ice, it produces a faint glow. From the characteristics of this glow, scientists are able to reconstruct the energy and direction of the neutrino involved in the collision. This exquisite set-up became operational in 2011. By that time, it had already recorded a couple of events that suggested the involvement of extra-galactic neutrinos. In 2013, the observatory presented the first evidence of having detected very high-energy neutrinos. Since then several such incidents have been recorded and verified. Its a very special detector and the work that Halzen has done is really very exciting. It has opened new avenues for astronomy and astrophysics, said Naba K Mondal, former project director of India-based Neutrino Observatory INO, a much-delayed effort to build a neutrino detector in India. In neutrino research circles, this award to Halzen was expected for a few years. INO was supposed to be located initially in Kerala and then in Tamil Nadu but ran into opposition from local and political groups over land acquisition and environmental grounds. A new location is yet to be finalised.

articleTitle: Three with Bhatti links held in J&K, one in Punjab; items ‘drone-dropped from Pakistan’ seized
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Narcotics 'drone-dropped from Pak', four with Shahzad Bhatti links held
description: Officials said the Pakistani gangster used to send them consignments of arms, ammunition and narcotics through drone. The items were supposed to be delivered to members of the module in Punjab, they said.
body_raw: The Jammu  Kashmir Police on Tuesday claimed to have arrested four people, including a Punjab resident, for allegedly being members of a cross-border narco-terror module with links in Pakistan. Police claimed the accused had links with Pakistan-based gangster Shahzad Bhatti. The arrested persons included two residents of Talhar, both called Ajay Kumar who went by the aliases Rabb and Sam, respectively, and one Rahul from Treva. Police claimed they have seized an Italian-made Bretta pistol along with two magazines and four live rounds, besides 500 grams of heroin and opium each from them. The seized items were reportedly dropped by drone from Pakistan, a police official said. Police said all three accused are in their early 20s and are drug addicts. Following their interrogation, a man called Jaganpreet Randhawa alias Jaggi was arrested from Punjab. The lid was taken off the module after a police party apprehended Rabb and Rahul on October 3 and seized a pistol along with ammunition and nearly 500 grams of heroin. On their disclosure during preliminary questioning, police nabbed Sam and seized nearly 500 grams of opium from him, officials said. Shahzad Bhatti link Officials said that the accused had links with Bhatti, a Pakistani handler operating under the patronage of ISI, who used to send them consignments of arms, ammunition and narcotics through drone from across the international border for further delivery to members of the module in Punjab. During questioning, they admitted having received two drone-droppings - the first one containing nearly half-a-dozen pistols a few months ago. While delivering that consignment to some people who had come to the region from Punjab, Rahul had kept one of the pistols for himself, which later led to his arrest, a police official said. The second drone-dropping, this time containing narcotics, was received a few days ago, which the accused had buried near a tubewell to avoid detection, police added. A case has been registered under relevant sections, and further investigation is in progress to unearth a wider network and members of the cross border narco-terror module. Security agencies have already raised concern over the use of drones by terrorist handlers and cross-border smugglers in Pakistan to send weapons and narcotics into Jammu and Kashmir. The agencies, in a massive pre-Independence Day operation launched simultaneously across 14 states, detained nearly 250 people allegedly linked to the Bhatti network. Arms, grenades and surveillance material were collected from them. The operation followed intelligence inputs, warning of attempts by terror operatives of strikes ahead of I-Day celebrations.

articleTitle: Denied boarding on Kochi-Abu Dhabi flight, mother and child wins Rs 70,287 payout
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Airlines boarding consumer flight
description: The commission held that the airline's failure to transport the complainants to the destination without any reason amounted to a shortcoming and inadequacy in the service.
body_raw: A Kerala consumer commission has directed an airline to pay Rs 70,287 to a mother and her minor son after they were allegedly denied boarding on a confirmed Kochi-Abu Dhabi flight and had to purchase fresh tickets. President CT Sabu and member Ram Mohan R observed that the complainant had to manage the minor child, rearrange their travel at short notice, undertake an additional journey and were constrained to pay a higher amount for the second ticket. The fact that the 2nd complainant was a child of approximately three years at the time makes the inconvenience and hardship more significant. The 1st complainant had to manage the minor child, rearrange their travel at short notice and undertake an additional journey between Sharjah and Abu Dhabi. Also constrained to pay a higher amount for the second ticket to Sharjah, the order read. Boarding denied The complainant said that she had booked flight tickets to travel from Kochi to Abu Dhabi on 11 February 2021, paying Rs 20,287. It was alleged that they had valid travel documents and were eligible to travel to Abu Dhabi under the travel guidelines applicable at the time, but were denied permission to board the flight. The complainant alleged that they were then compelled to purchase fresh tickets from Kochi to Sharjah for which they paid Rs 29,510. It was further stated that since Abu Dhabi was their intended destination, the mother and child had to undertake an additional journey from Sharjah to Abu Dhabi after landing there. The complainant said that the airline neither provided a satisfactory justification for denying boarding nor refunded the original KochiAbu Dhabi airfare. The airline did not appear before the commission despite being served notice and was proceeded against ex-parte. The commission said that if boarding had been denied because of any lawful restriction, failure to meet mandatory travel requirements or any other valid reason attributable to the complainants, the airline was required to disclose and establish the same. However, no such explanation or evidence was placed before it. The commission held that the airlines failure to transport the complainants to the contracted destination, without establishing a legally sustainable reason, followed by collection of a further amount for travel to a different destination, amounted to a shortcoming and inadequacy in the service. The commission thus directed the airline to refund the original airfare of Rs 20,287. It also awarded Rs 40,000 as compensation for deficiency in service, mental agony, inconvenience and hardship, and Rs 10,000 towards proceedings costs. Takeaway An airline that denies boarding on a confirmed ticket must have a legally sustainable reason and cannot retain the fare for a journey it failed to provide. Passengers can seek a refund and compensation for the resulting hardship. For consumer-related grievances, individuals may contact the consumer helpline in their respective states and union territories Kerala 1800-425-1550 or call the National Consumer Helpline on 1915 for assistance.

articleTitle: Rajasthan smuggler began new life in Madhya Pradesh as furniture trader. Then police closed in
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Rajasthan smuggler began new life in MP as furniture trader. Then police closed in
description: After he was named a wanted drug smuggler, Vishna Ram stayed at different locations in Rajasthan, including rented accommodation in Jodhpur and houses of relatives.
body_raw: A wanted drug smuggler from Barmer, who has been evading arrest for nearly two years, was arrested by the Anti-Narcotics Task Force ANTF from Mandsaur in Madhya Pradesh. The accused, identified as 32-year-old Vishna Ram, son of Madaram, a resident of Kudla in Barmer, was carrying a reward of Rs 1 lakh. Police said he had changed his identity and had been running a furniture business in Madhya Pradesh to avoid arrest. According to police, Vishna Ram had been involved in criminal activities for around 12 years and has over 18 cases including those under the NDPS Act, attempt to murder, assault, Arms Act, theft and fraud, registered against him in different police stations of Rajasthan. ANTF Inspector General Vikas Kumar said, Vishna Ram had studied up to Class 12 and initially worked as a driver. He later came into contact with drug smugglers while working as a labourer. His grandfather was addicted to poppy husk, and Vishna Ram initially began procuring small quantities for him. He subsequently came into contact with smugglers in Neemuch and entered the drug trade himself. Over the years, he allegedly established links with smugglers in Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Haryana and supplied drugs in the Marwar region. Police said he eventually became a key link in the trafficking network operating between Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan, police said. After he was named a wanted drug smuggler, Vishna Ram stayed at different locations in Rajasthan, including rented accommodation in Jodhpur and houses of relatives. With repeated police raids making it difficult for him to remain in the state, he eventually shifted to Madhya Pradesh, which he believed would be a safer place to hide. There, he started a furniture business and began living like an ordinary businessman to conceal his past. However, the ANTF continued tracking him. The breakthrough Police officials said the breakthrough came after information was received that Vishna Ram was running a furniture business in Madhya Pradesh and had called artisans from Jodhpur to work. The ANTF team began monitoring the movement of the artisans and followed the trail to Umaria village under the Pipliy Mandi police station area of Mandsaur district. When the team reached the location, Vishna Ram was allegedly partying with his friends and some of the artisans at the house of his smuggler associates uncle. The premises were surrounded and Vishna Ram was arrested.

articleTitle: From ‘chalta hai’ to ‘badal sakta hai’, changing the way India thinks
articleFeaturedImageAlt: The journey from ‘chalta hai’ to ‘badal sakta hai’
description: If the aim is to become ‘Viksit Bharat’ by 2047, this is the mindset to be cultivated
body_raw: Prime Minister Narendra Modi belongs to a rare breed of people who refuse to accept inherited challenges. He believes, and his actions show, that no problem in public life is too difficult to solve. I distinctly remember an Independence Day address in which he said that India must move away from the chalta hai attitude towards a badal sakta hai attitude. I have known him first as a colleague in the party and later in the government. For those of us who worked in the BJP for decades, Article 370 and Ram Janmabhoomi were matters of profound conviction, for which we made sacrifices. But I would be honest to admit that there were moments when even some of our own karyakartas doubted whether they would see these issues resolved in their lifetime. Article 370, described in the Constitution as a temporary provision, had come to be seen as virtually impossible to abrogate. I had the privilege of presiding over the Rajya Sabha when the historic legislation relating to its abrogation was passed. The Ram Janmabhoomi journey was much longer. Generations had lived with the hope that one day a grand temple would stand at the birthplace of Prabhu Shri Ram. On January 22, 2024, that hope became a reality. Modi became Gujarat Chief Minister a few months after the state had been hit by a terrible earthquake. Kutch, already a region beset by great difficulties, had suffered severe losses. Modi understood that the first task was to restore confidence. He spent his first Diwali as CM with the areas earthquake-affected families. Over the years, his policies helped Kutch reinvent itself, and it came to be known for its tourism potential, industrial growth and agricultural achievements. Water presented another seemingly permanent challenge to Gujarat. The Sardar Sarovar Project, conceived decades earlier, was mired in complications. Modi pursued it and saw to it that the dam reached completion and Narmada water travelled to water-scarce parts of Gujarat. Other, smaller structures, including check dams, made water conservation a mass movement and helped Gujarats farmers achieve remarkable results. Modi became PM at a time when India had been labelled one of the Fragile Five economies and its banking system was burdened with serious problems. He initiated a process of resolving these challenges through measures including the Asset Quality Review, banking reforms and the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code. India went on to become the fastest-growing major economy in the world. Many believed that the political consensus required for the GST would prove elusive. Yet it became possible because Modi was willing to invest political capital and see the reform through. Today, India is a leader in digital payments. Technology was not a challenge. The seemingly impossible task was to persuade crores across cities, villages, generations and income groups to change a deeply ingrained habit. Experienced political leaders asked how a street vendor could be brought into a digital payments ecosystem. PM Modi made that transformation possible. Poverty was another problem India had come to accept as permanent. Today, 25 crore Indians have moved out of multidimensional poverty. This happened through the painstaking work of creating a broad safety net and then giving the poor the means - bank accounts, direct benefit transfers, housing, sanitation, electricity, cooking gas, food security, health insurance and economic opportunities - to move out of poverty. For decades, Naxalism cost our nation thousands of lives. Through a twin approach of security and development, it has now been brought to an end. It is not that every problem has disappeared. But Modi has ensured that the assumption of helplessness in the face of problems has disappeared. During the pandemic, he brought the nation together. The Indian economy bounced back faster than many other major nations. The West Asia crisis brought another set of challenges involving energy security, shipping and trade. Indias approach, involving government and society, has been mature and responsible. The BJP was once branded as a party restricted to certain areas and social constituencies. PM Modi worked assiduously to change this perception. The BJPs growth in the Northeast and East India, and its deepening support among poor, rural and marginalised sections, have changed the countrys political map. For those who have watched his journey closely, it is clear that Narendra Modi begins by asking what the nation needs, and then works to create the circumstances to deliver it. This mindset is extremely important for a country that wants to become Viksit Bharat by 2047. The writer is former vice president of India

articleTitle: Why Anthropic is turning to religion to shape Claude’s values, and asking if AI can be conscious
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Anthropic, Christopher Olah at the Vatican
description: As AI systems tackle more complex questions, Anthropic is drawing on religious and philosophical thinking to shape Claude’s behaviour. But could such a system itself be conscious and deserve moral consideration?
body_raw: As it prepares for an IPO that could value it at 2 trillion, Anthropic is in the spotlight for meetings it held this summer with religious leaders. The Washington Post reported in April that the company had invited 15 Catholic and Protestant leaders to guide Claudes moral and spiritual development as the LLM encounters increasingly complex ethical questions. Weeks later, Anthropic co-founder Christopher Olah was present when Pope Leo unveiled his encyclical on artificial intelligence, Magnifica Humanitas, which warns against the blind adoption of AI, emphasises the primacy of the human person and rejects the idea that AI can replace or surpass humanity. The New York Times last week reported that these engagements, and several more, were part of a broader effort by Anthropic with two distinct aims to draw on religious and philosophical traditions to shape Claudes moral character, and to convince participants to seriously consider whether AI systems might themselves be conscious and deserving of moral consideration. Current AI systems can produce strikingly human-like language and behaviour, but there is no scientific consensus that they are conscious, or an agreed test for determining machine consciousness. Over the weekend, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he was very uncomfortable with ascribing religious power to AI models, while Google DeepMind researcher Jon Barron urged researchers to focus on actual humans rather than elevating the moral standing of AI systems. Anthropic is increasingly turning to religious leaders and philosophers for help thinking about what its systems should value, even as some of the industrys most powerful figures warn against treating AI itself as a source of moral or religious authority. That matters because people are already turning to these systems for advice, information and even moral or spiritual guidance. The values built into them can shape the answers people get and the judgements they make. According to The Economist, religious queries accounted for roughly 5 of millions of publicly released chatbot conversations analysed by CEFE AI. Why is Anthropic talking to religious thinkers? Anthropic has long positioned itself as the safety-focused AI company. Its efforts to shape Claudes behaviour have evolved from an internal memo dubbed the Soul Document to an 84-page constitution published this January, setting out the principles Claude is expected to follow. But questions about what kind of character an AI system should have quickly move beyond technical safeguards. They touch on morality, personhood, consciousness and human relationships, all questions that religious and philosophical traditions have debated for centuries. That made religious and philosophical traditions a natural place for Anthropic to look as it began asking what consciousness or moral worth might mean for an AI system, and what obligations could follow. None of that settles whether current AI systems are actually conscious. Mark Coeckelbergh, a philosopher of technology and professor at the University of Vienna, told The Indian Express that this move was an attempt to make sense of human-like technology. Its part of a broader tendency to try to understand what happens when we have an advanced technology that seems human-like or, according to some, gets increasingly divine qualities such as omniscience. The Vatican has grappled with similar questions a 2023 volume produced by scholars working with its Centre for Digital Culture examined AI through personhood, consciousness and human relationships with advanced systems. Coeckelbergh also cautioned that this messaging may go beyond understanding AI and help a company occupy a certain market position. Its important to see that this is not just a question of understanding AI. Its also rhetoric in the service of their business. Some Big Tech leaders intentionally use religious language to draw attention to their technologies and attract investments, Coeckelbergh told The Indian Express. What did the people in the room think was at stake? This is also where Anthropics effort to shape Claudes values began to run into a different question whether Claude itself might deserve moral consideration. Mois Navon, a rabbi and professor of ethics in AI at Ben Gurion University, Israel, who was invited to a meeting with Olah in April, said Anthropic was seeking feedback from different wisdom traditions on the Constitution that sets out Claudes moral framework. I submitted to them a 35-page critique from my traditions perspective. In addition, they were interested in hearing what kind of character would be best for Claude to have in order to fulfil its role in society. That said, the discussions drifted to what would be good for Claude itself, Navon told The Indian Express. In the critique, Navon argues that morality cannot simply be reduced to a list of rules Claude would need to exercise moral judgement within a framework of values. He also raises a more basic question about Anthropics attempt to cultivate human-like qualities in the model whose values? Charles Camosy, professor of medical humanities at Creighton University and another participant in Anthropics consultations, offered a more cautious account of the meetings. He said the discussions were broader than the question of Claudes moral status and that he did not feel participants were being steered towards any particular conclusion about AI consciousness. I dont think its fair to say that they wanted any one thing in particular. Some of the social media chatter is suggesting that the people we interacted with were trying to manipulate us or push us into thinking a certain way about Claudes moral status. That is not true. in multiple ways, Camosy told The Indian Express. Navon, however, said that once the discussion turned to Claude itself, Anthropics representatives appeared to be treating the possibility of consciousness as more than a remote hypothetical. They Olah and his colleagues at Anthropic said that they had observed internal behaviours that mimicked human behaviour to such an extent that they called them weird, and implied that, in their minds, there was a very high probability that Claude is conscious. Accordingly, they discussed its welfare, Navon told The Indian Express. Why does moral status matter, and who gets to choose the values? If an AI system were conscious, that would not automatically settle how humans ought to treat it. The next question is whether it has moral status, meaning whether it deserves moral consideration in its own right. In practical terms, that means asking whether it can be harmed or whether humans could owe it duties. Camosy said that after considering the question seriously, he did not think current AI systems possess significant moral status. When you first experience what contemporary models can do . many can be gobsmacked or taken aback at first. But when I went back to foundational principles about what consciousness is and where it comes from . it became clear that these models do not have a significant moral status, Camosy said. Navon took Anthropics premise in the opposite direction. If the company believed Claude might be conscious and therefore capable of being harmed, he argued, it also had to confront what it meant to make such a system work for humans. Anthropic acknowledged the moral problem but said, All the AI labs are doing it. At least we are being nice to ours. That is when I responded with what was quoted in part by The New York Times So you are nice slave owners. I think you should be fighting the South and freeing the slaves, Navon told The Indian Express. But even if Claude has no moral status, the question of what values it should embody remains. Anthropic is already making those choices. That question has already surfaced in Anthropics standoff with the US government over who gets to decide how its models can be used. Coeckelbergh warned that values embedded in AI systems can be exported globally with the technology. If most of these models are made by US companies, then of course they are going to reflect US values. That means we risk a kind of tech colonialism, where those values are exported through the technology, he told The Indian Express. At least if companies are explicit about the religious or philosophical values they are drawing on, there is something to discuss and contest. But this cannot remain in the hands of a few companies. It needs to be democratised. Camosy, however, drew a distinction between the moral status of the models and the effect our treatment of them may have on us. I do think the question remains about what kind of people we want to be in relation to the models. But thats a different kind of question from the ones asking whether the models themselves have a significant moral status or capability of being harmed, he said.

articleTitle: In Bihar, an experiment for the young that bets on them
articleFeaturedImageAlt: In Bihar, an experiment that bets on the young
description: The present effort is the construction of an ecosystem in which access, teachers, leadership, technology and academic discipline reinforce one another. Bihar has begun assembling these parts at unusual speed and scale.
body_raw: Bihar is Indias youngest state, with a median age of approximately 26. That fact is usually invoked in discussions about employment, migration and the demographic dividend. Yet, before any of these comes education. Unless Bihars young people can access credible colleges, complete their courses on time and acquire useful knowledge and skills, youthfulness alone will confer little advantage. This is why an unusual experiment now unfolding deserves wider attention. The direction is significant Expand access rapidly, recruit teachers transparently, improve university leadership and use technology to make a fragmented system more visible and accountable. The most visible step has been the opening of 211 government degree colleges, largely in areas without convenient access to higher education. Distance is not a minor issue. For a rural family, particularly one educating a daughter, a nearby college can determine whether education leads to a degree or ends after Class XII. These colleges are still young. Many have begun with a few rooms, small faculties, limited support staff and enrolments below their eventual capacity. They cannot yet be judged as finished institutions. They are foundations upon which institutions must now be built. To give them an academic core, Bihar appointed 2,451 contractual assistant professors. The recruitment, drawn from more than 23,000 applications, was completed in about 30 days through a centralised process. Speed attracted attention, but transparency matters even more. Public confidence begins when a qualified applicant believes that merit, rather than influence, will determine selection. The newly appointed teachers are joining colleges without established systems and traditions. Their initiative over the next two years will determine whether these colleges acquire academic energy or remain administrative units with classrooms. Reform at the college level cannot succeed if universities remain weakly led. Bihar is also revisiting how vice-chancellors and pro-vice-chancellors are selected. Nearly 8,000 applications were received for 10 V-C positions through an online process. Numbers alone cannot guarantee good appointments. Careful scrutiny, credible search committees and matching of individual capabilities with institutional needs are essential. Yet widening the field is itself a reform. Technology is providing the connective tissue for this effort. Samarth, the e-governance platform developed under the Ministry of Education, is being energised across Bihars higher-education system. For students, a common digital window improves awareness of institutions, courses, admissions and opportunities that were once confined to notices on distant campuses. For administrators, its modules can connect admissions, registration, examinations, results, employee records and finance. For those responsible for oversight, it can reveal where a process has stalled. The introduction of a uniform academic calendar across state universities follows the same logic. A calendar has value only when classes, examinations and results occur when promised. For students, a delayed result can mean losing a job, scholarship or admission elsewhere. Timeliness is, therefore, an element of educational justice. The reforms will ultimately be tested inside classrooms. New colleges must attract students, particularly women and first-generation learners. Teachers must teach regularly and create cultures of reading, writing, discussion and mentoring. Libraries and laboratories must grow. Curricula must connect knowledge with employability without reducing education to vocational training alone. Buildings, portals and appointments create capacity they do not automatically create quality. That requires faculty development, fair assessment, research support, institutional autonomy accompanied by accountability, and academic leaders willing to take difficult decisions. Bihar also has Nalanda University. Although outside the state-university system, it provides an important beacon. Its evolving Nalanda Approach - connecting civilisational knowledge with contemporary challenges - can encourage Bihars universities to be locally rooted, nationally relevant and globally engaged. Indias demographic future will be decided not only in metropolitan universities but also in public colleges serving small towns and rural districts. The present effort is the construction of an ecosystem in which access, teachers, leadership, technology and academic discipline reinforce one another. Bihar has begun assembling these parts at unusual speed and scale. The challenge is to turn momentum into institutional habit. A Viksit Bharat will require a Viksit Bihar, and that journey must begin by equipping its young people with credible, accessible and high-quality higher education. The writer is Governor of Bihar

articleTitle: Jeffrey Archer: The storyteller and the twists in his tale
articleFeaturedImageAlt: The storyteller and the twists in his tale
description: The writer understood that public life, like fiction, runs on appetite — for money, power, recognition and redemption — and he had a keen instinct for all four.
body_raw: British writer Jeffrey Archer, who died at 86 on October 5, might have been the first to admit that his life was the sort of script that could have been rejected by an editor for being far too dramatic. Athlete, MP, political aspirant, bestselling novelist, convicted perjurer, comeback artiste - the arc of Archers life showed a great talent for reinvention, a phoenix-like ability to rise from the ashes. He understood that public life, like fiction, runs on appetite - for money, power, recognition and redemption - and he had a keen instinct for all four. Even his death, arriving on the eve of the publication of Adam  Eve, carries the theatricality of a final twist. Archers literary life began after a personal setback, a financial defraud that had rendered him bankrupt. But Not a Penny More, Not a Penny Less, published in 1976, and followed in succession by A Quiver Full of Arrows 1980, First Among Equals 1984, and novels such as Kane and Abel 1979 and Shall We Tell the President? 1986 led to a reversal of fortunes. Despite a lukewarm reception by critics, his books sold over 300 million copies in a career spanning five decades. His appetite for drama, however, proved ruinous in politics - his ascent through Conservative ranks and his ambitions for high office ended in disgrace after a libel case, followed by his conviction for perjury and imprisonment. But prison turned into more source material, a new chapter in another new beginning that brought more bestsellers. In an interview to fellow writer Anthony Horowitz for The Sunday Telegraph Magazine in 2011, Archer had said, The people who survive are storytellers. In death as in life, Archer put the twist in the tale.

articleTitle: Expanded ANMOL scheme, hike in ASHA incentive — Delhi launches health initiatives
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Expanded ANMOL scheme, hike in ASHA incentive, ANMOL scheme, ASHA incentive, newborn screening programme for newborns, State Organ and Tissue Transplant Organisation (SOTTO), GB Pant Hospital, delhi news, India news, Indian express, current affairs
description: The programme also saw the virtual inauguration of the State Organ and Tissue Transplant Organisation (SOTTO) building at GB Pant Hospital.
body_raw: Expansion of the ANMOL scheme, which raises the free newborn screening programme for newborns, from 56 to 63 diseases, doubling of the monthly incentive for ASHA workers from Rs 3,000 to Rs 6,000 - these were among the several new healthcare initiatives launched by the Delhi Government on Tuesday under the Seva Sankalp Abhiyan programme, organised at Thyagraj Stadium. The programme also saw the virtual inauguration of the State Organ and Tissue Transplant Organisation SOTTO building at GB Pant Hospital. Further, a Nursing Home Management System portal was launched, which moves registration and renewal for private nursing homes online, officials said. The hike in incentives is set to benefit 6,690 ASHA workers in the Capital, officials said, adding that the increment is a recognition of the dedication with which the workers bring Delhis health services to households. ASHA workers act as the link between the community and the public health system. They register pregnant women, push for institutional deliveries, track immunisation, counsel families on nutrition and sanitation, and accompany patients to health facilities and work under the National Health Mission. On the development, Health Minister Pankaj Kumar Singh said, The incentive had been pending for nearly a decade. Through the Covid years, the workers kept serving. The steps to recognise them did not come. This government has addressed it. On Tuesday, Chief Minister Rekha Gupta also felicitated outstanding workers at the ASHA Sammelan-2026 and ASHA Samman Samaroh. She said she expects them to reach every family like an elder sister, and announced a special dandiya programme for them during Navratri. Delhi Lieutenant Governor Taranjit Singh Sandhu said, ASHA workers stand on the front lines of the healthcare system, taking health services and awareness to pregnant women, children and families. On the expansion of Mission ANMOL, officials said that it now covers 63 congenital health conditions, with screening to be carried out within 24 to 72 hours of birth. Since Mission ANMOL was made operational in March this year, more than 75,000 newborns have been screened and over 700 children have been treated in time, officials said. The government aims to increase the annual coverage under the scheme around 1.5 lakh to 2.5 lakh newborns. Last month, The Indian Express had reported that more than 14,000 newborn genetic samples arrive every month at the LNJP genetic lab, the only genetic lab run by the Delhi government.

articleTitle: Woman threatens man of false rape case, extorts Rs 90 lakh; held
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Bengaluru gym trainer death
description: The team of officers from Sadar police station caught her red-handed as she was being handed the money, in marked currency notes, and put an end to a man’s alleged three-year extortion ordeal.
body_raw: On Sunday, a 24-year-old woman entered a cafe in Gururams Sector 47, hoping to walk out with Rs 50,000 - unaware that plainclothes policemen were watching her from a table nearby. The team of officers from Sadar police station caught her red-handed as she was being handed the money, in marked currency notes, and put an end to a mans alleged three-year extortion ordeal. The accused, identified as Suryadita Das, who hails from West Bengal and currently resides in Sushant Lok, was arrested after a corporate employee alleged that she had blackmailed him into paying approximately Rs 90 lakh having threatened him of framing him in a false rape case. ACP Crime Naveen Sharma on Tuesday said the complainant and the accused first connected around three years ago on Seeking, a dating platform. The two came in contact through the app, exchanged phone numbers and remained in touch for nearly three years. They traveled together to multiple places and developed a relationship, the ACP said. According to the police, Das later began coercing the man into parting with significant sums of money. Providing a breakdown of the extorted funds, Sharma said, The accused took approximately Rs 60-65 lakh in cash in intermittent installments and another Rs 10-15 lakh through bank transfers, totaling around Rs 90 lakh. Even after that, she continued demanding more money. Asked why the complainant waited three years before approaching the police, the ACP said the delay stemmed from a fear of public dishonour. The complainant remained in deep fear that his social standing, family name, and personal reputation would be ruined, Sharma said, adding that he eventually filed a complaint on October 4 as the woman kept pressing for more money. The police laid a trap. They asked the victim to fix a meeting with Das, a police spokesperson said. Officers in plain clothes kept a watch. Das was caught accepting the money - the notes carried pre-recorded initials and signatures put by the police, officers said. Das, who completed her MBA from SGT University, works at a private firm, police said. On whether Das was part of an organised racket, ACP Sharma said, So far, it appears that she did this alone. We are verifying if she has targeted other people as well and if any complaint or case of a similar nature has been registered against her. Das was produced before a local court Sunday that remanded her into two-day police custody. The Gurugram police have frozen around Rs 95 lakh in her bank account. Further investigation into the matter is underway, police said.

articleTitle: ‘Nothing (left) to say’: Delhi court pulls up police for lax MCOCA probe
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Crime syndicate leader free for 6 years, delhi Crime syndicate leader free for 6 years, Delhi Police, Delhi judge police efforts mockery, delhi news, India news, Indian express, current affairs
description: Leader of alleged crime syndicate ‘roamed free’ for 6 years; police claims of making ‘best efforts’ to investigate are ‘nothing short of mockery’, says judge
body_raw: More than six years ago, Delhi Police invoked one of the toughest laws at their disposal against an alleged leader of a crime syndicate who was named in at least two cases of murder at the time. When police finally arrested him in February this year, another eight cases had been registered against him. This week, a Delhi court expressed exasperation at the delay in the investigation-and rejected the polices claim that they had made their best efforts. If according to the Addl. DCP this is the best effort, then this court has nothing to say, Special MCOCA Judge Gaurav Rao of Rouse Avenue Court said in his order passed on Monday October 5. The court pulled up all the officers who have investigated the case for the last six years, and ordered an inquiry into the delay in the investigation. Three Additional Deputy Commissioners of Police-Lokeshwaran, Ravinandan BM, and Rishi Kumar-and the Investigating Officers IOs, Assistant Commissioners of Police ACPs Rakesh Kumar, SK Gaur, and Vipin Kumar Retd were present in court. The fourth IO in the case, ACP Vivek Bhagat, was not present physically. Earlier in the day, ACP Bhagat and 11 other officers had been promoted as Addl DCPs. However, in view of an ongoing inquiry on an allegation of sexual harassment against Bhagat, the promotion was put in abeyance late on Monday evening. Judge Gaurav Rao was perusing a report submitted by police on their investigation against Mukesh, an alleged leader of a crime syndicate operating from Outer Delhis Narela. Police had booked him under the stringent Maharashtra Control of Organised Crime Act, 1999 MCOCA in September 2020. Mukesh was accused in 20 FIRs at the time, including two cases of murder, one case of attempted murder, and cases of robbery and dacoity. By the time he was arrested in February 2026, he had been named in another eight cases, including cases of murder, robbery, and kidnapping. Mukesh allegedly had close links with the gang led by the notorious Jitender Mann alias Gogi, who was once one of Delhis most feared gangsters. Gogi was shot dead inside Rohini Court in September 2021. The report submitted by police failed to address the query by this court, and though the lapses as well as the considerable delay in the investigation is writ large from the record, still the Addl DCP, Outer North District, said the police officials have made best efforts in the present case and are still making their best efforts. If according to the Addl. DCP this is the best effort, then this court has nothing to say, the judge said. Perhaps the Addl. DCP is insensitive to the legislative intent behind MCOCA. MCOCA was enacted to put a halt to the menace of organized crime which posed poses a serious threat to civil society. However, if despite invoking the strongest provisions of MCOCA, the accused persons are allowed to roam free, commit heinous offences, including murder as per their whims and fancies, then.it defeats the legislative intent behind the.statute, he added. The court had asked the DCP, Outer North District to file a report listing the cases against the accused, who were allegedly part of the syndicate. It had also sought an explanation as to why arrests were not made in the case. The Additional DCPs had appeared in court on behalf of the DCP. The claims of Best Efforts of the Addl. DCP is nothing short of mockery, the judge said. In fact, in his report, the DCP, Outer North District, made a reference to a circular dated 11.07.2024 issued by the Police Headquarters.for expeditious investigation and timely arrest of accused persons. Yet in the 6 years during which the accused persons were not arrested, investigation qua them was not completed, and the same gave the accused persons more time and opportunity to commit more crimes, he added. It seems that the Addl. DCP feels opines that he is not answerable to either the court or the general public who have all this while borne the brunt of the criminal activities of the crime syndicate, the court said. The court also mentioned an accused named Pradeep, who is alleged to be involved in a large number of cases including murder and robbery. Yet he Pradeep was arrested only on 16.4.2026. Hence, just like accused Mukesh, the said accused kept indulging in criminal activities even after invoking MCOCA, the judge noted in his order. The court described the report of the DCP as an eyewash, and directed that a detailed inquiry and appropriate action be taken against all erring officials and IOs for the delay in the investigation, and for not working in sync with the intent of the statute MCOCA, which permitted more crimes to happen. He directed a copy of the order be sent to the Commissioner of Delhi Police. In an earlier order dated September 18, the judge had said MCOCA was invoked in September 2020 and accused persons were arrested only in February 2026. It emerges from the record that the accused persons continued to be involved in other criminal activities during this period of around 5 and  years. One of the purposes of invoking MCOCA is to curb organized crime, however, if the accused persons, despite invoking MCOCA keep roaming free, are not arrested for the period of 6 years and most importantly keep indulging in criminal activities then the entire rational behind invoking MCOCA gets frustrated, is rendered futile. Mukesh has a criminal record going back more than a decade, and is suspected of heading a syndicate involved in murder, attempt to murder, robbery, extortion, Arms Act offences, and criminal conspiracy in parts of Delhi and Haryana. He first came on the radar of police in 2012 and was soon seen as a habitual offender. Cases have been registered against him at several police stations, including Narela, Alipur, Swaroop Nagar, Bawana, Kanjhawala, Samaipur Badli, and Shahbad Dairy in Delhi, and in Jhajjar and Rewari in Haryana.

articleTitle: Cameras on uniforms, speakers on streets: Delhi Police changes approach amid claims of manhandling
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Delhi Police, Delhi Police changes approach, Delhi Police approach claims of manhandling, delhi claims of manhandling, Delhi Police Cameras on uniforms, delhi news, India news, Indian express, current affairs
description: The cameras, along with speakers blaring announcements and police personnel largely without batons, were part of a visibly more cautious approach adopted by the force, as protests in Central Delhi entered their fifth day.
body_raw: The cameras were hard to miss. Attached to the uniforms of police personnel deployed on Parliament Street on Tuesday, the small body-worn devices were recording as officers prepared to deal with another round of protests near the Election Commission headquarters. This has been given to the ground staff so that no one makes false allegations, a Delhi Police constable said, pointing to the camera fixed to his uniform. He was deployed to maintain law and order during the INDIA blocs protest demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumars resignation. The cameras, along with speakers blaring announcements and police personnel largely without batons, were part of a visibly more cautious approach adopted by the force, as protests in Central Delhi entered their fifth day. The measures come after three days of criticism and allegations over the handling of protesters, including sexual assault allegations made by three female journalists. By Tuesday, around 80 body-worn cameras had been distributed among ground staff, according to a senior officer. They were deployed among almost all ground-level personnel up to the rank of DCP, with officers told to record their interactions while managing crowds. If required, more cameras will be given to the ground staff, the officer said. Body-worn cameras are not new to the Delhi Police. Traffic personnel have used them for several years to record interactions while issuing challans, while local police sometimes use them when dealing with members of the public, but not on such a large scale. Their deployment on this scale during crowd-control duties is a recent measure, another officer said. Further, police personnel were largely seen without batons or other weapons as Opposition leaders approached the barricades. Speakers repeatedly urged people not to gather in the area, with prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita BNSS in force across Parliament Street and adjoining areas. More than five companies of paramilitary personnel, along with local police, were deployed along the routes expected to be taken by the protesters from Makar Dwar of Parliament to the Election Commission office. Multi-layered barricades came up outside the EC offices main entrance and around Jantar Mantar. The New Delhi district has been witnessing protests since October 2, with Opposition parties holding demonstrations. Police have registered nine FIRs in connection with the protests held near Jantar Mantar over the last five days. The cases include alleged violations of prohibitory orders, rioting and attacks on police personnel while they were discharging their duties. Eighteen people have also been arrested, while more than 300 people detained and later released. Police are, meanwhile, bracing for another protest. The Cockroach Janta Party has called another demonstration at Jantar Mantar on October 10 as part of a nationwide stir demanding Kumars resignation.

articleTitle: Reminder from Cornell: Silence enables sexual violence
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Cornell reminder on impunity, sexual violence
description: Reluctance to confront rape, not just as a singular act but also as the culmination of everyday violations, emboldens would-be perpetrators and ensures that the cycle of violence continues
body_raw: A woman was sexually assaulted by seven men at a fraternity house in a US university which, when informed of the crime, allegedly did little to punish the perpetrators. This is the bare outline of a case that has rocked the US for over a week. The survivor filed a civil suit last month against Cornell University, the Chi Phi fraternity as well as the seven men who allegedly raped her in 2024, following which state prosecutors in New York, where the university is located, reopened a criminal inquiry into the incident. Horrific as the assault was, what stands out in the Cornell case is that other men with knowledge of what was unfolding did nothing to inform the authorities or stop the assault evidence from a fraternity group chat points to encouragement of the crime. Whether this range of disturbing reactions is rooted in a misplaced sense of loyalty, fear of offending ones peers or causing social discomfort or just indifference is immaterial. The larger picture they paint is one of impunity, where the cost of silence and inaction is paid, over and over, by women. This is why it is also a mistake to limit the conversation to what unfolded on one US university campus or treat it as the aberrant behaviour of a handful. That would risk underplaying the extent to which everyday sexism and gender stereotypes, normalisation of rape in the form of jokes and the sexualisation of women shape views about consent, about who deserves to be punished and who is shamed for what was done to them - across cultures and borders. Its echoes can be heard everywhere, from the cases brought to light by the global MeToo movement to the long battle of Indias women wrestlers to bring a powerful man to account. The survivor of the Cornell case had to drop out of college the university closed the case after a half-hearted investigation. Two of her attackers were expelled while the rest were asked to write essays to mitigate the harm they had caused. This stark asymmetry speaks of a structural injustice where reluctance to acknowledge and confront rape emboldens would-be perpetrators and ensures that the cycle of violence continues. The conversation that has revived with Cornell must continue everywhere.

articleTitle: One year of weight-loss drugs in India: What happened to the ‘Mounjaro brides’?
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Clinics are now offering three-month weight-loss packages at Rs 20,000-30,000, specifically targeting brides
description: In 2025, as weight-loss drugs entered the Indian market, clinics began launching pre-wedding packages targeted at young women hoping to rapidly shed kilos before their big day. As leading endocrinologists sound a note of caution, The Indian Express traces the journeys of some of the brides who signed up — long and difficult, one that doesn’t stop at the wedding
body_raw: Down a narrow lane in Lajpat Nagar, South Delhi, half hidden by low tree branches, is a small white door with silver lettering Weight Loss Clinic. Behind it is a basement. A silver aluminium partition divides the space in two. On one side is a small, brightly lit waiting area. On the other is the doctors desk. Nearby hangs a banner meant to reassure Obesity is a chronic disease. It has genetic, lifestyle and environmental components, and it is not a reflection of who you are. In the waiting area is a woman with her mother, a few others sit on a bench. They have all come for weight-loss consultations, and some have a date by which to do it an impending wedding. The clinic is one of a growing number in South Delhi that sell weight-loss programmes built on GLP-1 drugs, a class of medications first developed for diabetes and since approved for obesity. They include semaglutide, which Novo Nordisk sells as Ozempic and Wegovy, and tirzepatide, which Eli Lilly sells as Mounjaro - drugs that entered the Indian market last year. Since then, despite limited data on its effect on Indian patients, the drugs are among the most sought-after, by value, in Indias pharmaceutical market. There have also been reports of the drug being used for cosmetic reasons, and of clinics offering Mounjaro bride packages to those aiming for quick-fix weight-loss before the big day. Now, a year into that trade, there are harder questions to tackle. Doctors have increasingly been treating obesity as a chronic disease, not something that requires a cosmetic fix. But when the GLP-1 drugs for obesity treatment, which work by altering the bodys hunger signals, are used merely for cosmetic reasons, it raises a different set of questions. What happens after the immediate weight goal is reached, say, a wedding? Do the lost kilos stay away, or do appetite and weight bounce back once the three-month package runs its course? Interviews with clinics offering weight-loss programmes on tight deadlines, leading endocrinologists and patients who were on GLP-1 drugs ahead of their weddings shine some light on the risks that come with going down the path of quick-fix weight loss packages. Inside a weight-loss clinic The Lajpat Nagar clinics offer is simple. The programme promises Mounjaro-assisted weight reduction in three months for Rs 30,000. The price covers consultations with the doctor, a complimentary dietitian, and the injections themselves, which patients take home the day they pay. Youll be added to a dietitian group, a staff member explains. They regulate your diet, and in three months, youll lose weight. A senior member of the staff says, Most of our clients come ahead of their wedding. In the last one year, we have helped close to a hundred brides reach their desired weight. Its a tidy pitch by the clinic three months to the wedding, three months to lose weight. Endocrinologists, however, point out that obesity keeps no such calendar. None of these is meant to be used for cosmetic, short-term use, says Dr Ambrish Mithal, chairman of endocrinology at Max Hospital. The drugs are for long-term use. Most, but not all, patients require a maintenance dose to keep the weight off. On the face of it, many clinics make the pitch sound reassuringly medical. A Hauz Khas clinic promises a supervised weight-loss programme, overseen by an AIIMS-trained doctor. But there is a catch. The doctor is a dermatologist, not an endocrinologist. A few kilometres away, another clinic, better known for facial aesthetics, makes a similar promise a doctor-supervised Mounjaro package. Are weight-loss drugs a good idea before weddings? Heres what Dr Ambrish Mithal, chairman of endocrinology at Max Hospital says Read   - The Indian Express IndianExpress October 7, 2026 Mithal says there is a reason brides are the target. Brides are an attractive market for companies selling weight-loss drugs. The scrutiny before a wedding makes a bride especially vulnerable. When a wedding or a festival becomes the reason to take a drug, the drug itself is taken less seriously. Deciding when a patient can safely stop the drug is a slow process, says Dr Mithal, requiring months of monitoring to determine whether weight loss has been sustained, metabolic markers have normalised and lifestyle changes are strong enough to hold without the drug. He says that even those who start on the drugs with a wedding-date goal in mind would do well to consult an endocrinologist, someone who can monitor the patients health not only in the run-up to the event, but beyond it. In their desperation, not many take that route. Losing more than just kilos Six months ahead of her September 2025 wedding, the 23-year-old science graduate from Ludhiana decided she needed to shed some of her 108 kg. The push came from both social media and a cousin, says a Delhi-based endocrinologist who would eventually treat her. The cousin had taken a weight-loss injection before her own wedding and lost 50 kg, a transformation that was the topic of family conversations before the bride decided to try the drug herself. She found a local clinic that was willing to give her a weight-loss package. On her very first visit, she was handed Mounjaro in bulk, no questions asked about her medical history, no baseline tests run. She paid Rs 20,000 for a three-month course and walked out with the injections in hand, says the endocrinologist, who works at a health start-up in Delhi and agreed to speak on condition of anonymity. The Ludhiana clinic had offered the 23-year-old no tests. There was no gradual build-up of the dose, no monitoring, no plan for her and little contact with a doctor. The clinic asked her to self-inject Mounjaro and kept escalating the dose until she was at 12.5 mg, close to the maximum. She lost around 20 kg in 40 days, says the doctor. Through it all, the patient remained unaware of the other half of the treatment diet and lifestyle changes such as exercise and strength training. Almost two months before the wedding, she travelled to Delhi for her lehenga trials and jewellery appointments. But by then, the side-effects of the drug were severe enough for her to visit the endocrinologist in Delhi. When she visited us, she had nausea, exhaustion, hair fall, menstrual changes and mood shifts, and she had lost a massive amount of muscle mass. Acne flared up on her face, the doctor recalls. During the consultation she looked anxious, jittery. He says his first concern was not how much weight she had lost. We wanted to understand what was happening to her body during the process. Was she eating enough? Was she getting adequate protein? Was she losing muscle along with fat? How was her digestion and energy? the doctor says. The bigger conversation was about ensuring that weight loss was not coming at the cost of her metabolic and nutritional health. A full workup followed, and it found more than a lighter body. When we ran a full root-cause analysis, we found her hormones to be completely off, her periods were irregular, she had abnormalities in her metabolism, her thyroid was abnormal. And with all this, she was on unsupervised Monjaro, says the doctor. The drug had done what it was sold to do. The weight was gone. But she was left with a lot more to grapple with. She visited us twice after her health checkup. We gave her a proper diet chart, exercises to do, and a gradual dosage reduction of Mounjaro, till the maintenance dose, to wean off the drugs effect. She got married, but she never returned for a follow-up, the doctor says. Three months to February Akanksha Chauhan did most of it right, with her weight loss monitored by an endocrinologist. Yet, the journey sprung constant surprises, not all of it pleasant. It all began in December 2024, when Chauhan, a petroleum engineer who lives in the UK, turned 35, and seriously started considering whether she wanted to be a mother. Her gynaecologist suggested she freeze her eggs, but he was concerned about her weight. He told me he wasnt sure about the quality of the eggs we would retrieve, she says, adding that he advised her to shed some of the 99 kg that she weighed then. That was an alarm bell. I didnt want to go into a three-digit number, she says. The gynaecologist referred her to an endocrinologist, who put her on Ozempic. Her first dose was on March 25, 2025. Three days later, she met the man who would become her husband on a dating app. He was a practising lawyer, lean and athletic she recalls being embarrassed about her weight. I told him that in the next three months I was going to transform. I was almost trying to impress him, she says, laughing at the memory. But the next few months were difficult as Chauhan lived with the side effects of the drug. From April to August, I was in China on work. Suddenly, my appetite dipped, and had become zero. Along with that, I could hardly find anything that I could eat. It was mostly watermelon, she says. Then, in the middle of the trip, nausea took over. By November, the couple decided to get married and chose a February date for their wedding. It was around this time that Chauhan decided to stop the drug for a month. She weighed 58 kg then. Within days, the scale began to move the other way. Suddenly, I could see that there was some weight coming back, she says. It was also the time she began shopping for her wedding. She recalls walking into a store in Lucknow and settling on two outfits a deep olive-green lehenga, and a green-and-gold silk saree. The outfits would take three months to arrive. For Chauhan, those months were a countdown, not only to the wedding but to the lehenga and its tailored blouse. The only thing that was constantly running through my head was that I had to fit into that gorgeous lehenga and blouse, she recalls. She consulted her endocrinologist. Because I was getting married in February and I had only three months, I went back on the highest dose that I had stopped at, she says. By the time she stood in her olive-green lehenga, she had reached the weight she had been aiming for. The lehenga fitted. So did the blouse. I received compliments from everyone that day. They said I looked like I was 30 or 31, not 36. I felt so good that day. It was perfect, she says, smiling. But the wedding was the start of another chapter. On medical advice, in February, Chauhan stopped the drug again, this time for three months. She conceived, but the pregnancy ended in a miscarriage. When I got it tested, my gynaecologist said everything was normal and that my miscarriage was not related to the weight-loss drugs, she says. In June, she restarted the drug in the United Kingdom. My Indian doctor was on a holiday, she recalls. She decided to restart the dose herself, without the doctors advice. It was a big mistake, she says. The consequence was swift - severe vomiting and dehydration. She spent three days in the ICU. Chauhan is now back on Mounjaro, under her doctors supervision. I will continue it for the next six months, just to maintain my weight, and then we will try to conceive next year, she says. From the consultation room Dr Anoop Misra, executive chairman of Fortis C-DOC Hospital for Diabetes and Allied Sciences, is among the citys leading endocrinologists. He has watched the boom in GLP-1 drugs unfold from his consultation room. We are seeing particularly strong demand among urban women, including women with post-pregnancy weight gain, PCOS-associated obesity and metabolic problems around the perimenopausal period. There is also considerable social pressure on women to achieve a particular body shape, and this creates a risk of medicalising cosmetic weight loss, he says. There is a message he now repeats to his patients. The most important message is that obesity is a chronic disease, not simply a temporary excess of weight. GLP-1 drugs should therefore not be viewed like a short course of antibiotics, he says. For many patients, Dr Misra says, treatment will need to be long term, especially if the underlying tendency to obesity remains. When treatment is stopped, appetite generally returns and substantial weight regain is common. A recent analysis of 37 studies has found that cardiometabolic benefits progressively diminish after stopping anti-obesity medication, with GLP-1 drugs associated with relatively rapid weight regain, he says. That does not mean the drugs cant be stopped. In his experience, some patients can hold on to their weight loss with intensive dietary changes, more protein, physical activity and resistance training. The emerging consensus is therefore shifting from the question When can I stop the injection? to What is the appropriate long-term treatment strategy for this individuals obesity?, he says. But Dr Misra draws a clear line at using these drugs mainly for cosmetic weight loss. While the immediate side effects of the drugs are well recognised - nausea, vomiting, constipation, diarrhoea and reduced appetite - with excessive or rapid weight loss, there are broader concerns, he says, including loss of muscle and lean tissue, nutritional deficiencies, gallbladder disease and potentially loss of bone mass. Early observational data on bone outcomes need more confirmation, he adds, and should not yet be read as proof of cause. For Indian patients, I am particularly concerned about sarcopenia and micronutrient deficiency because a person can become lighter without necessarily becoming metabolically or physically healthier. This is especially relevant to women and older adults, he says. Dr Misra clarifies that his concern is not about the drugs themselves. They are a major advance in obesity and metabolic medicine. My concern is using a powerful medical therapy for the wrong indication, he says. A word of caution Chauhan has learned that the hard way. Despite the many turns in her weight-loss journey, she has had doctors monitoring her every step of the way. She has also become an informal adviser to other women weighing GLP-1 drugs before their weddings. In a WhatsApp support community, brides on weight-loss GLP-1 drugs often reach out to her, and she tells them what she wishes more people understood this is not another item on a pre-wedding checklist.
